lenses.L1: Opcodes and EVM semantics: supported fork, opcode behaviour and pricing differences, code size, call gas forwarding, SELFDESTRUCT, EIP-7702, non-EVM execution (WASM, precompile-only accounts)
lenses.L2: State model: transient storage lifetime, transaction boundaries and batching, state changes made outside normal EVM execution (system transactions, fee debits, deposits), account model, address aliasing
lenses.L3: Gas, native currency and token contracts: gas token identity and decimals, ERC-20 aliases of the native asset, enshrined or precompile tokens, issuer controls (freeze, blocklist, seize), fee payment in tokens, block and transaction gas caps
lenses.L4: System contracts, precompiles and predeploys that can move balances, change code, or read privileged state
lenses.L5: Deployment parity and governance: deployed bytecode versus this repo, constructor arguments, owner and protocol fee controller, cross-chain ownership path
lenses.L6: Block production, ordering, finality and upgrade roadmap: sequencer or validator powers, reorg depth, scheduled forks that change any of the above

leads.question: After the announced ArbOS upgrade (about four weeks after 2026-11-09), how are ElysiumCoreWriter result callbacks delivered: as ordinary transactions from a keeper account, or as system transactions or calls made by ArbOS, and does the upgrade add any system address that moves native HYPE?
leads.why: A callback delivered outside an ordinary transaction, or batched with other calls in one transaction context, would change the A1 transient storage boundary and the A8 sender model on this chain. A system address that moves HYPE would touch A3.

attempts.answer: The upgrade is unscheduled on 2026-11-23 and the documentation still does not say how result callbacks are delivered. It says a keeper signs intents for HyperCore and that outcomes are delivered back to the originating contract with gas refunded from a HYPE escrow on the predeploy. If the delivery is a transaction from a keeper account it is an ordinary transaction with its own transient map. That reading is an inference and no code or address is published.

leads.question: Which Nitro commit does Elysium run (the RPC reports a locally built binary), and does it change anything in state transition, transient storage or precompile dispatch compared with the tagged release?
leads.why: Every cleared item for Elysium that cites client source assumes the stock code. The docs say stock ArbOS 61 at launch and announce custom precompiles next.

leads.question: Which v4 pools on Arbitrum One have a hook or currency whose code starts with the Stylus prefix, what do ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft return for them, and on what date was activation gas raised relative to the ArbOS 61 activation on 2026-08-20?
leads.why: This sizes the Stylus finding. A Stylus hook still at version 2 with remove liquidity flags means LP funds are frozen today.

leads.question: In the verified source of the stock token logic 0xb35490d6f9163de4f80d88dc75c3516eb64c5ae2 and the registry 0xe10b6f6b275de231345c20d14ab812db62151b00, which of from, to and msg.sender does transfer check against isBlocked, who holds the block, pause, burn and upgrade roles, and is the upgrade delayed?
leads.why: The issuer control finding rests on selectors and view calls. If transfer also checks msg.sender or the recipient, a blocked recipient or caller changes which PoolManager calls revert.

leads.question: Which compliance rules does the Robinhood sequencer apply: are token Transfer events to a restricted address inside a hook or token enough to reject a transaction, is the burn exception enabled, and are the PoolManager and Uniswap periphery exempt from listing?
leads.why: If event rules are on, a pool whose hook or token emits a transfer involving a restricted address is unusable on this chain, and an unprivileged party who can choose a payout address in a hook could block other users of that pool.

leads.question: Who holds EXECUTOR_ROLE on the Elysium upgrade executor 0xce4ceced412aa9359840c7d52bbd99827a5d42b9, who are the validators and batch poster of the rollup on HyperEVM, and what force inclusion delay does its SequencerInbox set?
leads.why: With one sequencer, one data availability server and permissioned proving, these accounts decide whether LPs can exit during an outage and who can rewrite chain state.

leads.question: Who controls the Robinhood Chain owners 0x2a153c6a1b66dbc930a8d7017230ab0253005c09 and 0x5eb36fd3a11f3a123c046e3bf84195bb4f5a2690, and what does the SequencerInbox on Ethereum set as the force inclusion delay?
leads.why: The chain owners appoint filterers and schedule ArbOS upgrades. The 4 day force inclusion bound comes from a secondary source only.

leads.question: ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 says collectProtocolFees reverts while the manager is unlocked and the currency is synced, but ProtocolFees.sol:49-52 tests only the synced currency and never calls _isUnlocked (declared at ProtocolFees.sol:60). Does a collection made inside an unlock through the permissionless controller create any accounting gap?
leads.why: On these two chains anyone can trigger collection at any point of a transaction. I found no gain from it, because it only lowers the balance by accrued fees, but a reader of the core code should confirm and correct the assumption text.

attempts.answer: No accounting gap. See the answer to L-030. The guard depends on the synced currency only, and the lock state is never read (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52, 60; src/PoolManager.sol:392-394).

leads.question: Does the deployed PoolManager bytecode on these three chains match a build of this repository?
leads.why: This unit did not make the comparison because the review owner's instruction for the run forbids diffing this code against any other copy. The owner should decide whether a bytecode comparison against the deployed contracts falls under that rule.

leads.question: Has any chain owner called setNativeTokenManagementFrom or added a native token owner or a transaction filterer since 2026-11-22?
leads.why: Native token owners can mint the gas token without limit, which would let them buy out the other side of every native pool. Both switches have a 7 day delay, so a periodic read of ArbOwnerPublic gives warning.

leads.question: Which hooks or tokens used by v4 pools are EVM contracts that forward to a Stylus program, for example a proxy whose implementation has code starting with 0xeff0 or a Solidity hook that calls a Stylus library?
leads.why: My scan read only the code at the hook and currency addresses and found no Stylus program on Arbitrum One. An indirect dependency fails the same way when the program expires or needs a newer Stylus version, and activation is closed on both chains.

leads.question: Who operates the stock token role accounts 0xcd8c6182e7c6ca3b5156d6a90a67719d7e2be094 (beacon upgrader), 0x957b6de6525c63349f7619743ef1e0ad93cd74d4 (admin burner), 0x913ca87347391218e5de2c17c5a0aeba8b0b28fd (blocker) and 0xe7bcb188254bc6ebbff63014dfed4cd4a024f22a (pauser), and is any of the 247 blocked accounts a contract that pools or routers pay out to?
leads.why: Each account has no code, so one signature can upgrade every stock token, burn the PoolManager balance, block the PoolManager or pause all transfers with no delay. A blocked recipient makes a take of a stock token revert for that caller.

leads.question: In the USDG facet 0x58cab81e3d8468a0e90df8cbfacb34535e1de942, what do wipeFrozenAddress and the claim functions do, is the PoolManager registered in a payout group, and can any payout group name the PoolManager as claim destination?
leads.why: USDG is a claimable rewards token. A claim credits the destination from the claim source without a call by the destination. A credit to the PoolManager between sync and settle of one transaction would be booked to whoever settles (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). I read the main logic and found the destination is set by a Paxos role, and I did not read the facet.

leads.question: Do any contracts on Robinhood Chain share a code hash with the 26 activated Stylus programs, and what does ArbWasm.programTimeLeft return for each?
leads.why: A new contract with the code of an activated program is callable without a new activation, so Stylus hooks or tokens can still appear on this chain. All of them stop answering together when the activation expires from 2027-07-25 or when the Stylus version changes.

leads.question: What liquidity sits in the Arbitrum One pool whose hook 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 is an EIP-7702 delegated account, and who holds that account?
leads.why: The holder can change or clear the delegation at any time, which changes the hook code after pool creation (A7). The address has the before swap, before swap returns delta, after add liquidity and before initialize flags and no remove liquidity flag, so swaps and additions depend on the holder and removals do not. Six other hook addresses and 13 currency addresses used by pools on this chain hold no code. None of those hooks has a remove liquidity flag.

leads.question: Once forge and the three submodules are available, does a build of this checkout with the foundry.toml settings pass its own test suite, and which tests fail?
leads.why: I could only read the tests and replay their concrete math vectors in Python. A failing test marks a place where the source no longer does what the tests expect, and I already found one fuzz condition (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129) that disagrees with src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-320. A full run is the cheapest way to find any other such place. This unit did not compare the source with deployed bytecode or any other copy, so whether the deployed contracts correspond to this source is also open.

leads.question: What does lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol at submodule commit 4b47a19038b798b4a33d9749d25e570443520647 contain once it is checked out: is onlyOwner a plain msg.sender == owner check and is transferOwnership the only other state changing function?
leads.why: setProtocolFeeController is the only owner gated function in src and its gate lives in a file that is absent from this checkout. The on chain probes show the existing deployments revert for a non owner, which says nothing about the file the CTF build will compile.

attempts.answer: lib/solmate is checked out at commit 4b47a19 in this session. Owned.sol declares one storage variable, owner. onlyOwner is require(msg.sender == owner, "UNAUTHORIZED"). The constructor sets the owner and transferOwnership, guarded by onlyOwner, is the only other state changing function (lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol:17-43). In the PoolManager the owner role reaches only setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32).

leads.question: For each of these networks, is every TSTORE made in one user transaction invisible to the next user transaction in all execution modes (parallel execution, protocol batches, phased or sponsored transactions, system transactions)?
leads.why: The code leaves the synced currency and reserves in transient storage after unlock returns and lets anyone call sync while locked (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). If those two slots survived into a later transaction, the party that wrote them could call settle and be credited the whole increase of the PoolManager's balance of that token since the sync, then take it. Under EIP-1153 semantics this cannot happen, so the answer per network decides between no issue and a critical one.

attempts.answer: For Monad and MegaETH the client sources confirm that a TSTORE does not reach the next transaction. Monad keeps transient storage inside the per-transaction State object (cycle 1) and rolls it back with the state version stack on a failed frame. MegaETH ends every transaction, including one that errors or panics, with the revm journal finalize step that clears transient storage, and the KeylessDeploy sandbox does not share it. Chains 137, 43114 and 4217 are outside this unit.

leads.question: Do the PositionManager and Universal Router deployed on each network call sync for the exact currency immediately before every payment, including sync(address(0)) before a native settle, with no external call between sync, transfer and settle?
leads.why: Core credits whoever calls settle with the balance increase since the last sync and accepts settle from any caller while unlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307, 349-364). A periphery contract that transfers before syncing loses the payment (test/Sync.t.sol:207-253), and one that makes an external call between transfer and settle lets a hook or token callback claim it with settleFor. A native settle without a prior sync reverts if an earlier call in the transaction left an ERC-20 synced.

attempts.answer: Yes for all 77 Universal Router and PositionManager deployments listed in state/networks.json. Each pays through DeltaResolver._settle, which calls sync(currency) for the exact currency, then either settle with value or the token transfer and settle. For the native currency that is sync(address(0)). The only external call between sync and settle is the token transfer itself, made directly or through Permit2. 54 deployments were read from verified source and 23 were matched to them by runtime code with PUSH20 to PUSH32 operands zeroed, with the MegaETH first router read from Blockscout.

leads.question: Does any PoolManager hold a token whose totalSupply in base units exceeds 2^127 - 1, and how much liquidity sits in pools that use it?
leads.why: Positions in such pools can become impossible to update once uncollected fees in that token reach 2^127 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:192, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59).

leads.question: On each network other than Ethereum that has EIP-7702 active, which initialized pools use a hook address whose code is a delegation indicator, an upgradeable proxy or empty, which of those addresses carry bits 9, 8 or 0, and how much liquidity do the pools hold?
leads.why: Core calls the hook on every removal and has no path around it (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-245, src/PoolManager.sol:156-183). An account that can change its code can turn a harmless hook into one that blocks or reprices removal. The ethereum-reference unit asks this for mainnet and the arbitrum-family verifier for one pool. The address 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 on Arbitrum One holds a delegation indicator today.

leads.question: For pools that hold a token with a base unit supply above 2^127 - 1, how close are the largest positions to 2^127 uncollected fee units, and do the PositionManager or common vault contracts collect fees often enough to stay below it?
leads.why: A position whose uncollected fees in one currency reach 2^127 can never be updated again, and the principal in both currencies stays in the PoolManager (src/libraries/Pool.sol:192, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). Ordinary swap volume against a passive position can reach the bound without an attacker. This extends the researcher's lead on such tokens from supply to accrued fees.

leads.question: Does Owned.sol at the pinned solmate commit declare exactly one storage variable, so that _pools sits at slot 6 as StateLibrary.POOLS_SLOT assumes, and does the Unichain predeploy, whose bytecode length differs, keep the pools mapping at slot 6?
leads.why: The PositionManager, quoters and hooks read pool state through extsload at slots derived from POOLS_SLOT. If the layout differs they read empty or unrelated slots, which can misprice or block periphery operations even though core accounting is unchanged.

attempts.answer: First half answered: Owned declares exactly one storage variable, so _pools is at slot 6 as StateLibrary.POOLS_SLOT assumes (lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol:17, src/ProtocolFees.sol:21-24, src/ERC6909.sol:15-19, src/PoolManager.sol:93, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:11). Second half open: I did not examine the Unichain predeploy, because the owner has ruled out comparing this code with other copies.

leads.question: With solc 0.8.26 and the foundry.toml settings available, do the repository fuzz tests for Pool, SwapMath, SqrtPriceMath, TickMath, TickBitmap, BitMath and FullMath pass on the compiled build, and does the compiled Pool.swap give the same deltas as the Python transcription on the 28,000 fuzz sequences?
leads.why: Both source reading units cleared the math from the text and from transcriptions. Neither could compile. A compiler or optimizer effect on the assembly blocks would not show in a transcription.

leads.question: eth_estimateGas priced the 4,394 byte probe creation at 22,573,027 gas on MegaETH against 536,325 on Ethereum and HyperEVM and 535,533 on Monad. What do a first liquidity add, which writes up to 11 new storage slots, and a removal cost under the MegaETH gas model, and does any per transaction limit apply to them?
leads.why: Liquidity removal is the exit path for LPs. If MegaETH prices or caps storage writes far above Ethereum, the gas bound used to clear A9 for the math files needs its own number on that network.

attempts.answer: A new storage slot in a bucket of minimum size costs no storage gas, and the measured cost is about 22,500 gas per new slot (22,357,175 gas for 990 slots in a creation). Every transaction pays 60,000 intrinsic gas, and each LOG topic adds 3,750 storage gas. A first liquidity add with about 11 new slots and a removal therefore cost close to their Ethereum gas plus the intrinsic difference, far below the limits of 200 million compute gas and 1,000 new state entries per transaction. The high estimate for the 4,394 byte probe comes from the storage gas charged on deployed code. No modifyLiquidity call was simulated.

leads.question: How many initialized tick crossings and empty bitmap words of Pool.swap fit in a 3,000,000 gas HyperEVM small block, and do the routers and hooks deployed on HyperEVM split large swaps or send them to big blocks?
leads.why: A swap that must cross many ticks in one transaction, for example inside a liquidation or a hook, can fail on small blocks. This does not lock LP funds through core, and it can lock funds in contracts that depend on such a swap.

attempts.answer: From the repository snapshots and the gas constants of EIP-2929 and EIP-2200, one loop iteration of Pool.swap costs at least 2,242 gas for the bitmap read, a crossing about 14,342 gas when both fee growth slots change and about 48,542 gas when both are written for the first time, all before the swap step and TickMath. A 3,000,000 gas small block transaction therefore fits at most about 200 crossings, about 59 first time crossings, or about 1,283 empty bitmap words. The values are upper bounds and were not measured on HyperEVM. A swap from tick 0 to the extreme limit in a spacing 1 pool needs 3,468 iterations and cannot fit. I did not read the routers and hooks deployed on HyperEVM, so the second half of the question stays open and is repeated as a lead.

leads.question: Do the block producing clients of the 21 networks, as opposed to the public RPC nodes, return the same 66 probe words (one marker and 65 results), and does a wider differential test of MULMOD, SDIV, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND and SAR on random operands agree with the specification on Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM?
leads.why: Pool prices and amounts depend on exact 256 bit arithmetic. The probe in this cycle covered one node per network and 65 vectors. A single differing opcode result in a custom interpreter or compiler backend would change swap amounts.

leads.question: Does the PoolManager bytecode change when the sources are rebuilt with a solc 0.8.26 that carries the fix for the Yul optimizer bug YulOptimizerKnowledgeBaseStaleBookkeeping (checks 1 to 3 in the Solidity team's post of 2026-10-22), and does the 24,050 byte Unichain predeploy pass the same comparison?
leads.why: The Solidity bug list marks 0.8.26 as affected. The bug is present from 0.8.19 to 0.8.37 whenever the Yul optimizer runs: a load can be replaced with an outdated value, or a needed store can be removed, when two addresses derived from a reassigned variable coincide at run time (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ethereum/solidity/develop/docs/bugs_by_version.json, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ethereum/solidity/develop/docs/bugs.json, https://blog.soliditylang.org/2026/10/22/yul-optimizer-knowledge-base-stale-bookkeeping-bug/). foundry.toml sets solc 0.8.26, via_ir and optimizer_runs 44444444, and eth_getCode on all 21 networks returns code whose metadata trailer names solc 0.8.26. The post says the conditions cannot be checked from the Solidity source, so the two source reading units, which worked from the text and from transcriptions, cannot exclude it. Pool.swap reads and writes storage and memory through computed addresses inside a loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437), and Extsload reassigns a memory pointer inside a loop (src/Extsload.sol:20-36). An effect is unlikely: the post reports that rebuilding about 283,000 via-IR compilations from Sourcify with and without the fix gave identical bytecode, and Sourcify lists the Ethereum PoolManager as verified with solc 0.8.26, viaIR and the optimizer enabled (https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x000000000004444c5dc75cB358380D2e3dE08A90?fields=compilation). That scan used a development compiler, and Sourcify has no entry for the Unichain address (https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/130/0x1f98400000000000000000000000000000000004 returns 404), so the question stays open until someone with a compiler runs the comparison. I did not compare the Unichain bytecode with the other deployments. The other bug list entries for 0.8.26 need a recursive storage struct with a dynamic array, mutual recursion, named arguments in a require with a custom error, the legacy pipeline or an array at the end of storage. I saw none of these in the files I read.

attempts.answer: I fetched the Solidity team's post and the bug list. The handwritten assembly in src/ does not contain the reproducer pattern: the only address variables that are reassigned sit in the loops of Extsload and Exttload, which never load what they stored, and every other block uses constant addresses or a pointer assigned once. The other seven entries listed for 0.8.26 need constructs that src/ does not contain. The condition on the intermediate Yul code of the compiler generated parts cannot be decided from the text, and I had no compiler, so the bytecode comparison the lead asks for is still open.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on 2026-12-08, what does the client implementation of CAS20 return for transfer and balanceOf when called by the PoolManager, has the ActivationRegistry opened token creation, and which CAS20 tokens have pools?
leads.why: The finding on CAS20 rests on a Draft BEP. Return data shape, static call behaviour and gas metering decide whether sync, settle and take work at all with these tokens.

attempts.answer: From the client source and from 12 live tokens on Chapel: transfer returns a 32 byte true and moves exactly the amount, balanceOf returns 32 bytes and works under STATICCALL, a transfer above the balance reverts with InsufficientBalance, and a policy that does not list the sender or the recipient makes the transfer revert for every amount. sync, settle and take therefore work with a CAS20 token whose policies admit the PoolManager. Token creation on mainnet stays closed after the fork until an administrator appointed through GovHub activates it. No CAS20 token can have a pool before 2026-12-08, and a new lead asks for the list after activation.

leads.question: Can any sequence of hook callbacks, token callbacks or ERC-6909 operations profit from calling the fee adapter's collect while the PoolManager is unlocked, given that collectProtocolFees in src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 never checks the lock?
leads.why: Fee collection is reachable by any address on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain and moves tokens out of the shared balance in the middle of an unlock. This unit found no gain but did not read Pool.sol in full.

attempts.answer: No sequence profits. A model run with a third party fee withdrawal allowed at every point, except for the ERC-20 that is synced, found no gain and no shortfall in three currency settings (75,072, 67,659 and 100,064 states). collectProtocolFees writes no delta and no transient slot, subtracts from protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction before the transfer, and reverts for the synced ERC-20 in both lock states (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). Hook callbacks, token callbacks and ERC-6909 operations add nothing, because none of them can raise protocolFeesAccrued or change the recipient that the adapter fixes.

leads.why: The owner path finding inferred these checks from bytecode strings.

leads.why: Anyone can move accrued protocol fees from the PoolManager into the jar, so the jar's release rule decides who ends up with them.

leads.why: The onlyOwner modifier at src/ProtocolFees.sol:29 cannot be reviewed from the repository as it stands.

leads.question: Who are the nine signers of the Safe 0xFa7D2a996aC6350f4b56C043112Da0366a59b74C that owns the StateSender on Ethereum, is any delay or timelock placed in front of StateSender.register, and which other roles can change that Safe?
leads.why: Five signers can register a new sender for FxChild and forge a message from the Uniswap timelock to the PoolManager owner proxy on Polygon. An eth_call of register from the Safe succeeds today. This lowers the precondition of the Polygon owner path finding from a Heimdall majority to one multisig.

leads.question: Do failedStateSyncHashes or the historic failed root at 0x1001 (leafCount 76, replayCount 9) contain a record addressed to FxChild whose payload targets the owner proxy 0x8a1b966ac46f42275860f905dbc75efbfdc12374, and who controls the gas oracle 0x5e3a5eafd4501332c0bc2acfd38df3ebc5152147 that sets the gas forwarded to receivers?
leads.why: The published StateReceiver source has replayFailedStateSync, replayFailedStateSyncWithData and replayHistoricFailedStateSync, all open to any caller, and the deployed selectors match. A governance message that failed on first delivery, for example for lack of receiver gas (the default is 160,000), can be executed later by anyone at a time of their choosing. That could restore a protocol fee controller that governance has since replaced.

leads.question: After Jenner, does the deployed CAS20 handler expose SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY as on client master or SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY as in the BEP-702 text, and does a call to a 0xCA52 address that holds no token revert with empty return data?
leads.why: The scope name decides which getter a monitor must read to learn whether the PoolManager is seizable. A4 assumes that a transfer call to a currency without code succeeds. In the reserved range it will revert, which changes take for any pool initialized on a token address that does not exist yet.

leads.question: Is the Avalanche owner 0x47eb0cf11a1626462da3c830bcde64c3f582b5a6 verified on an explorer, and does its source equal the BNB Smart Chain receiver apart from the chain id constant?
leads.why: Sourcify has an exact match for the BNB Smart Chain receiver and no entry for the Avalanche one. The Avalanche checks rest on bytecode strings and getters.

leads.question: Does a second, independent reading of PoolManager.sync, _settle and ProtocolFees.collectProtocolFees agree that a sync outside an unlock, or a fee collection inside an unlock triggered through a permissionless controller, can never change the amount credited in _settle or pay out more than protocolFeesAccrued?
leads.why: The lock is not checked on either path and ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 says it is. I found only same-transaction reverts, but this is the place where the code and its stated assumptions disagree.

attempts.answer: A second reading and a state search agree. A sync outside an unlock sets two transient slots and nothing else (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). The credit in _settle is the checked rise of the balance since the last sync of that currency, or msg.value when no ERC-20 is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). A fee collection can only lower a balance, cannot touch the synced ERC-20, and is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-56). So neither can raise a credit or pay out more than was accrued.

leads.question: Who will be the owner and the protocol fee controller of the CTF build on mainnet, and will the controller expose collectProtocolFees or setProtocolFee to arbitrary callers as the current V4FeeAdapter does?
leads.why: All governance facts in this cycle describe the existing deployment. A different owner or a controller with an arbitrary recipient would change who can reach accrued fees.

leads.question: Among pools initialized on the mainnet PoolManager, how many use a hook address whose code is an EIP-7702 delegation indicator or is empty, and how much liquidity do they hold?
leads.why: This turns the EIP-7702 hook finding from a possibility into a measured exposure. It needs a scan of Initialize events and eth_getCode on each hook.

leads.question: When Glamsterdam gets a mainnet date, how much gas does one initialized tick crossing in Pool.swap cost under EIP-8038 and EIP-8037, and how many crossings fit under the 16,777,216 gas cap?
leads.why: The storage write surcharge rises from 2,800 to 10,000 gas and each crossing writes two fee growth slots. The answer sets how finely large swaps must be split and whether any periphery flow that cannot split would stall.

leads.question: What does lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol at the pinned submodule commit do on ownership transfer, once the submodule is checked out?
leads.why: lib/ is empty in this checkout, so the code behind onlyOwner and transferOwnership was not read. A one-step transfer to a wrong address would permanently fix the protocol fee controller.

attempts.answer: transferOwnership writes the new owner in one step and emits OwnershipTransferred. There is no pending owner, no renounce function and no check that the new owner is nonzero (lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol:39-43).

leads.question: Which other tokens among the largest balances of the mainnet PoolManager have issuer freeze, seize, pause, upgrade or rebase functions, and what is the combined value exposed?
leads.why: This cycle checked USDC, USDT, PYUSD, stETH, wstETH, WETH, DAI, WBTC and AMPL only. A full list sizes the issuer finding.

attempts.answer: On-chain balances at block 26471602 add 56.25M USDS, 32.36M RLUSD, 404.31 WBTC, 369.89 cbBTC, 35.17M WLFI, 2.80M USDG, 2.47M GHO, 1.66M EURC, 1,496 XAUT and 1,145 PAXG to the list. Block or freeze views exist on cbBTC, EURC, WLFI, USDG, PAXG and XAUT and a pause view on RLUSD, WBTC and LBTC. I did not read these tokens' sources, so the roles and any seize function are unconfirmed, and I did not total a dollar value.

leads.question: How much of the stETH balance of the mainnet PoolManager is surplus above the sum of pool reserves, ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees for stETH?
leads.why: It measures the yield already stranded by rebases and confirms the rounding argument in the stETH finding.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the mainnet PoolManager have a function that any account can call to raise balanceOf(PoolManager) without a transfer from the caller, such as a public rebase, a reward claim on behalf of a holder or a distributor push, and how much value does each call move?
leads.why: sync needs no unlock and _settle credits any balance increase since the last sync to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). A caller who places such a call between sync and settle is credited value that belongs to no delta. The researcher checked stETH, where only oracle members can do this, and AMPL, where the PoolManager holds dust.

attempts.answer: Recorded as the finding in this file. Public triggers exist (Ampleforth rebase behind an origin check that EIP-7702 defeats, Compound claimComp for any holder, Olympus rebase). None paid the PoolManager at block 26471590, and AMPL holdings are 16 base units.

leads.question: Who holds the pauser and proxy admin roles of USDC, the pause and upgrade roles of PYUSD and the owner role of USDT that controls pause, and are any of these separate from the blocklist roles already recorded?
leads.why: transfer in all three tokens reverts while the token is paused, and USDC and PYUSD are upgradeable. Each of these roles can stop take and collectProtocolFees for every pool in that currency in the same way as a blocklist entry (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/ProtocolFees.sol:56).

attempts.answer: USDC reports pauser 0x4914f61d25e5c567143774b76edbf4d5109a8566, blacklister 0x0a06be16275b95a7d2567fbdae118b36c7da78f9 and owner 0xfcb19e6a322b27c06842a71e8c725399f049ae3a, so the pauser is a separate account. USDT reports owner 0xc6cde7c39eb2f0f0095f41570af89efc2c1ea828, the same account as XAUT's owner. PYUSD reports owner 0x3af3e85f4f97de7ad0f000b724fb77fe5ffc024b. I did not read the proxy admin of USDC or the role members of PYUSD.

leads.question: Does computeFee of the policy contract 0x1cd822b70a0591420f65e94b9b3a0d0b0fb3a314 read state that a swapper or a hook can change inside one transaction, so that a call to triggerFeeUpdate before a swap lowers the protocol fee for that swap?
leads.why: triggerFeeUpdate on the mainnet adapter is open to anyone and setProtocolFee does not check the lock (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41). The effect would be limited to protocol fee revenue, since the value stays under the 1,000 pip cap.

leads.question: MegaETH seals an EVM block once cumulative state growth reaches 1,000 new entries. What does it cost per block to reach that cap with one transaction, at the base fee and bucket multipliers seen on chain, and are L1 deposit transactions included regardless of the cap?
leads.why: If the cost is small, a paying spammer could shrink every block to a few transactions and delay liquidity removals for as long as it pays. If deposits are also subject to the cap, the forced inclusion route in the sequencer finding is weaker than documented.

attempts.answer: One creation that writes 999 new slots reaches 1,000 new state entries and costs 22,559,525 gas, about 0.0000226 ETH at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei. A transaction that brings the block counter to 1,000 is included and the limiter then skips every later candidate of that block. The state growth test also runs for deposit transactions. Recorded as a low finding with effect degrade. The ordering rule of the sequencer was not confirmed.

leads.question: Read the MegaETH node and derivation rules for deposit transactions: do the sequencer-configured gas cap, the 1 MB size limit and the MegaEVM runtime limits apply to a forced PositionManager call, and does SystemConfig gasLimit (60,000,000 read on L1) bound it?
leads.why: The forced inclusion route is the only exit when the sequencer censors. A limit that a normal liquidity removal exceeds would turn the 12 hour delay into a freeze.

leads.question: List every currency with a non-zero balance at the two PoolManagers and classify each for issuer controls and for balances that change without transfers. Start with iTRY on MegaETH, which the token list calls interest-bearing with a separate non-rebasing wrapper, and with sUSDe, syrupUSDC and STCUSD.
leads.why: A token whose balanceOf rises between sync and settle credits the settler with the increase (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Only the main dollar tokens were classified in this cycle.

attempts.answer: MegaETH: Blockscout lists 67 tokens at the PoolManager, about 17,000 dollars in total, with eight aTokens below one dollar each and wiTRY but no iTRY. Monad: 65 of 147 listed tokens have a balance, and GHO, syrupUSDC, apxUSD and shMON were added to the issuer control record. Tokens outside the lists on Monad were not enumerated, and the liquid staking tokens were classified by type and not by source.

leads.question: Read the verified source of AUSD, mUSD and USD1 on Monad and of USDm on MegaETH: can the issuer burn or move a frozen balance, and do they refuse transfers to a frozen address?
leads.why: This decides whether an issuer action against the PoolManager is a reversible freeze or a loss, and whether swaps into the token also stop.

leads.question: Survey the hooks used by v4 pools on MegaETH for try/catch or unchecked low-level calls around reads of block fields, the Oracle contract at 0x6342000000000000000000000000000000000001 or the high-precision timestamp contract.
leads.why: A hook with a failure-tolerant path around a volatile read can be steered by any caller through MegaAccessControl. Finding one would turn the low severity hazard into a concrete loss path.

leads.question: When the MONAD_NEXT revision is specified, read the list of EIPs and MIPs it activates (the client maps it to EVM revision Amsterdam) and check each against transient storage lifetime, SELFDESTRUCT, call gas forwarding and new precompile addresses with hook flag bits.
leads.why: A revision that changes any of these alters assumptions A1, A7 or A10 for a PoolManager that holds over 200 million MON.

leads.question: ASSUMPTIONS A12 says collectProtocolFees reverts while the manager is unlocked and the currency is synced. The code at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49 tests only the synced currency, and _isUnlocked declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 is not used in that function. Should the assumption text or the code reading be corrected by the source-reading unit?
leads.why: No fund path was found from this difference, because a fee withdrawal of the synced currency is still blocked. The assumption list should match the code so later cycles reason from the right guard.

attempts.answer: The code reading is right. ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 in this checkout already says that collection reverts when the currency is an ERC-20 that is currently synced, whatever the lock state, and that _isUnlocked is declared and never called. That text matches src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-60 and the three tests at test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039.

leads.question: A forced exit through the OptimismPortal can buy at most 20,000,000 gas per L1 block (resourceConfig read on L1), and MegaETH charges 20,000 times (bucket multiplier minus 1) storage gas for each zero to nonzero SSTORE. How are storage slots assigned to SALT buckets, can a third party fill the bucket that holds a chosen PoolManager slot, and what does it cost to push that bucket's multiplier above 1,000?
leads.why: Removing liquidity writes the position's fee growth fields (src/libraries/Position.sol:100-101), and keeping the proceeds as a claim writes an ERC-6909 balance (src/ERC6909.sol:80). If one of those writes goes from zero to nonzero in a bucket with a multiplier above about 1,000, its storage gas alone exceeds the deposit budget. A sequencer that censors and also inflates the bucket would turn the 12 hour delay of the sequencer finding into a freeze for that position. The gas model page and the L1 value are confirmed. The bucket mechanics and the cost are not.

attempts.answer: Slots map to buckets by a fixed-seed hash of address and slot modulo the number of buckets, a bucket doubles above 80 percent fill, and the multiplier comes from the parent block. Inflating one bucket to multiplier 2^k costs about 2.7 million times 4^k gas. Multiplier 1,024 costs about 2.8 ETH and adds 20.5 million gas to one new write, which is negligible on the normal path and above the 20 million gas that the lead reports for a forced deposit. That case needs the sequencer to censor the user as well, and the user can avoid new writes in a targeted bucket by choosing a recipient that already holds the token. The bucket count was not read.

leads.question: Have any MegaETH network upgrades (MiniRex through Rex6) executed deposits with from set to the zero address, as the OP Stack Ecotone and Isthmus upgrade bundles do, and does the node accept arbitrary targets in such bundles?
leads.why: The protocol fee controller on MegaETH is the zero address. A fork bundle that calls as the zero address could set protocol fees up to 0.1 percent per direction and collect them (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-57). The reach is protocol fees only, and naming a real controller through governance closes it.

leads.question: The mUSD implementation 0xc2e2fbcef84dea88025a5b2599039c912ef6b61c contains the selector of forceTransfer(address,address,uint256) and the AUSD implementation 0xc1e3c7d486d6a92fbe920232e439eec2ceb112da contains burn(address,uint256). Which role may call each, and does the call require the source account to be frozen first?
leads.why: This extends the open lead on issuer powers with two concrete entry points. The PoolManager holds 1.64 million mUSD and 1.52 million AUSD. A role that can move or burn an unfrozen balance is a direct loss path for those pools without any prior freeze event to watch for.

leads.question: The admin of the USDC proxy on Monad (0xc66bf3ef02d30e942bbab7f871d07b14d0ccc619) and its blacklister (0x17864246c1edb4a5da2e2ca891564e3dff01d6cd) are accounts with no code. Does Circle document how these accounts are held, and is the owner 0xf62c8e636d61840ec9f8c3ab518aa65306af26e0, which can reassign the blacklister, a contract with a threshold?
leads.why: USDC is 16.06 million of the PoolManager's balance on Monad. The stablecoin finding treats the issuer as one actor. If one signing account can upgrade the token, the precondition is weaker than a multi-party issuer decision and monitoring should watch that account.

leads.question: How does HyperCore choose and authorise the sender addresses of AQAv2 rebalancing system transactions? Must the treasury address or the linked contract sign or send an authorization, or can the treasury deployer name any EVM address, including a contract that cannot sign?
leads.why: If an address can be named without its consent, a validator vote plus two staked deployers could make HyperCore send transfer calls from the PoolManager and drain a currency. If consent from the address is required, the PoolManager can never be bound and the AQAv2 finding drops to info.

attempts.answer: Same evidence as for L-116 and L-074. The archive client shows that the node accepts any 20 byte address as sender of a system transaction, and recent blocks contain such transactions from the CoreDepositWallet and from the treasury address. How HyperCore authorises the choice of these addresses is not public.

leads.question: The PoolManager's first storage slot holds the owner, which HyperCore accepts as finalizer for linking a spot token to the PoolManager address, and the owner contract can call CoreWriter action 8 through a governance message. What does HyperCore do with a linked contract beyond calling transfer and reading Transfer logs, in particular under AQAv2 where system transactions are sent from the linked contract?
leads.why: A link is harmless under the documented transfer behaviour, but a rule that sends system transactions from the linked contract would turn a governance or guardian compromise into a drain of pool balances.

leads.question: Has Hyperliquid announced a move of HyperEVM from Cancun to Prague or later, and would it include EIP-7702?
leads.why: EIP-7702 lets an account with a mined hook address change its code after pool creation, which breaks assumption A7. No dated statement was found in this cycle.

attempts.answer: No announcement of a move to Prague was found. The hard fork of 11 November 2026 at block 50,988,232 only reprices seven precompiles and switches MODEXP to the Osaka formula. Both spec ids of the archive client map to CANCUN and the Prague precompile addresses still answer like empty accounts, so EIP-7702 is not active.

leads.question: How do pools behave when a hook calls read precompiles or CoreWriter inside swap or modifyLiquidity callbacks? A precompile error consumes all gas passed to the call, results are fixed per block, and CoreWriter actions run after the block.
leads.why: A hook that depends on HyperCore state can make removeLiquidity revert whenever a precompile input becomes invalid, for example after a delisting, which would freeze LP funds in that pool.

leads.question: What were the 18 improper self destructs that the replay client patches between blocks 1,467,569 and 1,531,366, and does the production node now follow EIP-6780 exactly?
leads.why: If SELFDESTRUCT can still remove code outside the creating transaction, a hook address could be emptied and redeployed with different code.

attempts.answer: The archive client carries the same list of 18 patched transactions between blocks 1,467,569 and 1,531,366 (src/node/evm/patch.rs) and no later entry, and it uses the stock revm instruction table for all later blocks while matching every block header. That supports standard EIP-6780 behaviour since block 1,531,366. What the 18 cases were is still not documented.

leads.question: The sender rule in the public replay client (run.rs lines 223 to 227) covers only the HYPE bridge address and token system addresses. Has the client been updated for AQAv2 senders, and does the updated code still create one EVM per system transaction?
leads.why: The clearance of assumption A1 rests on this client matching the production node. A newer execution path for system transactions should be read once it is public.

attempts.answer: The public replay client was not updated: its sender rule at run.rs lines 223 to 227 is unchanged. The archive client nanoreth was. It recovers any 20 byte sender from the fabricated signature of a system transaction, runs each transaction through one transact call, and its pinned revm fork clears transient storage after every transaction. It also checks gas used, receipts root and logs bloom of every block against the validator node's header.

leads.question: Read lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol once the submodule is checked out and confirm what the owner can do besides setProtocolFeeController.
leads.why: The governance finding assumes the owner has no power over pool funds. The file was not available in this checkout, so that statement rests on the files under src/ only.

attempts.answer: Besides setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32) the owner can only call transferOwnership (lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol:39-43). No other function in src/ uses onlyOwner or reads owner.

leads.question: Can the USDT0 OFT contract on HyperEVM, 0x904861a24f30ec96ea7cfc3be9ea4b476d237e98 as returned by oftContract(), burn tokens from an arbitrary holder such as the PoolManager without a prior blocklist entry, and who can change that contract through the owner gated setOFTContract?
leads.why: The OpenZeppelin audit says the authorized sender in the OFT extension can burn any amount from any account. On HyperEVM the OFT contract and the token share the owner 0xb64a89ad247a2d691a728bb6822a85eedd7fc541. A simulated burn(address,uint256) from the OFT address reverted without a message, so the entry point is unconfirmed. If such a path exists, the PoolManager balance of USDT0 can be removed without a BlockPlaced event, which defeats the monitoring proposed in the issuer finding and adds the cross-chain message configuration to the trusted set.

leads.question: Was the PoolManager at 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F created by an EOA through CREATE or by a factory contract, and does HyperCore accept the create variant of finalizeEvmContract for it?
leads.why: The docs give three finalizer variants. In the create variant the EOA that deployed the contract finalizes a link with its deployment nonce, without the owner in storage slot 0. If the PoolManager was created by an EOA, that deployer account alone can link a HyperCore spot token to the PoolManager address, which lowers the bar assumed in the AQAv2 finding and in the clearance on linking from Uniswap governance to one deployer account.

leads.question: Is the AQAv2 treasury address always the account that signed authorizeAqav2Role with role treasury, or can the treasury deployer name a different EVM address afterwards?
leads.why: The exchange API action has only the fields token and role, which suggests the role attaches to the signer. If that is the rule, the PoolManager can never be a treasury address and the system transaction finding drops to info. If a separate designation exists, staked deployers plus a validator vote could point per block transfer calls at the PoolManager balance.

attempts.answer: The treasury address is not the signer. 0xc20699185c15d0a2fd65779bb5d69f5b0b113c00 has no HyperCore user role, no stake and no HyperCore balance, while the docs say the authorizations are sent from the staking accounts and that the treasury deployer designates a treasury address. Whether the designated address has to consent, and whether it can be changed later, was not found.

leads.question: Is the risk control filter or the bridge interceptor enabled on the X Layer mainnet sequencer, and has any transaction that touches 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32 or a pooled token been denied or held for audit?
leads.why: This decides whether the freeze finding describes a live control or a dormant one. Sequencer flags and rules are not public, so the answer needs operator statements or evidence of valid transactions that stayed unincluded.

attempts.answer: Whether the builder filter is enabled on mainnet is still unknown. New in this cycle: the execution layer has a separate rule that voids blacklisted L1 deposits, its contract is deployed on mainnet, and one account without code owns it. See the high finding.

Operator only hazard. Whether the filter or the bridge interceptor is enabled on the mainnet sequencer is still unknown. No evidence of a denied or held PoolManager transaction was found, the deposit blacklist is empty at block 76,668,710, and chain data cannot show the flag (see L-263).

leads.question: What is the address of the gasless whitelist predeploy on X Layer, who can upgrade it, which caller address does the client use for the getGaslessAllowance system call, and can that contract make an onward call during the check?
leads.why: protocolFeeController is address(0). If the system call uses address(0) as caller and the whitelist contract were ever replaced by one that forwards calls with delegatecall semantics, the controller role could become reachable. The current reading says the call is uncommitted, which would rule this out.

attempts.answer: The gasless whitelist is the proxy 0x19787404b0c70021b4752028f7e3a92313885B27 with implementation 0x2cd362cd1079057f61459c7cef13042a3aca1672. Its owner and the owner of its proxy admin 0x86ef647bd5e009bbc63944a6753535bce3dd1057 are the account 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, which has no code. The client calls it from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe and drops the resulting state, so no call can reach the PoolManager as address(0) through it.

leads.question: When Uniswap governance sets a protocol fee controller on Celo, can anyone trigger its collection inside a transaction of their choice?
leads.why: The guard at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49 skips currency address(0). On Celo a native fee collection lowers the same balance that a synced CELO token settlement measures, so a collection between another party's sync and settle would under credit that settlement or make it revert. The path needs a permissionless collector and attacker code between sync and settle, and neither exists today.

leads.question: Which wrapped native address did the periphery deployments on Celo (PositionManager 0xf7965f3981e4d5bc383bfbcb61501763e9068ca9 and the Universal Routers) receive in their constructors: the CELO token, the 0x4200...0006 predeploy, or the bridged WETH?
leads.why: A router that wraps or unwraps through the mislabelled predeploy, or that treats the CELO token as a wrapper with deposit and withdraw, would mishandle user funds on the way to or from the PoolManager.

leads.question: Does any token registered in FeeCurrencyDirectory call code outside Governance control during debitGasFees or creditGasFees?
leads.why: The credit call runs while the transaction's transient storage is still present. A fee currency with a callback to arbitrary code would run that code with msg.sender address(0) one hop away and with a possibly stale synced currency in the PoolManager.

leads.question: When will Celo and X Layer activate Karst, and will they adopt the L2 Contract Manager for predeploy upgrades?
leads.why: Karst adds the 16,777,216 gas cap per transaction and a consensus level route to replace predeploys, including the messenger that the PoolManager owner trusts.

leads.question: How will the Espresso fast finality integration change who can reorder or revert Celo blocks before L1 finality?
leads.why: A new confirmation layer changes the sequencer trust model that bridges and fast withdrawal services around the pools rely on (A14).

leads.question: Do the issuer control findings raised for stablecoins on other OP Stack chains apply to USDT0 and USDC on X Layer and to USDT and USDC on Celo with the same roles and upgrade paths?
leads.why: The PoolManager on X Layer holds about 5.83 million USDT0, which is an upgradeable proxy with a blocklist getter. A block on the single PoolManager address would stop every USDT0 pool (A6).

leads.question: Who administers the bridge at 0x2a3DD3EB832aF982ec71669E178424b10Dca2EDe on X Layer after the move to OP Stack, and can it still mint or burn the wrapped WETH, WBTC and old USDT that pools hold?
leads.why: The EIP-1967 admin slot of the bridge proxy reads zero, so its upgrade path was not identified. A bridge that can burn from arbitrary holders could lower PoolManager balances outside take (A2).

leads.question: Can the holders of the X Layer L1 upgrade authority (Safe 0xC290be56089bCC83C6993583ce2cF51a7951D45A on Ethereum, threshold 2, three owners without code, owner of the ProxyAdmin 0x313ce9cec2070b519f13bdafe07eabb4f215fee6 of OptimismPortal 0x64057ad1DdAc804d0D26A7275b193D9DACa19993) replace the portal with one that emits TransactionDeposited with an arbitrary from, and does the X Layer derivation accept such a deposit without any further check or delay?
leads.why: The OP deposit specification says the sender of a deposited transaction is the value in the portal event. A forged sender could call the PoolManager as the zero address, which is the current protocolFeeController, or call PositionManager as any position owner and withdraw that owner's liquidity. This would put pool reserves on X Layer within reach of two signers, which is a wider reach than the fee control described in the ownership finding. The same question applies to Celo with a 2 of 2 Safe of two 6 of 8 Safes.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the X Layer PoolManager are OptimismMintableERC20 tokens whose bridge() is the L2StandardBridge predeploy 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000010, and how much of each does the PoolManager hold?
leads.why: The admin slot of that predeploy holds the ProxyAdmin 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000018, whose owner is the 2 of 3 Safe on X Layer. A replaced bridge could mint such tokens without backing and sell them into pools for the paired assets.

leads.question: PositionManager 0xf7965f3981e4d5bc383bfbcb61501763e9068ca9 on Celo returns the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 from WETH9(), and the first Universal Router contains the same address. How do the wrap, unwrap and sweep actions of these contracts behave when the wrapped native token has no deposit or withdraw function and its balanceOf equals the contract's native balance?
leads.why: This answers part of the research lead on periphery constructor arguments: the predeploy and the bridged WETH are not used. A sweep of the CELO token moves the contract's native balance, so native value left in the PositionManager or a router between actions could be taken under the token face on its way to or from the PoolManager.

leads.question: Does the deployed CELO token implementation 0xFeA1B35f1D5f2A58532a70e7A32e6F2D3Bc4F7B1 (version 1.2.0.0) match the monorepo source for transfer, transferFrom and balanceOf, and does it contain any function that passes a from address other than msg.sender or an allowance checked account to the transfer precompile?
leads.why: The CELO governance finding was checked against master source that reports version 1.3.0.0. A function in the deployed version that debits an arbitrary account would turn a governance only path into an unprivileged one.

attempts.answer: The deployed CELO implementation has the same 24 functions as GoldToken.sol at tag core-contracts.v15 (version 1.2.0.0). Every call to the transfer precompile passes msg.sender or an allowance checked source. I compared function lists and read the tagged source. I did not rebuild the bytecode.

leads.question: Which protocol hardfork did X Layer mainnet activate with the coordinated upgrade to xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 and op-node xlayer/v0.1.7 that was due by 10 November 2026, and did it change transaction validity, gas rules or system calls?
leads.why: The v0.0.7 release notes mention support for a protocol hardfork and the same release introduced the risk control filter. The CLZ probe shows Osaka rules are not active, so the content of the fork is unknown to this review.

attempts.answer: The notes of xlayer/v0.1.7 and xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 list Glamsterdam L1 header compatibility, wider gasless support with a GASLESS_WHITELIST predeploy and a fix of the gasless base fee bypass. They do not name a protocol hardfork. The CLZ probe still fails with NotActivated on 2026-11-22.

leads.question: Which B20 tokens does the Base PoolManager hold, and for each one what are the bound TRANSFER_SENDER, TRANSFER_RECEIVER, TRANSFER_EXECUTOR and SEIZE_EXEMPT policies, who administers them, and is the PoolManager authorised under each?
leads.why: It turns the B20 finding from a class of hazard into a list of pools with a live freeze or seize exposure. The log query for the factory was rate limited and the Base explorer blocked the request in this cycle.

leads.question: In Base Transactions (EIP-8430, type 0x79, planned for Everest), is transient storage cleared between call phases, can a failed phase leave earlier phases committed, and at what point is the payer's token reimbursement debited?
leads.why: A phase boundary that keeps transient storage while reverting part of the transaction, or a token debit outside EVM execution, would touch assumptions A1, A2 and A5. Everest has no activation date yet.

leads.question: When Lagoon is scheduled, do the sequencer defined gas refunds credit only tx.from as the draft says, and what can the activated SuperchainTokenBridge and SuperchainETHBridge do to balances of tokens that implement crosschainBurn?
leads.why: The draft credits ETH to senders outside EVM execution and activates bridge predeploys that mint and burn. The PoolManager cannot be a tx.from, but the final spec and the token bridge rules should be read before activation. OP Mainnet and Zora also have the legacy ETH view that turns any native balance change into a readable ERC-20 balance.

attempts.answer: The Lagoon specification credits the refund to tx.from only, after the EVM frame of the transaction has ended, and debits the block beneficiary and two fee vaults. The PoolManager cannot be tx.from, and a credit applied after execution cannot fall between a sync and a settle, also not through the legacy ETH view on OP Mainnet. The SuperchainTokenBridge burns only from the caller of sendERC20 and mints to the recipient named on the source chain, so a balance of the PoolManager in a token with crosschainBurn can rise and cannot fall. SuperchainETHBridge pays out by self-destruct, which adds a second route for forced ETH and no credit for anyone. Lagoon is targeted for 11 January 2027 on OP Mainnet and Unichain. The specification is not final and Zora, Ink and Soneium have no date.

leads.question: How should bytecode parity for the Unichain PoolManager (24,050 bytes against 24,009 elsewhere) be established, given that the review owner forbids diffing against other copies?
leads.why: The findings and cleared items for Unichain assume the deployed code behaves like src/. A method that the owner accepts, such as a reproducible build of this repository compared by hash, is needed to close lens L5.

leads.question: Who controls 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59, the single owner, pauser and blacklister of Soneium USDC.e, and what kind of contract is its 133 byte code?
leads.why: One account can freeze about 517,000 USDC.e at the PoolManager and can change the token's roles. Its threshold and signers decide how likely a freeze or a compromised role is.

leads.question: Do USD₮0, USDG and USDSC have a function that destroys or moves the balance of a blocked or frozen holder, and who holds that role on each chain?
leads.why: A balance destroying function applied to the PoolManager would be a loss for LPs, where a plain freeze is only a lock. Only the existence of isBlocked and isFrozen was confirmed.

leads.question: Which World Chain upgrade activated the Osaka opcodes, does the EIP-7825 gas cap apply there, and does the World Chain node add any execution rule beyond PBH ordering?
leads.why: World Chain runs its own node build and is not in the Upgrade 19 chain list. Only the CLZ probe and the PBH documents were checked.

leads.question: Who controls the L1 addresses behind the L2 ProxyAdmin owners 0x8cc51c3008b3f03fe483b28b8db90e19cf076a6d (Base), 0x5b5a62275df8c60a80d3a25faec5aa7de116b857 (Zora) and 0xb2aa0c2c4fd6bfcbf699d4c787cd6cc0dc461a9d (World Chain)?
leads.why: These owners can replace L2CrossDomainMessenger and L2StandardBridge, which decides who can act as PoolManager owner and who can burn bridged tokens. Only the Optimism governed owner was matched to a documented multisig.

leads.question: For OUSD at 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344, of which the PoolManager holds about 5.34 million, who holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE, who controls the policy 122 admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246, and is policy 122 a blocklist?
leads.why: One account without code can stop every OUSD payout by listing the PoolManager under the sender policy, and a holder of BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE could then burn the balance. RoleGranted logs need an archive endpoint, which the public RPCs refused.

leads.question: Which other B20 tokens does the PoolManager hold, and do tokenised stocks such as AMDC at 0xB2000000000000000000000d8Ce462E99ee7A47B (policy 5 on four scopes, seize exempt policy 129) keep the PoolManager authorised under each bound policy?
leads.why: The two tokens found came from a sample of 50 transfers. The factory emits about 225 creations a day, so a full list needs an indexer. Removing the PoolManager from policy 129 would make its AMDC balance seizable.

leads.question: Who can call addToBlockedList and destroyBlockedFunds on USD₮0 (owner 0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8 on Unichain and 0xc95de55ce5e93f788a1faab2a9c9503f51a5dae2 on Ink), and what are the signers and threshold?
leads.why: The selectors are present in both implementations. A blocked PoolManager could lose about 1.53 million USD₮0 on Ink and 180,760 on Unichain, which turns the stablecoin finding from a freeze into a loss for this token.

leads.question: Do the Karst bundle or any scheduled fork bundle contain upgrade deposits sent from the zero address, and should the owner set protocolFeeController to an inert non zero address on these five chains?
leads.why: The zero address passes the controller check at src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48, and Ecotone and Isthmus used zero address senders for upgrade deposits. A non zero controller removes the dependency at no cost.

leads.question: Does the execution client source (op-reth, and the Reth V2 based client Base adopted at Beryl) reset transient storage at the start of every transaction, including user deposits and network upgrade deposits?
leads.why: The clearance of assumption A1 rests on the deposit specification. The exttload probe by eth_call cannot show leakage between transactions. A stale unlock flag or synced currency carried across a transaction boundary would be a siphon path.

leads.question: Which addresses hold BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE and DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on OUSD and pathUSD, and what kind of account is the policy 2 admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246?
leads.why: It decides how many signers stand between the PoolManager's 426,000 USD of TIP-20 balances and a burn or freeze. An explorer or an archive RPC without the 100,000 block log limit can answer it from RoleMembershipUpdated events.

leads.question: What does the verified source of the USDC implementation at 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6 do in transfer, transferFrom, mint, burn and any rescue function, and can any role other than the proxy admin move or burn the native balance of an arbitrary account?
leads.why: The token contract is the only caller of Native Coin Authority, which can move any native balance. A function that reaches it with a caller-chosen from address would turn the issuer freeze finding into a seizure path that needs no upgrade.

attempts.answer: I read the verified source of NativeFiatTokenV2_2 at 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6. transfer moves msg.sender's balance, transferFrom needs an allowance, permit and the EIP-3009 functions need the owner's signature or an ERC-1271 answer the PoolManager cannot give, burn takes from the calling minter, and rescueERC20 moves only what the token contract holds. No role other than the proxy admin, through an upgrade, can move the native balance of an arbitrary account.

leads.question: How do the PositionManager and Universal Router deployed on Arc handle address(0) and 0x3600 together, for example sweeping native value after an ERC-20 USDC operation, or wrapping and unwrapping steps?
leads.why: Core credits each inflow once, but periphery contracts that read both msg.value and USDC.balanceOf of themselves can double count the shared balance. Funds in transit through those contracts could then be taken by the next caller.

leads.question: After T14 activates on 8 December 2026, what do the ConfigurableAccount precompile at 0xaacc000000000000000000000000000000000000 and accounts with the 0xef marker return for transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address) and the hook selectors when called by the PoolManager?
leads.why: The address is codeless today and becomes a native shim at T14. Each new precompile is a new target for the arbitrary transfer call in take and for hook calls, so the on-chain selector test from this cycle should be repeated after each upgrade.

attempts.answer: T14 is not active on mainnet. The address 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 is still codeless and returns success with empty data for every call shape. The ConfigurableAccount interface in the v1.19.0 source has no transfer, balanceOf or hook function, so the dispatcher should answer those selectors with UnknownFunctionSelector after activation. The on-chain sweep must be repeated after 8 December 2026.

leads.question: Which interpreter does the mainnet release run (revm or evm2 with JIT), where does it clear transient storage between transactions and around block system calls, and what did the EVM execution fix in v1.18.4 change?
leads.why: The PoolManager keeps its lock, deltas and synced reserves in transient storage. A young interpreter with a recent execution fix is the place where TSTORE, TLOAD or MCOPY could differ from Ethereum.

attempts.answer: The mainnet RPC reports v1.19.0 at commit 697ea97, and the manifest at that commit pins evm2 at revision e25a95fb with the JIT crate as a dependency. evm2 clears transient storage in clear_transaction_state on commit, discard, detach and drop of every executed transaction and after system calls. I could not confirm whether the JIT is enabled or what the v1.18.4 fix changed.

leads.question: What is the verified source of the Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver at 0xcfb43dc56b55be9611ded8384201cecf06a9811b (Tempo) and 0xbca30b5429935205037069cf5b8a165f55d05a75 (Arc), and are the Wormhole core contracts they point at the official deployments with the current guardian set?
leads.why: The receiver is the owner of the PoolManager. A receiver bound to an unofficial or outdated core contract would lower the bar for setting a protocol fee controller.

leads.question: What do a liquidity removal and a swap across 50 never-crossed ticks cost in gas on Tempo with storage credits in Refund mode, and how are non-payment transactions ordered when the 30M general budget is full?
leads.why: This cycle estimated gas from the specification. If credits or the reservoir model change what counts against the 30M cap, large swaps or exits could need more splitting than estimated, or a cheap spam campaign could delay exits for longer than a tip auction suggests.

leads.question: When Stablecoin Services ship, will gas payment in EURC or other ERC-20 tokens debit and refund token balances outside normal execution, and can the payer be a contract?
leads.why: A protocol-level fee debit or refund in a pooled ERC-20 is the kind of balance change that sync and settle would credit to whoever is settling.

leads.question: Does the EIP-7825 transaction gas cap of 16,777,216 apply on Arc, given the 30M block gas limit and the Osaka baseline?
leads.why: It sets the largest swap that fits in one transaction. I read the block gas limit on chain and did not confirm the per-transaction cap.

attempts.answer: The Arc EVM tests raise tx_gas_limit_cap explicitly to switch off the EIP-7825 cap, which implies that the default configuration keeps the 16,777,216 gas cap. eth_call accepts 30,000,000 gas, so the RPC does not confirm it. A liquidity removal needs far less than the cap.

leads.question: Who controls 0x79c6631fa15cda38777fb9dd7a6348baee794a4e (DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on OUSD and pathUSD) and 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246 (admin of TIP-403 policy 2)? Both carry the EIP-7702 designator for 0x000000fb7702036ff9f76044a501ac1aa74cbab16b. What does that delegate allow, how many signers or scoped credentials can act for each account, and did pathUSD get any burn or pause role holder at genesis without an event?
leads.why: A read-only simulation shows the first account can grant itself BURN_AT_ROLE and burn the PoolManager balance of either token in two calls, and the second can freeze both tokens at the PoolManager in one call. The log scan found no current holder of a burn or pause role, so these two accounts are the whole distance between about 424,000 USD of pooled stablecoins and a burn or freeze.

leads.question: Do the Universal Router and PositionManager deployed on Tempo take TIP-20 tokens to themselves and forward them, or take straight to the user's recipient, and does either call validateReceivePolicy first?
leads.why: A redirected transfer records its sender as originator. If a router forwards the tokens, the router is the originator, and a receipt with recovery authority address(0) can then be claimed by nobody. That would move the receive policy loss from direct PoolManager users to every user of the periphery.

leads.question: When the USDC pauser pauses the token on Arc, do native value transfers keep working while the ERC-20 face reverts?
leads.why: The EVM differences page lists only the blocklist as a runtime rule on native transfers. If a pause stops 0x3600 and leaves address(0) open, claims in 0x3600 are frozen while claims in address(0) still exit from the same balance, and a pool that pairs the two faces becomes the only way out for 0x3600 holders. An eth_call with a state override on the paused flag can answer it.

attempts.answer: Yes. With the paused bit set by a state override, USDC.transfer from and to the PoolManager reverts with 'Pausable: paused' and a native send from the PoolManager succeeds. The EVM checks only the blocklist on value transfers. Recorded as a variant of F-032.

leads.question: Does an Arc validator that includes its own transactions recover the whole base fee, and how many sync and settle rounds on 0x3600 fit in one 30M gas block?
leads.why: The sub-unit rounding of USDC.balanceOf lets a caller gain just under 10^12 wei of native claims per round. The clearance rests on gas cost, and the base fee is paid to the block beneficiary. The answer bounds what a validator could move per block, which I estimate at a fraction of a cent.

attempts.answer: The per round gain is bounded by 10^12 - 1 base units, 0.000001 USDC, in a model of the source, and each round needs one native send that reaches the PoolManager without a call, one sync, one settle and one native take. With the 20 gwei base fee read at blocks 32,596,992 to 32,597,012, a single 9,000 gas value call already costs 1.8 * 10^14 base units. I did not establish who receives the base fee or measure the gas of a full round, so the number of rounds per block for a proposer remains open. The loss per block cannot exceed the number of rounds times 0.000001 USDC.

leads.question: Where does the block production code of Arc (client arc/v1), Avalanche C-Chain (avalanchego 1.15.3), HyperEVM, X Layer (xlayer-reth v0.0.7) and World Chain (world-chain v2.8.2) discard transient storage between two transactions of one block, and does an RPC provider that offers eth_simulateV1 or eth_callMany for these chains return zero from TLOAD in a transaction that follows one that ran TSTORE on the same contract?
leads.why: sync needs no unlock and leaves the synced currency and reserves in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). If those two slots survived into a later transaction, any account could sync a token, wait for other users' deposits and settle the whole increase to itself (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). That would be a critical siphon. On 2026-11-22 the critic ran a read only two transaction simulation with a state override contract. The second transaction read zero on 13 endpoints through eth_simulateV1 (chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 130, 7777777, 57073, 1868, 42161, 4663, 99901, 137, 56, 4217) and on MegaETH through eth_callMany. The endpoints of these five chains and of Celo and Monad refuse both methods. Celo and Monad have a client source reading from this cycle. Arc has none, Avalanche rests on documentation, World Chain and X Layer rest on the OP Stack deposit text, and the HyperEVM clearance uses a replay client that does not model the AQAv2 system transactions. A simulation shows the RPC path only, so the place in the source is still needed.

attempts.answer: For X Layer only. The executor and the flashblocks builder run each transaction with Evm::transact, which ends in the journal's finalize, and finalize, commit_tx and discard_tx clear transient storage. The two X Layer system calls are finalized or discarded before the user transaction runs. The other four chains of this lead belong to other units.

leads.question: Does HyperCore require a signature or a CoreWriter action from the EVM address that becomes the sender of an AQAv2 system transaction, or can a treasury deployer name any EVM address, including a contract that cannot sign?
leads.why: This one fact settles the plausible finding on unsigned system transactions. If the address must consent, the PoolManager can never be a sender and the finding drops to info. If an address can be named, a system transaction could call transfer on a token with the PoolManager as msg.sender and lower its balance with no take and no delta (assumptions A2 and A8, src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The researcher and the verifier each asked part of this. The exchange API description of authorizeAqav2Role and one observed AQAv2 sender traced back to its authorisation answer it.

attempts.answer: No requirement of a signature or CoreWriter action from the sender address was found in the docs, and the USDC treasury address has never existed as a HyperCore user. The CoreWriter action table (ids 1 to 17) has no AQAv2 action. This points toward designation without a HyperCore side action by the address, and it does not rule out an EVM side proof of control.

leads.question: On Robinhood Chain, what does each of the 6,234 entries added by the filterer account identify (a transaction hash, a sender, or any address touched during execution), is the list provider automated, and can an ordinary account cause an entry or a rule to match transactions that call the PoolManager 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951, for example by sending funds from a restricted address through a pool or by creating a pool whose hook or token touches a restricted address?
leads.why: The confirmed filtering finding assumes the operator has to act against the PoolManager. All pools, claims and protocol fees sit at one address (assumption A6), and the filter also fails force included transactions. If entries match addresses touched in execution and are added by an automated provider, a third party could make every exit through the shared address fail without holding any role, which would move the finding from the operator class to the unprivileged class.

attempts.answer: Each entry identifies one transaction hash, never a sender or a contract. The provider side is automated: the sequencer reports a filtered delayed transaction and the filterer service adds its hash, which matches a median gap of 10 blocks and one hash that a loop added 4,741 times on 2026-07-15. An ordinary account cannot cause an entry or a rule to match transactions of others that call the PoolManager, for the reasons given under L-315. The finding F-001 stays in the operator class.

leads.question: Without a compiler, does the source text satisfy every concrete expectation in the repository tests that no unit has replayed yet: test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol, Position.t.sol, TickBitmap.t.sol, SafeCast.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol, LPFeeLibrary.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol and BitMath.t.sol, test/CustomAccounting.t.sol, ERC6909Claims.t.sol, ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, PoolManager.clear.t.sol, PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol, NoDelegateCall.t.sol and DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, and the expectRevert cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol?
leads.why: The organisers say this build contains at least one path to frozen or siphoned funds, and no unit found one that an ordinary account can use. Both source readers worked from the text and replayed the vectors of SwapMath, SqrtPriceMath, Tick and TickMath and parts of the DynamicFees, Sync and PoolManager tests. They found one fuzz condition that the source does not meet, for a zero amount at a 100 percent fee (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-320), and one boundary where test and source differ (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:143 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:328). A test whose expected value or revert the source cannot produce marks a place where the source departs from what its own tests describe. The check uses only files in this repository and compares nothing with another copy.

attempts.answer: Covered in this unit and all satisfied by the source text: test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol, Position.t.sol and SafeCast.t.sol, the modifyLiquidity fuzz conditions of test/libraries/Pool.t.sol, the salt tests and the two fixed cases of test/ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, and the modifyLiquidity and donate cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol.
