Not covered here: Hooks.t.sol, LPFeeLibrary.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol, BitMath.t.sol, CustomAccounting.t.sol, ERC6909Claims.t.sol, PoolManager.clear.t.sol, PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol, NoDelegateCall.t.sol, DynamicReturnFees.t.sol and the remaining expectRevert cases of PoolManager.t.sol. The JavaScript reference used by the ffi fuzz test in ModifyLiquidity.t.sol was not run.

I replayed the parts that belong to the swap path in a transcription of the source and found no expectation that the source text fails. Covered: the 19 fixed cases and both fuzz properties of test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol; the fixed values and fuzz identities of test/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.t.sol and test/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.t.sol; the swap section of test/CustomAccounting.t.sol (lines 73-266), including the constants maxPossibleIn -6018336102428409 and maxPossibleOut 5981737760509662 and the revert conditions for HookDeltaExceedsSwapAmount and SwapAmountCannotBeZero; the swap cases of test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol; the Swap event values and the protocol fee fuzz of test/DynamicFees.t.sol and test/PoolManager.t.sol (lines 496-506, 589-611, 779-818); and the bit index functions of BitMath for every single bit value and random values, which is a property check and does not replay test/libraries/BitMath.t.sol. Not covered by this unit: test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol, Position.t.sol, SafeCast.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol and FullMath.t.sol, the liquidity section of CustomAccounting.t.sol, ERC6909Claims.t.sol, ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, PoolManager.clear.t.sol, PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol, NoDelegateCall.t.sol and the remaining expectRevert cases of PoolManager.t.sol.

For the bit level files and the revert cases I found no expectation that the source text fails. Covered by reading and, where numeric, by transcription: test/types/Slot0.t.sol, test/types/BalanceDelta.t.sol, test/CurrencyReserves.t.sol, test/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.t.sol, test/libraries/PoolId.t.sol, the revert bounds of test/libraries/SafeCast.t.sol, the validity and permission cases of test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:191-990, the revert order of test/PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol:55-85 and its fixed cases, test/PoolManager.clear.t.sol, test/NoDelegateCall.t.sol, the expectRevert cases of test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol and of test/PoolManager.t.sol:96-1039. Not covered by this unit: the hook call sequences in test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:46-190 and 992-1046 beyond their revert selectors, test/libraries/FullMath.t.sol and Position.t.sol, test/ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, the liquidity section of test/CustomAccounting.t.sol and the value assertions of test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol. I read the tests and did not run them.

Partly answered. The settlement related tests agree with the source text: test/Sync.t.sol, test/PoolManager.clear.t.sol, test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol and the take, settle, mint, burn, fee collection and unlock cases at test/PoolManager.t.sol:917-1039 and 1173-1189. The other files named in the lead were not replayed by this unit.

leads.question: Which functions of the B20 token precompile, the B20 factory 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000 and the Policy Registry 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000002 can an account with no role call, and can any of them change balanceOf of another holder, make a transfer to or from the PoolManager return true while the tokens are held or sent elsewhere, or change the PoolManager's membership in a policy that a pooled token references?
leads.why: The cycle read the issuer roles of B20 and did not list what an ordinary account can do. The PoolManager holds about 5.34 million OUSD, and settle credits any rise of balanceOf since sync to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). Currency.transfer accepts any call that returns true (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). On Tempo a transfer that the recipient's receive policy rejects returns true and parks the tokens in a guard contract, which is a confirmed medium finding there. A similar rule in B20, or a balance component that a third party can add and later remove, would give a credit that is not backed or a payout that does not arrive. The B20 rules also changed at the Cobalt and Denim forks, so the documentation of the current fork must be used.

leads.question: Which tokens make up the twenty largest balances of the Arbitrum One PoolManager 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32, and for each one: who can freeze, seize, pause or upgrade it, does USDT0 there carry destroyBlockedFunds, and does any function that an ordinary account can call change balanceOf(PoolManager) without a transfer (rebase, reward claim for a holder, reflection)?
leads.why: The issuer control finding is confirmed on eleven chains and nobody checked Arbitrum One. The second half of the question looks for the unprivileged case: a balance rise between sync and settle is credited to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and a balance drop without a take leaves pools short (assumption A2).

leads.question: For the twenty largest token balances of the PoolManager on Polygon and on Avalanche, who holds freeze, seize, pause and upgrade roles, and can an ordinary account change balanceOf(PoolManager) of any of them without a transfer? Should the cleared item on Circle USDC for these two chains become part of the issuer finding?
leads.why: The unit recorded the USDC blocklist on these chains as cleared while five other units rate the same hazard high, and it listed no other pooled asset. The rebasing stETH finding on Ethereum shows that balances which move without transfers do sit in the PoolManager. PoS bridged tokens on Polygon and bridged tokens on Avalanche have their own mint and upgrade paths.

leads.question: Which tokens does the PoolManager hold on OP Mainnet, Zora and World Chain beyond the main stablecoins, and does any of them have issuer controls or a balance that an ordinary account can change without a transfer?
leads.why: The three profiles repeat the generic OP Stack text for this lens, and Zora has no delta of high relevance at all. The stablecoin finding of this unit covers six chains and leaves Zora out without saying why.

leads.question: Does USDG on Ink (0xe343167631d89B6Ffc58B88d6b7fB0228795491D, about 767,000 held by the PoolManager) use the claimable rewards design that the verifier found in USDG on Robinhood Chain, is the PoolManager registered in a payout group or named as a claim destination, and who can trigger a claim?
leads.why: On Robinhood Chain balanceOf excludes unclaimed rewards and a claim moves tokens from a claim source to a destination without a call by the destination. A claim that credits the PoolManager between a caller's sync and settle is booked to that caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). If any account can trigger such a claim, rewards meant for the PoolManager's balance can be taken by whoever times the call. The op-stack-eth verifier could not find where the freeze logic of USDG on Ink lives, so the implementation there is unread.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain on 2026-12-08, does any CAS20 token or reserved address expose the native BNB balance of an account through balanceOf and transfer? On Base, does any B20 token, precompile or planned Base Transactions fee token expose native ETH in the same way?
leads.why: A second face of the native asset is confirmed on Celo, Arc, Polygon, OP Mainnet and Zora, and the code handles it only because settle rejects msg.value while a token is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356). Each new face is a new currency id that shares the native balance, and its transfer and balanceOf rules decide whether the two ledgers stay jointly covered. Both chains are adding token logic that runs in the node, and nobody asked this question for them.

attempts.answer: BNB Smart Chain part: no. No CAS20 token, singleton or reserved address reads or moves a native BNB balance, all of them reject value, and 0x70 returns a timestamp. BNB gets no second face from Jenner. The Base part of the lead belongs to another unit and was not examined.

leads.question: On Elysium, which contracts on HyperEVM hold the rollup's inbox, bridge escrow and assertion logic, does a delayed inbox message and a forced inclusion call fit into a 3,000,000 gas HyperEVM block, and can HyperCore system transactions move tokens held by the bridge escrow?
leads.why: Elysium settles to HyperEVM. Every hazard recorded for HyperEVM (small blocks, system transactions that move token balances, the bridge to HyperCore) applies to the parent chain contracts that back all bridged assets in Elysium pools and to the only exit that does not depend on the single sequencer. The unit treated Elysium as stock Nitro and did not look at the parent chain.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the system contracts of BNB Smart Chain (0x1000 to 0x1008, 0x2000 to 0x2006, 0x3000), of Polygon (0x1000, 0x1001) and every precompile address in the Avalanche C-Chain client source return for transfer(address,uint256) with zero and nonzero amount, balanceOf(PoolManager), each IHooks selector and empty calldata with zero value?
leads.why: take makes the PoolManager call transfer on any address the caller names, sync makes it call balanceOf, and initialize makes it call hook selectors (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). The sweep was done on Ethereum, the Arbitrum chains, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM. On these three chains only 0x1010 on Polygon was tested and the Avalanche list came from documentation. A target that returns true or empty data to transfer, or a changing number to balanceOf, needs a follow up.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the predeploys 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff, the Base registries 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000001 and 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000002 and the World Chain PBH contracts return for transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(PoolManager) and empty calldata with zero value, and what does a native take with value to L2ToL1MessagePasser 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016 do?
leads.why: The unit tested predeploys as hook addresses and tested WETH and LegacyERC20ETH as currencies. The full sweep with the currency call shapes is not recorded. The message passer has a receive function that calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data) (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/develop/packages/contracts-bedrock/src/L2/L2ToL1MessagePasser.sol, lines 60 to 62), and an eth_call with from set to the PoolManager, value 1 wei and empty calldata succeeds on OP Mainnet and Base. A native take to it would send the amount to the PoolManager's own address on L1, which is the same pattern as the confirmed HyperEVM finding on payouts to the HyperCore bridge address. The caller is debited the amount (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the expected result is a loss for the caller only, and that should be confirmed.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the OP Stack predeploys on Celo and X Layer, the Celo core contracts LockedGold and FeeHandler, the transfer precompile at 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000fd and the X Layer gasless whitelist contract return for transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(PoolManager), each IHooks selector and empty calldata with zero value?
leads.why: Same sweep as on the other chains. On Celo the CELO token and the fee currencies were tested, and the critic tested the four fee currency adapters, which answer balanceOf and revert on transfer. The other system contracts on both chains have no recorded test. Celo's native asset can be moved by contract calls through a precompile, so a second caller path into that precompile would matter for every native pool (assumption A3).

attempts.answer: The sweep ran on 365 Celo addresses and 302 X Layer addresses with the P1, P2, P3 and P5 call shapes. Results are in the three sweep items of the cleared list and in the low finding on native payouts. LockedGold reverts on every shape, FeeHandler accepts every shape and returns nothing, 0xfd rejects every call from the PoolManager, and the X Layer gasless whitelist and blacklist revert on transfer, balanceOf and hook selectors.

leads.question: Do the Karst bundle or any fork bundle scheduled for Celo and X Layer contain upgrade deposits sent from the zero address, and does failedMessages of the L2CrossDomainMessenger on either chain hold a message from the Ethereum timelock that anyone could replay?
leads.why: protocolFeeController is the zero address on both chains. Two verifiers rejected the clearance of the zero sender on the other OP Stack chains because the Ecotone and Isthmus bundles used zero address senders, and the clearance for Celo and X Layer did not consider this. The replay question transfers the Polygon lead on failed state syncs: a stale governance message that failed on first delivery could restore an old controller. The reach in both cases is the protocol fee (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-57).

leads.question: Do the X Layer release notes, node configuration published by OKX or operator statements show the risk control filter enabled on the mainnet sequencer, and is there a valid transaction to 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32 or to a pooled token that was visible to other nodes and stayed unincluded?
leads.why: This one fact settles the plausible finding on the X Layer filter. If the filter is off, the finding is a dormant capability and stays low. If it is on with a rule that can match the PoolManager, the verdict says medium applies.

attempts.answer: No operator statement or node configuration was found. The release notes of xlayer/v0.1.7 and v0.0.7.3 do not mention the filter state. The deposit blacklist found in this cycle is active by construction for chain id 196 and does not depend on a node flag.

leads.question: Has any transaction that touches a contract on the Soneium restriction list been included after it was submitted through an RPC endpoint not run by the operator?
leads.why: The Soneium finding is confirmed with secondary evidence for blocking at the sequencer. The primary source describes blocking at the RPC only. One included transaction shows the block is at the RPC, and then any other endpoint is enough and the L1 route is not needed.

leads.question: On Tempo and Arc, does any protocol rule read an account's token or native balance during a transaction and grant something that lasts beyond it (fee sponsorship, payment lane access, validator or channel deposits, storage credits), so that tokens taken from the PoolManager for the length of one unlock have value?
leads.why: take hands out any pooled balance before payment, and the only condition is that deltas net to zero when unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-297). Assumption A5 was tested on Ethereum, Celo and HyperEVM. The two chains whose protocol is built around stablecoin balances were not asked.

attempts.answer: No rule found on either chain that reads a balance inside a transaction and grants something that outlasts it. Fees are debited before execution, payment lane status depends on the calls, storage credits depend on cleared slots, and neither chain stakes pooled tokens.

leads.question: What does it cost in each currency to fill the lowest and the highest usable tick of a pool to tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick for tick spacings 1, 60 and 200, and is there a deployed hook or vault that must add a position on those ticks inside its withdrawal path, so that a full tick blocks an exit?
leads.why: The accounting unit computed about 1.9e12 base units at spacing 60 and filed the result under cleared because removals are never gated by the cap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:165-173). Blocking deposits alone is griefing. It becomes a freeze only for a contract that has to add liquidity on a full tick before it can pay out. The numbers were not checked by the verifier.

attempts.answer: Cost to fill the highest usable tick to the cap with a range one spacing wide, in base units of currency0: 519,766,372 at spacing 1, 1,878,783,905,959 at spacing 60 and 20,966,766,746,469 at spacing 200. Cost at the lowest usable tick, in base units of currency1: 519,766,206, 1,878,783,895,257 and 20,966,766,629,403. The figures come from a transcription of the source and were reproduced to the wei by eth_call through the PositionManager on 20 networks. The cost does not depend on the pool price. Recorded as the low finding in this file. Second half: no deployed contract was found that must add on those ticks in its exit path. The Zora coin hook adds liquidity inside afterSwap, but next to the current tick, where the fill cost exceeds the token supply. The search for other vaults and hooks is carried forward as a lead.

leads.question: Once the announced ArbOS upgrade activates on Elysium, what do the HyperCore read precompile and the ElysiumCoreWriter predeploy return to the PoolManager call shapes: does the predeploy accept HYPE with empty calldata and credit a gas escrow to msg.sender, does it answer balanceOf(address) or transfer(address,uint256), and are result callbacks delivered as ordinary transactions?
leads.why: A predeploy that credits an escrow on plain value and reports it through balanceOf would be a new face of HYPE reachable through take, sync and settle. A callback made outside an ordinary transaction would change the transient storage boundary. The upgrade is expected around 2026-12-07 and getScheduledUpgrade() will show it first.

attempts.answer: The upgrade is still not scheduled: getScheduledUpgrade() returns zeros on mainnet and on the testnet 99801, both report ArbOS 61, and a code scan of both shows the stock precompile set only. The documentation pages, last updated 2026-09-21 and 2026-11-02, give no address, selector or funding function for the read precompile or the ElysiumCoreWriter predeploy. They say a dapp prefunds a HYPE gas escrow on the predeploy and that outcomes are delivered back to the originating contract, without saying how either is done. The three questions of the lead cannot be answered before the code is on a chain. The lead stays open and should be re-run when getScheduledUpgrade() changes. Until the new ArbOS version activates, a precompile address registered for it answers as an address without code.

Still not answerable on 2026-11-23. getScheduledUpgrade() returns zeros on Elysium mainnet and on the testnet 99801, both report ArbOS 61, and the two documentation pages are unchanged since 2026-11-02 and 2026-09-21. They give no address, selector or funding function for the read precompile or the ElysiumCoreWriter predeploy. The lead should be re-run when getScheduledUpgrade() changes.

leads.question: Does the Conduit G2 sequencer that produces Elysium blocks execute transactions with the Nitro state transition code, and which commit is the locally built RPC binary?
leads.why: All opcode and precompile results for Elysium come from the RPC node. The documentation names a separate sequencer stack. A sequencer that differs in transient storage or call handling would produce blocks that the probes of this cycle do not describe.

attempts.answer: The Elysium rollup pins the official consensus-v61 module root, the same as Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain, so the accepted state follows stock ArbOS 61 regardless of the sequencer stack. The commit of the locally built RPC binary could not be identified.

leads.question: The Elysium Outbox on HyperEVM executes child chain messages as calls made by the Bridge contract, which holds 298,480 HYPE. What happens when such a call targets a HyperCore system address or the HyperEVM CoreWriter: is the Bridge credited a HyperCore balance, and can a later message move it?
leads.why: The Bridge balance backs all HYPE on Elysium, including the 9,751 HYPE in the PoolManager. HyperEVM gives every address a HyperCore account that system contracts act on by msg.sender, which the stock Nitro bridge was not designed around. I did not fetch HyperEVM sources for this in this cycle.

attempts.answer: A call from the Bridge to the HYPE system address credits a HyperCore account of the Bridge, and a later message can make the Bridge move that HyperCore balance through CoreWriter. The amount is what the withdrawing account sent there, so only that account loses. The native HYPE held by the Bridge on HyperEVM leaves only with outbox calls whose value was burned on Elysium. The Bridge has no HyperCore account today. A lead covers the untested finalize action.

leads.question: Which currencies and hooks do the more than 10,000 pools on Elysium use, and do any of the larger PoolManager balances belong to tokens with rebasing, fee on transfer or issuer controls?
leads.why: The pool count after 13 days points to launchpad tokens and hook based pools. This cycle looked only at HYPE, WHYPE and USDC.

attempts.answer: The pools use 129,516 currencies. Native HYPE is a currency in 124,372 pools, followed by WHYPE, KNTQ, bridged USDC, wNVDAx, VOLTA and xyz:NVDA3L. The cycle 4 reconcile found no currency whose PoolManager balance moved without matching Transfer logs, and the cycle 5 transfer test found 21 tokens with unusual transfers, with ELO recorded in F-059. The larger balances read in this cycle (9,964 HYPE, 14,726 WHYPE, 3.32M KNTQ, 193,719 USDC, 175.6 wNVDAx, 68,227 xyz:NVDA3L) show no rebase or transfer fee. Their issuer side controls (proxy upgrade of WHYPE, bridge minting, the minter of the leveraged token) were not read in depth and belong to the issuer class.

leads.question: Which event rules and which restricted list does the Robinhood Chain sequencer run with, and does the list contain or exempt the PoolManager 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951, the routers and Permit2?
leads.why: The client source shows that a rule matches on 4 bytes of topic 0 from any contract and that the list is an off-chain hash file. Whether a widely used contract could be listed, by the provider or by a rule that reads a topic as an address, cannot be seen from the chain.

attempts.answer: The event rules and the restricted list are files on the sequencer and are not on chain. What can be seen: the documentation names ERC-20, ERC-721 and ERC-1155 transfer events and the opcodes CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 and SELFDESTRUCT; 144 filtered transactions carry the restricted wallet only in calldata, for example as the recipient of a token transfer sent by an unrelated account, which fits a rule on the ERC-20 Transfer event; the filtering start time is 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC and the filtered funds recipient is 0xbbbd433db8700d8927faaaaf482e007e293ed568. No filtered transaction ever had the PoolManager, the PositionManager, a Universal Router, the Quoter or Permit2 as recipient or in calldata, and swaps through them execute daily, so none of them is on the list today. Whether a rule exists for the claim event 0x1b3d7edb, and whether any contract is exempt, cannot be read from outside.

leads.question: What are the twenty largest token balances of the Arbitrum One PoolManager from an indexer, and what is the token that reports symbol xUSD at 0xe80772Eaf6e2E18B651F160Bc9158b2A5caFCA65?
leads.why: This cycle classified 29 addresses chosen by hand because the Blockscout token list was not reachable. A rebasing or reflection token with a larger balance, or one whose rebase can be triggered by anyone inside a transaction, would change the low rating of the aToken finding.

attempts.answer: Ranking by value from live balances and the cycle 5 price list, which stands in for an indexer and covers the 845 priced currencies: USDC, WBTC, USDG, Dinari USD+, cbBTC, USDT0, VSN, ARB, ESP, DOT, PENDLE, UNI, LINK, wstETH, WOO, AAVE, wSOL, HDN, WETH and EQB, with 4,425.84 native ETH beside them. USDG (1.71M) and Dinari USD+ (1.07M, 34.4 percent of supply, share based with an operator moved index and a transfer restrictor) were missing from F-036 and are added by the finding of this cycle. The token that reports xUSD at 0xe80772Eaf6e2E18B651F160Bc9158b2A5caFCA65 is a rebasing token with credits per token accounting, and the PoolManager holds 62.35 units that follow rebases, which is too little to change the low rating of F-037. Two entries of the price list, Varlamore USDC Growth and EVA, have prices I did not confirm, and a lead covers them.

leads.question: What is the full facet table of USDG at 0x5fc5360D0400a0Fd4f2af552ADD042D716F1d168, and what do the values returned by globalTransferSettings() restrict?
leads.why: A facet that credits balances without a transfer, or a global transfer limit that applies to the PoolManager, would touch the balance assumptions for 16.8M USDG. Twenty candidate names were tried and the setting semantics are unknown.

leads.question: Were any hand-crafted Stylus programs activated before the pause on 2026-10-02, and can new contracts with the same code hash still be deployed and called?
leads.why: The Security Council report ties the known liveness bugs to hand-crafted programs. Activation is closed, but an activation covers every contract with the same code. A liveness attack would stop exits from the PoolManager for its duration.

leads.question: Which go-ethereum commit does the build nitro v3.13.0-rc.9+b72783f pin, and do StartTxHook, StateDB.Prepare, the precompile dispatcher and the precompile registry in that build match what was read at v3.11.3 and commit f3a966e?
leads.why: Both public endpoints report v3.13.0-rc.9 built on 2026-11-16, and the research read the source of v3.11.3. The tag did not resolve on raw.githubusercontent.com in this session. The on-chain probes agree with the older source, yet a new precompile or a changed transaction hook in the running build would not show in a sweep of known addresses.

leads.question: Who can call the payout function of the exchanger behind xUSD at 0xe80772Eaf6e2E18B651F160Bc9158b2A5caFCA65, and can the call be made from a contract inside one transaction?
leads.why: xUSD is a credit based rebasing token: it answers rebasingCreditsPerTokenHighres() and creditsBalanceOf(address), the PoolManager is in the rebasing state, and changeSupply(uint256) reverts with 'Caller is not the EXCHANGER'. If any account can trigger the supply change, that account can call sync before it and settle after it and take the PoolManager's share of the rebase (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-364). The PoolManager holds 62.35 xUSD today, so the amount at risk is small. The role is not enumerable and I did not find the exchanger address.

leads.question: Who controls the proxy contract 0xce4ceced412aa9359840c7d52bbd99827a5d42b9 that owns the beacon 0x659f40efd07d70224b7ac61e4721f6f3e11b625e of the standard bridged tokens on Elysium?
leads.why: The beacon owner can replace the logic of Elysium USDC and of every other standard gateway representation in one call. The PoolManager holds 182,936 USDC of this kind. This is a governance class control that the research file does not record.

leads.question: Which deployed vaults or hooks on the 21 networks keep a position whose tickLower or tickUpper is the lowest or highest usable tick and call modifyLiquidity with a positive delta inside their withdrawal path or inside a swap hook, for example to reinvest fees before paying out?
leads.why: Filling such a tick to the cap costs dust (519,766,372 base units at spacing 1, 1,878,783,905,959 at spacing 60). For a contract of that kind the fill turns from a blocked deposit into blocked withdrawals or blocked swaps until the filler removes its position. The Zora coin hook was checked and adds near the current tick, where the fill is out of reach.

attempts.answer: For Celo and X Layer only, and for the pools GeckoTerminal lists. Celo: 20 pools, none with a hook. X Layer: 110 pools with seven hook addresses, none of which contains the modifyLiquidity or unlock selector. No hook there adds liquidity in a swap or withdrawal path. Vaults that hold positions through the PositionManager were not searched.

leads.question: On Tempo, does an add that is paid in a TIP-20 currency cost exactly the amount the source formulas give, for example 519766372 base units for the highest tick at spacing 1? The check needs an account with a TIP-20 balance and a Permit2 allowance, or an eth_call with a state override of the TIP-20 balance.
leads.why: Tempo is the only network where the liquidity path could not be probed with a payment, because the node rejects calls that carry value. Its client uses a separate execution engine, and the stablecoin unit has an open question on whether a JIT backend is active.

attempts.answer: Yes. 288 liquidity adds on 12 hookless pathUSD, OUSD and USDC.e pools were simulated with a payer that held real TIP-20 balances by state override. Each unlock completes when exactly the amounts of the transcribed source formulas are transferred and reverts with CurrencyNotSettled when one unit less is paid. That includes the highest and lowest usable tick pairs at spacings 1 to 5000 and the liquidity value 519,766,372,000. Add followed by remove leaves 0 or 1 unit of debt per currency.

leads.question: Has any pool with meaningful liquidity already had its lowest or highest usable tick filled to the cap? Read liquidityGross of both boundary ticks for the largest pools of each network through extsload and compare with tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick.
leads.why: The fill is cheap and silent. On Ethereum the two largest ETH/USDC pools and the ETH/USDT 0.05 percent pool were clean at block 26471794. Other pools and networks were not read.

leads.question: With the deployed PoolManager bytecode on HyperEVM, what do debug_traceCall or eth_estimateGas report for one empty bitmap word and for one initialized tick crossing in Pool.swap, and which price limit do the Universal Router and the other routers deployed there pass to swap?
leads.why: The finding of this unit gives upper bounds of about 59 to 200 crossings and about 1,283 empty words per 3,000,000 gas, derived from repository snapshots and gas constants. Measured values decide how small a price move an attacker can force into several transactions, and a router that always passes the extreme limit turns a swap that exceeds the liquidity on its side into an out of gas failure.

attempts.answer: Measured with debug_traceCall on the deployed PoolManager: 5,871 gas per empty bitmap word, 39,059 gas fixed for the swap frame, 10,917 to 31,243 gas per tick crossing, about 60,500 gas for a liquidity removal. A small block fits about 504 empty words where F-039 estimated 1,283. Universal Router 2.1.2 and seven other callers pass the extreme price limit and one caller passes its own. Recorded as a finding that extends F-039.

leads.question: Does a swap in a pool with tick spacing 1 that runs from tick 0 to the extreme price limit through empty words (3,468 loop iterations in my transcription, at least 7,775,256 gas from the bitmap reads alone) fit under the 16,777,216 gas cap per transaction of EIP-7825, if that cap is active, and how many initialized spacing 1 pools sit more than that many words away from the nearest position?
leads.why: A pool created by a third party at an extreme price has to be walked to the market price with swaps that take no tokens. If one transaction cannot cover the distance the walk needs several, and a pool id that people expect to use stays unusable until somebody pays for them.

leads.question: Can native USDC reach the Arc PoolManager without a call into it, for example as the beneficiary of SELFDESTRUCT, as a block reward recipient or through a system credit, while 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 is the synced currency?
leads.why: The ERC-20 face reports floor(native / 1e12). In my model of sync and settle a native amount that arrives without a call between sync(0x3600...) and settle is rounded up to one whole unit of the face, which gains up to 1e12 - 1 base units per round at the cost of other holders of native claims. The gain is below 0.000001 USDC per round, so it matters only if a round can be repeated at almost no gas cost. This adds the mechanism to lead L-114.

leads.question: When this checkout is compiled with solc 0.8.26 and the foundry.toml settings, does the optimized Yul of PoolManager.swap, modifyLiquidity and the ABI coders contain a variable that is reassigned in a loop or branch and then used with two different constant offsets as a memory or storage address, as the Solidity team's reproducer test reassigned_offset_base.yul does?
leads.why: The source level screen of this unit covers only the handwritten assembly. The Solidity team says the condition for SOL-2026-7 depends on the intermediate Yul code. A positive answer would mean a stale load or a dropped store in code that moves pool funds on all 21 networks. It needs a compiler and can be done on this repository alone, with --ir-optimized output, without any other copy.

attempts.answer: Not answered. The lead needs the optimized Yul from solc 0.8.26, and this environment has neither solc nor forge and the rules forbid installing them.

leads.question: Does this checkout produce identical PoolManager bytecode, apart from the metadata hash, when compiled with the foundry.toml settings by solc built at commit ce5702db (last commit before the fix of SOL-2026-7) and at commit 00d5ee65 (the fix)?
leads.why: The Solidity team names this comparison as the decisive test for the Yul optimizer bug in 0.8.19 to 0.8.37. The build uses 0.8.26 with via-IR and the optimizer, so it is in the affected range, and a source level screen cannot settle it. A difference would mean a stale load or a dropped store in code that moves pool funds on all 21 networks. The test compiles this repository twice and compares no other copy of the code. It refines lead L-028.

leads.question: Does any precompile, system contract or execution feature on these networks run code inside a call that is already in progress in a context whose transient storage is separate from the caller's, while its token transfers and storage writes are kept? Two shapes matter. In the first the inner context starts from a copy of the outer transient storage and its transient writes are dropped on return. In the second it starts empty and its final transient values are written back over the outer ones.
leads.why: unlock is one call frame, so no batching at transaction level can split it, and only a mechanism that acts inside a running call can separate deltas from payouts. In the first shape a take made in the inner context moves tokens and leaves no debit (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). In the second shape an inner unlock ends by writing zero to the counter and the flag (src/PoolManager.sol:112-113, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:28-34), which lets an outer unlock return with an open debit. Either would expose every token the PoolManager holds to any account. Two candidates are answered: the MegaETH KeylessDeploy sandbox runs only as a top level call, and the Arc CallFrom child is an ordinary frame on the parent journal. Candidates that no unit has read in client source for this exact property: Tempo precompiles that call out to contracts, Stylus programs on the Arbitrum family, HyperEVM system calls and CoreWriter, the Celo fee currency calls, and the parallel executors of Monad, Polygon and Avalanche.

attempts.answer: Neither shape exists on the Nitro chains. Stylus programs use the same StateDB transient map and the same call path as EVM code (arbos/programs/api.go lines 119 to 128 and 186 to 190 at v3.12.4), and a retryable redeem requested inside a call runs later as a transaction of its own. See the cleared item on L-153 and L-202.

leads.question: Is the 20 gwei base fee seen on Arc a protocol minimum, who receives it, and can it be changed without a hard fork? If the fee per gas could fall below about 0.03 gwei, or a block proposer recovered the base fee of its own transactions, how many rounds of sync on 0x3600, forced native send, settle and native take fit in one 30,000,000 gas block?
leads.why: Each round of the scaled face sequence nets less than 10^12 base units, which is 0.000001 USDC, and today a single value call costs about 180 times that. The loss to pools is bounded by the number of rounds times 0.000001 USDC, so the answer decides whether the item stays a rounding curiosity for a block proposer as well.

leads.question: For each currency with a large balance at each PoolManager, does a second contract address exist whose balanceOf(PoolManager) is derived from the same underlying balance in a different unit or at a rate, and whose transfer(address,uint256) works when the PoolManager is the caller? For each such pair, what is the largest value of one unit of rounding and can the finer side be moved in amounts below one unit of the coarser side?
leads.why: The model shows that a second face is harmless when it is one to one or cannot transfer, and that a scaled face with a working transfer yields up to one coarse unit minus one fine unit per bracket whenever the fine side can be moved while the coarse side is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). On Arc that unit is 0.000001 USDC. A pair with a valuable unit, such as a whole token face over an 18 decimal balance or a share face over an asset balance with a public rate change, would turn the same sequence into a real loss. The hyperevm unit found one share and asset pair (stHYPE and wstHYPE). The other networks have no survey.

leads.question: On each network, do the deployed routers and position managers call sync(address(0)) before a native settle, and can operations of different users run inside one transaction there (ERC-4337 EntryPoint bundles, sponsored or batched transaction types)?
leads.why: sync needs no lock and its two transient slots survive until the transaction ends (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). An ERC-20 sync left by an earlier operation in the same transaction makes a later settle with msg.value revert with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356), and the comment at line 348 says integrators should sync first. The settlement unit cleared the stale sync for a transaction of one party. With several users in one transaction the effect on the later user is a reverted operation and lost gas, with no transfer of funds, so this is a griefing path against native payers whose router skips the sync.

attempts.answer: The canonical routers and the PositionManager call sync(address(0)) before a native settle on all 21 networks. Operations of different users do run in one transaction on every network at the contract level: the four EntryPoints, Multicall3 and Simple7702Account hold code on all 21, and bundles of two or three operations with PoolManager swaps were seen on World Chain, Soneium and Base. Several third party routers settle value without sync and revert after a stale sync, which is recorded as a low finding.

leads.question: Where does the opcode fusion feature of pull 3395 (super-instructions) live in the BSC client that validators run today, which opcode sequences does it fuse, and does the deployed PoolManager bytecode at 0x28e2ea090877bf75740558f6bfb36a5ffee9e9df give the same results with the feature on and off for unlock, sync, settle, take, swap and modifyLiquidity?
leads.why: The changelog records a bad block and a stack bound fix for this feature in v1.7.1. A fused sequence that mishandles one opcode pattern in the PoolManager would change deltas or the lock for every caller. The interpreter files read on master show no such code, so the feature was not reviewed.

attempts.answer: The superinstruction feature was removed from the client in v1.8.0-alpha (pull 3759) and cannot run on any validator after Jenner, for which v1.8.2 is mandatory. Until then validators on v1.7.x may still run it. 420 Quoter simulations through the deployed PoolManager at one block gave 409 identical answers on Geth v1.8.2, Geth v1.7.8 and reth-bsc, and the remaining 11 were rate limited on one endpoint and identical on the other two. Open parts: whether the v1.7.8 endpoint has the optimisation enabled, and the list of fused sequences, since the v1.7 source was not read.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on 2026-12-08, what do the millisecond timestamp precompile 0x70 and an uncreated address in the 0xCA52 range return to transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address) and the afterSwap, beforeDonate and afterDonate selectors when the PoolManager is the caller?
leads.why: 0x70 has a valid hook flag combination and will answer calls with a changing number. If it ignores its input, sync(0x70) stores a timestamp. The value is constant inside a block, so no credit should arise, and this needs one on-chain run to close.

leads.question: Do the PositionManager, Permit2, the Universal Router or any hook with liquidity on Avalanche use constant storage slots (EIP-1967, ERC-7201 or hand-written assembly) of which two differ only in bit 248?
leads.why: The C-Chain treats such a pair as one slot. Core is unaffected, and a periphery contract or hook with such a pair would have a write path on Avalanche that does not exist on other chains.

attempts.answer: No. The PositionManager, PositionDescriptor, Quoter, StateView, ReservesLens, the three Universal Routers, Permit2 and the owner contract on Avalanche, and all 282 hooks with code named by the 5,779 Initialize logs, hold no two PUSH32 constants that differ only in bit 248. The test reads constants in bytecode and does not cover slots computed at run time.

leads.question: Among the tokens the PoolManager holds on these three chains, which have a balanceOf(PoolManager) that any account can raise inside one transaction without transferring to it, for example through a public rebase, a reward claim paid to the holder or a reflection mechanism?
leads.why: settle credits the whole rise since sync to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). The sweep of this cycle covered protocol addresses only. Reflection and rebasing tokens are common on BNB Smart Chain, and yield that accrues to the PoolManager balance could be claimed by whoever triggers it between sync and settle.

leads.question: In Bor's BlockSTM executor and its serial fallback, is the transient storage of a task ever copied into the state database that the next task reads, for example when results are merged in transaction order?
leads.why: This cycle confirmed the reset in StateDB.Prepare for every message. The merge step in core/blockstm was not read line by line, and a copy of the journal there would break A1.

leads.question: What is the function behind selector 0xed9ef524 in the code at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010, and can an ordinary account call it?
leads.why: It is the only entry of the native token contract that this cycle could not name. The contract holds 6.9 billion POL and mirrors the native balance of every account.

leads.question: Among the tokens the PoolManager holds on these three chains, which change state for the sender when the PoolManager sends a zero amount transfer, for example a reward that is auto-claimed to the sender in a second token, a per-sender transfer cooldown, or a fee swap-back?
leads.why: take(X, to, 0) records no delta (src/PoolManager.sol:294, src/PoolManager.sol:369) and still makes the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, 0) (src/types/Currency.sol:73), so any account can trigger sender-side token logic in the PoolManager's name at no cost. A reward paid to the PoolManager in token R between sync(R) and settle is credited to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). A cooldown that restarts on every transfer could block later takes of X for every pool. This narrows the open lead on balances that rise without a transfer to one concrete trigger.

attempts.answer: Covered for the 12 to 15 largest pooled tokens on BNB Smart Chain, Polygon and Avalanche, and for 248 tokens over all 21 chains. A zero amount transfer from the PoolManager changes sender state in one token: qiAVAX on Avalanche, where it runs Benqi reward accounting for the PoolManager, and the public claimReward(0, PoolManager) would pay 14.84 accrued QI to the PoolManager if the Comptroller held it (it holds 0.11 QI, so the claim pays nothing today). sAVAX rejects zero amount transfers. No token in the samples has a per sender cooldown, an automatic claim to the sender, a fee paid by the sender or a swap back. On BNB Smart Chain SPCXB emits a second event with a display amount and nothing else changes. On Polygon all twelve tokens log only Transfer. The samples do not cover every pooled token.

leads.question: Do any BNB Smart Chain validators still run a v1.7.x client with the opcode fusion interpreter, and from which block is a v1.8 client required?
leads.why: The BSC changelog says v1.8.0-alpha removed the superinstruction feature of pull 3395 entirely (pull 3759), which explains why master has no such code. The v1.7.1 and v1.7.3 notes list three fixes to fused opcodes, one for a wrong LT comparison. The public endpoint reports Geth/v1.8.2, and v1.8.2 is mandatory before Jenner on 2026-12-08. Until every validator has moved, blocks can still be produced by the fused interpreter. A divergence there is a consensus fault and was not tied to any PoolManager opcode pattern.

leads.question: Among the 66,554 token rows of the mainnet PoolManager, which tokens other than the 12 sampled have a rebase, reward claim or airdrop claim that any account can trigger for a holder, and what does one trigger pay to the PoolManager?
leads.why: Each such token lets the first caller book the payment through sync and settle. The sample found no paying trigger today, and the long tail is unchecked.

leads.question: On each other network, is there an address that answers balanceOf(PoolManager) from a ledger which a plain value transfer or a zero amount call from the PoolManager raises, as EntryPoint.balanceOf and WETH9 do on mainnet, and that also answers transfer(address,uint256) from the PoolManager by releasing native value or a pooled token, at a rate, unit or fee other than 1:1?
leads.why: On mainnet the two halves meet only in WETH9, where the rate is 1:1 and both legs are booked, and in EntryPoint, which cannot pay out. A predeploy with a deposit ledger, a transfer function and a different rate or unit would turn take(address(0), X, amount) with sync(X) and settle around it into a credit larger than the native debit.

attempts.answer: On the three chains the only address with both halves is the wrapped native token, which exchanges one for one. The EntryPoints and the PositionManager have a ledger or a balanceOf answer and no transfer(address,uint256). No precompile or system address answers either call as an inner call from the PoolManager. Application contracts outside the swept list were not examined.

leads.question: On which other networks can an account run code while msg.sender == tx.origin holds (EIP-7702 or a native batch or account abstraction transaction type), and which pooled tokens there guard a public rebase, reward push or mint with that check?
leads.why: The finding in this file needs only that check to fall. Networks with native account abstraction may have had this property since launch, and a rebasing or reward token with real liquidity there would make the amount material.

leads.question: Do the sweep results of the other units change when the call is made by the PoolManager address with a different transaction origin, using a small forwarder placed at the PoolManager address by state override, for every target that did not revert under plain eth_call and for every target that reverted with an origin or EOA message?
leads.why: With from set to the PoolManager a plain eth_call makes tx.origin equal to msg.sender. On mainnet that mode showed the OP Mainnet L1StandardBridge accepting a payout that it refuses in the real call shape, and it hid the aliased sender of portal deposits. A predeploy that treats an origin caller differently could be misfiled as safe or as unsafe.

leads.question: Do the second entry points of TUSD (0x8dd5fbCe2F6a956C3022bA3663759011Dd51e73E) and SNX (0xC011A72400E58ecD99Ee497CF89E3775d4bd732F) still forward transfer and balanceOf for the PoolManager's balance, and does a self transfer of any pooled token, take(X, PoolManager, amount), raise balanceOf(PoolManager)?
leads.why: The double entry clearance rests on the accounting argument and was not exercised on chain. A token whose self transfer credits the recipient without debiting the sender would give a free credit between sync and settle.

leads.question: How does the MegaETH sequencer order candidates inside a block (arrival order or priority fee), and are transactions that were skipped for a block-level limit placed ahead of newer arrivals in the next block?
leads.why: This decides whether one sender who fills the state growth budget each block delays other users by one block or can keep them out for as long as it pays.

attempts.answer: The order is not by priority fee. In 232 of 300 sampled blocks a transaction with a lower priority fee precedes one with a higher fee from another sender (525 of 3,316 neighbouring pairs). That fits arrival order per mini-block. Whether skipped transactions keep their place could not be established, because the sequencer's pool is closed source, the documentation is silent, and no block with a full state budget exists in 400,000 recent blocks to observe.

leads.question: Are L1 deposit transactions placed before sequencer transactions in every MegaETH block, and what does the node do when a deposit itself brings the block's state growth counter to 1,000 while further deposits of the same L1 block remain?
leads.why: The block limiter applies the state growth test to deposits. If a later deposit can be skipped, the forced inclusion path that F-017 relies on has a gap, and a derivation mismatch would be an operator-level fault.

attempts.answer: Deposits sit at index 1 in 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks, ahead of system and sequencer transactions. One L1 block can carry at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits (resourceConfig on the L1 SystemConfig), which pays for fewer than 900 new slots, so deposits alone cannot bring the counter to 1,000, and the transaction that reaches the limit is itself admitted. The forced inclusion route of F-017 has no gap from this limit.

leads.question: Which currencies outside the Monad token list, the Uniswap list and the documentation page have a balance at the Monad PoolManager? Enumerate currency0 and currency1 from the Initialize events and repeat the classification for issuer controls, second entry points and balances that change without transfers.
leads.why: The list checked covers 147 tokens. A token with two entry points or a rebasing balance outside that list was not looked at.

attempts.answer: Enumerated from Initialize logs since deployment: 19,402 pools, 11,268 token currencies, 8,375 with a balance. New holdings of size are ten wrapped stock tokens worth 7.9 million dollars, 40 cbBTC, 337 bridged WETH and 1.7 WBTC. The wrapped stock tokens and cbBTC carry pause, sanctions, freeze and burn rights and are added to F-015. No second entry point to a pooled balance and no mirror of the native balance was found. Balances that change without transfers are Aave and Neverland deposit tokens with at most 24,696 nWMON (about 300 dollars) and unwrapped stock tokens at dust size.

leads.question: Who holds the proxy admin of GHO (0x06ba20fb633cbf38b7acfdc243829fb5f897e19c) and of mUSD (0x685e7f8c9414bfa716b254b349153e2317929ac9), the owner of shMON (0x48a3267bcc4cf230e9bc4cae0c11eebdb9a6a687), BURNER_ROLE on syrupUSDC and the upgrade right on apxUSD, and does burn(address,uint256) on syrupUSDC and apxUSD need an allowance from the account?
leads.why: This decides whether an issuer action against the PoolManager address is a pause that can be undone or a loss, for about 6.2 million units of dollar tokens and 269,214 shMON.

leads.question: What is NUM_KV_BUCKETS in the SALT repository, and can entries for a chosen bucket be found without brute force given the fixed-seed hash?
leads.why: The cost estimate for inflating one bucket assumes the attacker can place entries at will. The estimate also bounds a combined case in which the sequencer censors a user and the user's forced removal through L1, which an earlier lead puts at 20 million gas, needs a new slot in an inflated bucket.

leads.question: Obtain the full BlockSec report for MegaEVM and the Runtime Verification report for Monad execution and read the notes on fixed gas calls, sender balance taint and reserve balance proofs.
leads.why: Only the index of the BlockSec report and a search extract of the Runtime Verification report were read. A note could describe a behaviour of value calls that matters for native payouts.

leads.question: Does a run of N transactions that each create 1,000 new state entries, submitted together from several accounts, close N consecutive MegaETH blocks for every transaction that arrives after the run, and what limits per sender or per block does the sequencer's pending pool apply to such a run?
leads.why: The finding assumes the sender must win the first place in every block. Under arrival order a queued run would hold that place for N blocks at 0.0000226 ETH each, which is about 1.95 ETH for a day in which no PoolManager withdrawal is included. That would move the finding from a delay inside one block to blocked liquidity operations.

attempts.answer: Not observed and not excluded. Blocks are not ordered by fee, so under arrival order a queue of N filling transactions from several accounts would hold N blocks and delay later arrivals by N seconds at about 0.0000226 ETH per second. The only documented pool limit is 500 pending transactions per account. The delay is bounded by the queue length at arrival and does not reach L1 deposits, which are placed first. F-042 is updated with this bound and stays low.

leads.question: Is there a mainnet block in which a transaction with 1,000 new state entries is followed by further sequencer transactions in the same block? Search for transactions near 22.5 million gas that write about 1,000 fresh slots and read their position in the block.
leads.why: The block-level skip is confirmed in the reference limiter and the specification and was not observed on chain. One counterexample would show that the live sequencer does not apply the block limit as written, and one positive example would confirm it.

attempts.answer: No example in either direction. Headers of blocks 32,206,276 to 32,606,276 were read. 359 blocks exceed 20 million gas. The 30 transactions above 12 million gas in blocks of 20 to 80 million gas were traced, and the largest state growth is 27 entries. The heavy transactions are contract deployments. Blocks before 32,206,276 were not scanned.

leads.question: Which currencies appear in pools of the HyperEVM PoolManager? The public RPC limits eth_getLogs to 1,000 blocks, so the Initialize events of about 52 million blocks need an archive node or an indexer. For each currency, is it rebasing, does it have a second entry point, or is it a contract whose balanceOf can rise without a transfer?
leads.why: This cycle checked balances of 16 known tokens by hand and found the stHYPE and wstHYPE pair by reading issuer docs. A full list would show whether a pool already uses the stHYPE face or another token of this kind.

attempts.answer: The archive endpoint https://rpc.purroofgroup.com serves eth_getLogs over 100,000 blocks, which made a full list possible. 344 pools, 308 currencies, 53 hooks since block 45,998,366. For 306 of 307 ERC-20 currencies the PoolManager balance equals its Transfer logs. The exception is a test token without logs. No Transfer log naming the PoolManager comes from a contract outside the list, so no pooled token has a second entry point. stHYPE and wstHYPE are in no pool. Value held is small: 11.38 HYPE, 14.78 WHYPE, 997.75 USDC and test or launch tokens.

leads.question: What does the Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c do in mint, burnAndRedeemIfPossible and redeem: can any of them call stHYPE.syncSupply, and how is getNewSupply computed from read precompiles while HYPE is in flight between HyperCore and the EVM?
leads.why: The contract is not verified on Sourcify. If a public function can trigger syncSupply with a supply below the current one, for example while funds are in flight and the precompiles under-report, the loss shift between the stHYPE and wstHYPE ids described in the finding would no longer need the rebaser.

attempts.answer: Measured on the official node inside one eth_call from a real holder's address: mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible change the stHYPE supply by exactly the amount minted or burned and leave balancePerShare, syncStart, syncEnd and rewardsToSync unchanged, so neither calls syncSupply. redeem reverted for the test caller and is left as a low lead. The implementation is still unverified. No pool holds stHYPE or wstHYPE.

leads.question: How does HyperCore bind an AQAv2 treasury address to a token: does the named address have to send an EVM transaction or sign a message, and can the treasury deployer change the address after activation? The treasury address for USDC has no HyperCore account and no stake.
leads.why: This is the remaining open link of F-020 and of leads L-065, L-074 and L-116. If no consent is needed, two staked deployers and a validator vote can make HyperCore send transfers from the PoolManager.

attempts.answer: The treasury address does not have to send an EVM transaction, sign a HyperCore action or hold a HyperCore account. Its first transaction (nonce 0, block 37,597,803) is an unsigned system transaction that moved 2,001 USDC out of it, it held 0 HYPE before, and the info API reports userExists false and userHasSentTx false. The designation is separate from the authorizeAqav2Role action, which carries no address and was sent by the staking account 0x4E5319dEb1072B01439EE674db5C321d11fd96F8. Whether the deployer can change the address after activation is still unknown and is a new lead. F-020 is re-reported with this evidence.

leads.question: On HyperEVM testnet, send two transactions that land in one block: the first calls PoolManager.sync on a token and nothing else, the second reads the synced currency slot through exttload. Does the validator node return zero in the second?
leads.why: It would test assumption A1 on the closed validator binary directly. The present clearance rests on the archive client reproducing every block header. The test needs transactions, which this review does not send.

leads.question: Does a complete swap through unlock, with settlement in ERC-6909 claims, fit in the 200,000 gas of a linked contract's system transaction, and in which order does HyperCore place several system transactions in one block?
leads.why: It decides how useful the first position of a block is to an account that links its own contract, and so whether the ordering finding deserves more than low.

leads.question: What does MRB stand for, and has Hyperliquid stated whether further repricing or per block resource limits are planned? The change is visible in the archive client release of 10 November 2026 and not in the HyperEVM docs.
leads.why: A change of execution rules with one day of public notice is a hazard for hooks and routers that budget gas tightly. A statement of intent would show whether opcode prices that core depends on could change the same way.

leads.question: What bounds the gasLimit of a sendToEvmWithData action, is the gas of the resulting coreReceiveWithData system transaction left out of the block total like other system transactions, and where in the block is it placed?
leads.why: The exchange API lets the sender of this HyperCore action choose a gas limit and a data payload for a call into a linked contract, and anyone can link a contract of their own. If the limit is large, the 200,000 gas bound in the ordering finding does not hold, and uncounted execution ahead of signed transactions could also lengthen blocks. Neither the cycle 1 state nor the cycle 2 research file mentions this action.

attempts.answer: The documentation gives sendToEvmWithData a gasLimit field and no maximum. On chain all 60 coreReceiveWithData system transactions in 4,725 blocks carry 200,000 gas, target the CoreDepositWallet and sit before the signed transactions, like every other system transaction (1,927 of 1,927). The archive client leaves the gas of system transactions out of the block total (executor.rs lines 225 to 227). I saw no transaction with another gas value, so the bound is not established. A testnet action with a larger gasLimit would settle it.

leads.question: Is there a past HyperEVM block in which one transaction called PoolManager.sync on an ERC-20 without a settle and a later transaction of the same block made a native settle with value that succeeded?
leads.why: Such a pair is a read only test of assumption A1 against the validator itself: with leaked transient storage the second transaction would revert with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). It needs an archive node or an indexer with traces, since sync emits no event and the public RPC limits eth_getLogs to 1,000 blocks.

leads.question: Does Overseer.redeem(uint256) or any other public function of the unverified Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c change stHYPE totalSupplyRaw or totalShares out of proportion inside one transaction?
leads.why: A simulation in this check showed that public mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible leave a holder's stHYPE balance unchanged. redeem and the remaining selectors of the 24,255 byte implementation were not tried. A public call that moves the rate would let an ordinary account open a sync window on the stHYPE id and be credited the rise, once the PoolManager holds stHYPE.

leads.question: Has any source hash been added to the TxBlacklist at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727, which accounts are operators, and which commit of the okx/optimism submodule does the mainnet sequencer build pin?
leads.why: The high finding on voided deposits rests on source at tag xlayer/v0.1.7 and on the deployed contract. An indexer with full log access can show whether the rule has been used and against whom. The public endpoint limits eth_getLogs to 100 blocks.

attempts.answer: Operator only hazard. I read the logs of the contract with eth_getLogs in windows of 100 blocks for blocks 66,955,423 to 67,242,822 (2026-08-06 10:24 UTC) and blocks 75,407,023 (2026-11-08 22:14 UTC) to 76,607,000 (2026-11-22 19:33 UTC), which is 15 percent of the range since its creation. The second range starts before the date by which operators had to run the release that contains the deposit blacklist rule (10 November 2026). The public endpoints limit the request rate, so blocks 67,242,823 to 75,407,022 were not read. The creation block 66,955,423 (3 August 2026) holds four logs: Upgraded, OwnershipTransferred to 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, Initialized and AdminChanged. The ranges that were read hold no other log. The OKLink page https://www.oklink.com/x-layer/address/0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 shows no transaction records for the contract. The owner of the contract and of its proxy admin is still 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa. Which commit of the okx/optimism submodule the mainnet sequencer runs could not be read: the endpoint reports reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with xlayer/v0.0.7 and the submodule commit is not visible through raw file access.

Operator only hazard. No source hash is listed and no operator is appointed at block 76,668,710 (2026-11-23): the storage trie of 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 has exactly four leaves (implementation, admin, owner, initialized flag), walked from the storage root and tied to the state root of that block from rpc.xlayer.tech. An entry added and later removed inside the unread log range would not show. The commit of the okx/optimism submodule in the sequencer build cannot be read from chain. The repository publishes tags named xlayer-dep with a commit hash, and at the newest one, a492b62bbecbdcf3be90719e042c9abca47c8cc6, the six consensus files (alloy-op-evm lib.rs, the blacklist and gasless contract files, op-revm handler.rs, evm.rs and precompiles.rs) are byte identical to tag xlayer/v0.1.7.

leads.question: Can any error that the OKX handler raises for a non-deposit transaction occur after contract code has run in that transaction, given that its catch_error leaves the journal in place?
leads.why: The executor aborts the block on such an error, and the builder skips the transaction and reuses the same EVM. If code could run before the error, transient storage written by the rejected transaction, such as a synced currency in the PoolManager, would be visible to the next transaction the builder simulates, and the builder would produce a block that validators reject.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the X Layer PoolManager besides USDT0, USDC, Wrapped OKB and the bridged WETH answer at more than one address or change balances without a transfer?
leads.why: The sweep covered system contracts and the largest holdings. A token with two entry points or a rebasing balance would be a second face of one balance (A2, A3).

leads.question: Does every future CELO token implementation keep the property that the token address calls no contract outside Governance control?
leads.why: The transfer precompile accepts a DELEGATECALL from any contract that the token address calls, because the caller field is inherited. A token upgrade that adds a callback to a recipient or to a registered hook would let that callee move native CELO from any account, including the PoolManager. The upgrade itself needs Governance.

leads.question: Which op-reth commit does the OP Mainnet sequencer run, given that the public endpoint reports op-reth/v0.0.0-dev-unknown, and does it include the reth trie fix from pull request 28264 and the op-revm error path that discards a failed transaction's journal?
leads.why: Every source based clearance for OP Mainnet in this cycle rests on the commit that Unichain, Ink and Soneium report. The largest OP Stack balances outside Base sit on this chain.

leads.question: In the World Chain node, does the parallel validation path for flashblocks with block access lists execute each transaction on its own journal, and is a transaction whose result disagrees with the access list re-executed from clean transient storage?
leads.why: Assumption A1 names parallel execution with speculative state as a way for an unlock flag or a delta to reach another execution. The sequential path was read and is safe. The parallel path was not read to the end.

attempts.answer: At world-chain v2.8.2 the parallel flashblock validation builds a new State and a new EVM instance for every transaction and executes it without commit, so each transaction has its own journal and an empty transient map. The results are committed in index order and the access list hash, receipts root, state root and block hash must match the sequencer's, otherwise the flashblock is rejected with an error. No re-execution with shared transient state exists in that file.

leads.question: reth v2.10.0 names a new execution engine, evm2, in its SDK changes, and the Base workspace has a crate base-common-evm2. When a chain in this unit moves block execution from revm to that engine, do TSTORE rollback on revert, clearing at transaction end, rollback of precompile state on a failed frame, and calls to addresses without code keep the behaviour read in this cycle?
leads.why: All opcode and transient storage clearances of this cycle were read from revm. A second engine needs the same reading before it produces blocks.

attempts.answer: No chain of the unit runs evm2. All seven endpoints report the client builds of cycle 2, and the Base crate base-common-evm2 is documented as not wired into the node. The question is open again when a release moves block execution to that engine.

leads.question: Does Base plan a third B20 variant byte, and at the fork that defines it, can any address that was a plain account without code before the fork already hold ERC-6909 claims or pool state in the PoolManager under its currency id?
leads.why: Before a variant is defined its addresses accept transfer calls silently. This cycle found no way to hold credit in such an id, and the check should be repeated against the fork's token logic.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the PoolManager on Base and OP Mainnet raise a holder's balance through a call that any account can make, such as a rebase payout or a claim on behalf of the holder? The PoolManager holds 112.55 USD+ on Base, a token that rebases for every holder, and the caller of its payout function was not read.
leads.why: A caller who runs sync, the trigger and settle in one transaction is credited the whole increase on the PoolManager balance (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). Cycle 1 raised this for stETH on Ethereum. The balances found here are small, and a larger rebasing or reward token would make it a loss of yield for LPs.

attempts.answer: No token was found. The trigger probe called 70 public functions on each of 1,594 tokens on OP Mainnet and 9,108 on Base and no balance of the PoolManager changed. The USD+ payout on Base is not public: changeSupply needs the exchanger and payout() on the exchange reverts for an account without a role. The PoolManager holds 112.37 USD+. The Base list covers tokens that moved in one day, and triggers that live on a second contract are outside the probe.

leads.question: Do the deployed Universal Router and PositionManager on these chains accept a predeploy such as L2ToL1MessagePasser or an EntryPoint as the recipient of a native payout, and how did 0.0588 ETH reach the Base PoolManager address on Ethereum?
leads.why: The stranding finding of this cycle needs a user facing path to matter. A router that filters recipients would close it, and the L1 balance may show that it has already happened.

leads.question: What did the v1.18.2 item 'EVM call input hardening' and the v1.18.4 'fix for EVM execution' change in evm2 or in Tempo's handler, is the evm2 JIT backend enabled in the mainnet build, and does the PoolManager bytecode give the same results under the interpreter and the JIT for its call, return data and transient storage sequences?
leads.why: Tempo runs a new interpreter that received two execution fixes in November 2026 without a public description. The PoolManager's payout check reads return data size and memory right after a CALL, and its accounting lives in transient storage. A defect in either area would be specific to this network.

attempts.answer: Answered in part. The jit feature is optional at the mainnet commit 697ea97 and is absent from the default features and from the release Dockerfile, so the stock build runs the evm2 interpreter only. I could not confirm what each validator builds. Through the deployed PoolManager bytecode, 256 swaps and 288 paid adds gave the amounts of the source formulas, and 1,008 arithmetic opcode cases matched. The commits behind the v1.18.2 and v1.18.4 notes remain unidentified, because the commit history could not be read from this environment.

leads.question: Can the Universal Router deployments, the PositionManager or Permit2 on Tempo be made to call TIP403Registry.setReceivePolicy as themselves through any command, callback or subscriber path, and do they take TIP-20 payouts to themselves before forwarding?
leads.why: Anyone who can make a forwarding contract set its own receive policy can name themselves recovery authority. Every later TIP-20 payout from the PoolManager to that contract would then be credited to ReceivePolicyGuard and be claimable by the attacker. All policies were unset at block 50,287,321.

attempts.answer: No. The setReceivePolicy selector 0xdda03d86 is absent from the bytecode of the PositionManager, both Universal Routers and Permit2, and none of them forwards caller supplied calldata to an address other than their immutable position managers, the PoolManager, tokens and subscribers with fixed selectors. Their receive policies are unset at block 50,363,131. The routers do take TIP-20 payouts to themselves before forwarding, and those payouts are credited normally.

leads.question: Do the Universal Router and PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle, and how do they treat a pool or a route that names both address(0) and 0x3600?
leads.why: sync needs no unlock, and three EntryPoint contracts are deployed on Arc. An earlier user operation in the same bundle can leave 0x3600 synced, after which a native settle without a fresh sync reverts with NonzeroNativeValue. The bundler collects the gas of the failed operation.

attempts.answer: Both routers and the PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle. With sync(0x3600) or sync(EURC) left by an earlier call in the same transaction, a native SETTLE through each of the three contracts succeeds at block 32,662,000, while a direct settle with value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue. The contracts treat address(0) and 0x3600 as unrelated currencies, and their wrapped native immutable is a contract that always reverts.

leads.question: Which arc-node release do mainnet validators run behind the client string arc/v1, is Zero8 active, and does that release contain the ruint correction listed for v0.8.0?
leads.why: All source claims for Arc in this cycle rest on the main branch. The ruint note concerns shift and overflow handling in EVM arithmetic, which the pool math depends on.

leads.question: Is a TIP-20 amount sent by plain transfer to the FeeManager, StablecoinDEX or TIP20ChannelReserve address recoverable by anyone, for example through a reserve sync in the Fee AMM or the exchange?
leads.why: It decides whether a mistaken payout from the PoolManager to these addresses is lost or can be collected by the next caller of those precompiles.

leads.question: For each chain, name every feature that runs caller-chosen code against live state with a transient storage map other than the one of the surrounding transaction: Tempo zone contracts and the T14 ConfigurableAccount, Base Transactions of type 0x79, Stylus host calls and retryable redeems on the Arbitrum family, coreReceiveWithData system transactions on HyperEVM, PBH bundles on World Chain, the fee currency calls on Celo, and any keyless deploy, simulation or sandbox precompile. For each one, can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call, does the inner run begin with an empty or a copied transient map, and are its storage and balance writes kept?
leads.why: This is the one chain property that turns the settlement code into a direct loss for every pool. sync needs no lock and keeps the reserves in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). If an inner run with an empty map can pay tokens in, settle and mint a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364, 322-329) and its writes are kept, the outer settle credits the same tokens a second time. If the inner run starts from a copy and drops its transient writes, a take inside it leaves no debit (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The settlement unit raised the question and no network unit answered it except for MegaETH, where the critic found that the sandbox starts only at depth zero.

attempts.answer: Stylus host calls: an ordinary contract can start them, they share the transient map of the transaction, and their writes are kept like any other call. Retryable redeems: an ordinary contract can request one inside a call through ArbRetryableTx.redeem, the redeem does not run inside that call, and it starts as a separate transaction with an empty map after the requesting transaction has ended. Node interface simulations run only in RPC calls. No feature gives an inner run with its own map inside a running transaction.

leads.question: On each client, is there any way for a call frame to carry a nonzero CALLVALUE while the caller's balance does not fall by the same amount in the same journal? Check the system caller rule (go-ethereum master and BNB Smart Chain master skip the balance check and the transfer when the caller is 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, read by the critic at core/vm/evm.go lines 311 to 347 of bnb-chain/bsc; Bor v2.11.0 does not), deposit transactions with a mint field on the OP Stack chains including the custom gas token chains, retryable tickets and unsigned L1 messages on the Arbitrum family, gasless transactions on X Layer, the sandbox signer on MegaETH, system transactions on HyperEVM, and fee payer or sponsored transactions on Tempo and Arc. Which sender addresses reach those paths and can any of them enter contract code that an ordinary account chose?
leads.why: A native credit is msg.value and nothing else (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). The code never compares it with a balance change, so a frame that reports value it did not pay receives a native credit for free and can take every native balance and, through pools, other tokens. Assumption A3 lists the unit of msg.value and the faces of the native asset and does not list this. The established L1 unit recorded the system caller rule on BNB Smart Chain with relevance none and no unit asked the question for the other clients.

attempts.answer: Every value frame is backed by a balance debit on all three live nodes. The system caller exemption is in the fork source and is disabled for Arbitrum chains below Amsterdam. Deposits create no call frame, retryables pay their call value from an escrow funded by the parent chain deposit, and unsigned messages spend the aliased sender's balance. A probe with code placed at the system address confirmed the balance check on each chain. A low priority lead covers the Amsterdam version.

leads.question: Does the source text satisfy every statement the repository makes about itself in the files no unit has replayed? Replay by reading or by transcription: test/libraries/TickMath.t.sol, SqrtPriceMath.t.sol, SwapMath.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol, BitMath.t.sol, UnsafeMath.t.sol, StateLibrary.t.sol and Lock.t.sol, test/types/Currency.t.sol (the transfer cases from line 122 on), test/Tick.t.sol, test/DynamicFees.t.sol, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, test/SkipCallsTestHook.t.sol, test/PoolManager.swap.t.sol, test/Extsload.t.sol, test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol and the hook and initialize cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol. Then compare every NatSpec sentence in src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol, IProtocolFees.sol and IHooks.sol with the function it describes, and compare src/PoolManager.sol with the two other implementations of the same interface inside this repository, src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol and src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol, function by function.
leads.why: The owner states that this build carries a planted weakness and has ruled out comparison with other copies. The tests, the interface comments and the test doubles in this repository are then the only reference for intended behaviour. Cycle 1 found four places where the source departs from them (F-006), two of them in Pool.swap, and lead L-118 is still open with the files listed here unread. A fifth departure in a path that moves funds would be the planted item or would point at it.

attempts.answer: The part assigned to this unit is answered and found no new departure with a fund effect.
