leads.question: Which pooled tokens count locked, staked or vesting amounts in balanceOf and let a third party assign such an amount to any address (stakeFor, lockFor, transferWithLock)? PYRE on Robinhood Chain has stakeFor, stakedBalanceOf and liquidBalanceOf.
leads.why: A caller could sync, assign a locked amount to the PoolManager, settle, and take the same amount in liquid tokens. The caller ends even and the PoolManager holds tokens it cannot transfer, so later withdrawals revert. The reconcile cannot see this because the logs match.

leads.question: Which earlier results for Base rest on eth_call at an old block through https://mainnet.base.org? Repeat them on a second endpoint with a block timestamp check.
leads.why: In this unit old-block multicalls on that endpoint returned the same balance for two blocks a day apart for 231 tokens, and direct calls on four endpoints later disagreed with those values.

leads.question: Does the hook named by the TURING tokens (hook() returns a nonzero address) account for the decay, and do the thirteen pools hold liquidity from anyone other than the deployer?
leads.why: The PoolManager holds 26.8 percent of what the stored amount says. If others provided liquidity, the last of them cannot withdraw.

leads.question: For the fee tokens PIT, ASS, CATE and GFH held by the BNB Smart Chain PoolManager, does a take lower the PoolManager balance by more than the amount it debits? Fetch a trace of 0x684dd1095e662464e1f2df720e4702c952177a2b586873a822888e3152d4c000 from an archive node with debug methods and compare the take argument with the balance fall of 483,124,851.67 PIT.
leads.why: A token that charges its fee on top of the amount sent would leave the PoolManager short on every payout, and the shortfall would fall on other pools and claim holders in that token. The RISE trace on Ethereum shows the safe behaviour. For PIT the same conclusion rests on arithmetic over one log, and three of the five tokens were not read at all.

leads.question: Among the 177 rows classed as lending receipt tokens by symbol, is there one whose balanceOf uses a stored index that a public call updates? The sampled tokens compute the index from the timestamp at read time. Read balanceOf(PoolManager) before and after each protocol's public accrual call in one Multicall3 eth_call.
leads.why: Such a token would belong with sLGNS and USDI: any account could book the accrued interest on the PoolManager balance with sync and settle. The class was assigned by a symbol pattern, and the eight tokens I sampled are time indexed.

leads.question: On an endpoint that serves eth_simulateV1 or debug_traceCall for World Chain, replay recent handleOps and PBH bundles with PoolManager.sync(token) placed first: which operations change their outcome, and do the NodeRouter 0xab73c8f3bf8ae4856c90faa5e6560442a4787020 or the unverified senders 0x575229dcc62cdab8b02e5c2115aa2725c35aafdf and 0x392a2f3bb87b20782c220057556bba36853e8ab7 pay native value inside bundles?
leads.why: Three quarters of sampled World Chain swap transactions are bundles of up to three operations, and the NodeRouter source settles value without sync. This would size the denial where shared transactions are the normal case.

leads.question: Who operates and who may call the contracts that reverted in the replay and have no verified source: the Eisen facet 0x0b20601669dbce7e14210e24ca2b748cfb6dfc08 on Soneium, 0x944fe8becf9a02a3e9378b4cadde1b14ef8d2ed9 on Arc, 0x29d8d0a5c38716ebb4ae1786a46cf0ab74d480db on Robinhood Chain and 0xfe807eb087439ec6e59ed5f93fad011223cb50f9 on Avalanche?
leads.why: A public router with many users makes the denial worth reporting to its maintainers. A single operator bot does not.

leads.question: Do routers that catch a failed PoolManager leg, such as aggregator executors with fallback routes, leave the user's input in a contract that a later caller can sweep when the leg fails with NonzeroNativeValue?
leads.why: The Base replay showed an account that swallows the failure and reports success. If a public aggregator does the same while it already holds the user's funds, a forced failure could turn the denial into a loss outside the PoolManager.

leads.question: Which addresses appear as operator in OperatorSet logs and as spender in Approval logs of each PoolManager, and does any of them execute calls that an arbitrary caller supplies (Multicall3, Across MulticallHandler, aggregator executors, relay forwarders, settlement contracts with user defined hooks)? For each such address, do the owners that approved it hold ERC-6909 claims today?
leads.why: transferFrom and burn accept an operator or an approved spender as msg.sender (src/ERC6909.sol:35-48, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). The shared carriers that this unit listed run calls for anyone, so a claim owner that approved one of them would let any account move the claims and take the tokens. No earlier lead or cleared item covers the approvals. A Blockscout log query for Unichain returned 69 OperatorSet logs with 58 distinct operators, none classified; the same query timed out or returned no data for Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Polygon.

attempts.answer: 30,347 OperatorSet and Approval logs were read on the 21 networks over the whole history. 765 addresses hold a live approval: 4 networks have none, and Ethereum (227), Base (200) and Robinhood Chain (143) hold three quarters of them. Owners that approved someone hold claims in 2,882 owner and id pairs, about 44,000 USD in the tokens that could be priced. No approved address runs calls that an arbitrary caller supplies: 489 contracts were negative on 25 call shapes with a working positive control, 714 were tested for a caller check in unlockCallback, 201 code groups were traced selector by selector, and the shared routers that do hold approvals (Universal Router on Base and Robinhood Chain, PositionManager on Base) have no call to burn or transferFrom. Details per network are in the cleared items of this file. Provenance: the log scans of 17 networks, the state reads, the call shape probe and the caller test were collected by the first run of this unit on 23 November 2026 and reused from its work directory. The second run repeated the log scan of the four networks without logs, finished BNB Smart Chain and X Layer, and added the bytecode triage, the reach traces, the reading of contracts and every simulation quoted here.

leads.question: Ask the ViciCoin owner to add the Polygon PoolManager 0x67366782805870060151383f4bbff9dab53e5cd6 to the exemptions of the transfer limit plugin, and check whether other tokens that use the same HybridViciERC20 plugin set are pooled on any of the 21 networks.
leads.why: The plugin caps the net flow of every address that is not exempt at 6 VCNT per day and the PoolManager is one address for all pools. Other issuers of the same token framework can install the same plugin with other limits.

leads.question: AGL keeps one transient quota per transaction in its hook PoolAGL. If one party of a shared transaction (an ERC-4337 bundle, a relayer batch) ends its unlock with claims minted and the quota still open, does the AGL payment or take of the next party in that transaction revert or pass against the wrong quota?
leads.why: The quota is added in afterSwap and consumed by token transfers, and nothing resets it between unlocks of one transaction. A leftover quota could let the next party move AGL without a swap of its own or make its sell revert.

leads.question: Who controls USDG payout group 2 on X Layer (claimer 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72), who enrolled the PoolManager, and can a multiplier record that a live group uses be deleted so that _getMultiplierAtTime reverts on every transfer of a member?
leads.why: The PoolManager is a member, so a revert on that path would stop every USDG take and payment on X Layer. The reward on 385,837 pooled USDG goes to that address today.

leads.question: Find an endpoint that serves debug_traceCall with state overrides on Zora, World Chain, Soneium, Celo and Arc and repeat the round trip and one way state diffs for the pooled tokens there.
leads.why: On these five networks a per sender counter with a cap above 25 times the PoolManager balance, or a net flow limiter with a cap above the balance, would not show in the behaviour tests of this unit.

leads.question: Mikami (0x8581703a4c8db2cbcec42e883dee0404d4f97d6e) on World Chain answers Sender is frozen for the PoolManager, whose balance is 15,912e18 base units, and IDRX, WRC, CAKE and DogeX are paused or locked. What are these balances worth, who froze the PoolManager, and do the pools hold a second currency that users can still withdraw?
leads.why: A frozen PoolManager address stops every pool of the token, as G$ on Celo shows in F-056. These cases were found in passing and were not valued.

leads.question: uPEG (0x44b28991b167582f18ba0259e0173176ca125505) on Ethereum is an ERC-404 style token whose transfer of the full PoolManager balance mints and burns NFTs. How much gas does a take of the largest position need, and can it exceed the transaction gas cap?
leads.why: Twenty five round trips of the PoolManager balance needed more than 45 million gas in simulation. A take that cannot fit in a transaction would have to be split, and a position that cannot be split far enough would be stuck.

leads.question: Finish the access list sweep on World Chain (about 820 of 851 tokens remain) with an endpoint that does not rate limit eth_createAccessList, and identify the contract 0x796dff6d74f3e27060b71255fe517bfb23c93eed that seven Celo tokens read on every transfer.
leads.why: eth_createAccessList with the PoolManager as sender works on the five networks that refuse debug_traceCall and shows every contract and slot a transfer touches. A limiter of the ViciCoin kind shows as extra contracts with many slots. World Chain has the longest token list and the least coverage.

leads.question: The registrar 0x55f78e37adb9d1f6931c1da7314b374558ae9684 enrolled the X Layer PoolManager in USDG payout group 2 on 2026-11-19 (transaction 0xe22247f81654f1f438c3c24c9f35372ecf76441624009ad466aa82432569a621, registrarRegisterRewardAddressBatch). Which other addresses were in that batch, who is the claimer 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72, and has the same registrar address the role on Ethereum, Ink, Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain?
leads.why: The enrolment changes the transfer path of 390,000 pooled USDG and routes its rewards to a third address. The same role could enrol the PoolManager on Robinhood Chain, where it holds 17 million USDG.

leads.question: AKARII (0x643098f125e765081fec0b67384bfe5ca498f24a) on Arc: a transfer of half the PoolManager balance touches 1,914 storage slots of the token, and eth_estimateGas from the PoolManager address fails with gas required exceeds 16,777,216 for half and for the full balance. What is the largest take that fits in one transaction, and can every position be withdrawn in pieces of that size?
leads.why: A take that cannot fit under the transaction gas cap must be split. The research file raises the same question for uPEG on Ethereum only.

leads.question: 64 pooled tokens on Arc are clones of one launch platform (implementation 0x1b74922c01ddfd9c77b37d02c0a236611e8fe500) that call setShare on a reward tracker clone (implementation 0x72ee4bf0445d4fc2acaff82e6a1b7bb45238fc06) on every transfer. The PoolManager is excluded. Does an account that takes the PoolManager balance of such a token for one unlock receive shares, and can it trigger deposit, syncDeposit, flushBank or distribute while it holds them?
leads.why: take lends the whole pooled balance for free inside one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 104-114). If shares follow the balance at once, the borrower could collect payouts in USDC that belong to the holders of the token. The victims would be token holders, and pool funds would not move.

leads.question: Take the four places where src/ is looser than the repository's own comments and test doubles: collectProtocolFees never reads the lock and skips the synced check for address(0) (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 against src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40), sync has no lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279 against src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111), a take of a currency without code succeeds (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 against src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:174), and unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn lack the noDelegateCall that src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol puts on them. For each one, which of the 21 networks has a feature that the missing guard would have stopped, and what does an ordinary account gain or block there? Start with Arc and Celo, where an ERC-20 address measures the native balance, and with the eight networks whose fee controller holds code.
leads.why: F-006, F-054 and F-055 judged these differences under Ethereum rules and found no fund effect. The organisers say the weakness follows from a network difference, and no unit has paired these source facts with the network facts in the state. A guard that is redundant on Ethereum and needed on one network is the shape to look for.

attempts.answer: No network feature turns one of the four places into a gain or a freeze for other users. Fee collection without a lock check was cleared in cycle 1. sync without a lock gives nothing that a sync inside an own unlock would not give, which was shown on all 21 deployed PoolManagers, and its one effect is the revert of F-071. A take of a codeless currency costs only its caller, and no claim, debt or funded position can exist under a codeless id, including the CAS20 range of BNB Smart Chain before 2026-12-08. The functions without noDelegateCall run in the context of the calling account on all 21 networks. On Celo, Arc and Polygon one payment was credited once across address(0) and the native face.

leads.question: Answer lead L-260 by reading: for each guard and each accounting statement in src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 279-378, src/types/Currency.sol:40-96, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57, src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-175, which test in test/ fails when the line is removed or its condition is inverted, and which lines are pinned by no test? For every unpinned line, name the network feature in ASSUMPTIONS.md A1 to A14 it would have to defend against.
leads.why: The tests of the repository run on a plain EVM with ordinary tokens and one model of a native face. A change made for the CTF would sit where no test looks. This is the one method left that locates such a line from the text alone, and no unit ran it in cycle 4.

attempts.answer: Answered by reading and recorded as the info finding of this file plus eight cleared items with the test that pins each statement. Pinned by no test: removal of the CurrencyNotSettled check (src/PoolManager.sol:112); the lock guard on settleFor and clear (305, 310); the toInt128 limit at manager level (294, 313, 326, 334, 364); the use of _burnFrom in burn (335); the id truncation in mint and burn (324, 333); the checked subtraction for a fallen balance (360); empty return data, the 32 byte minimum and the missing code check in the token transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74); the gas of a native payout (Currency.sol:48); the length checks on hook answers (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166); the missing lock check in collectProtocolFees. Pinned only when a test runs as one transaction, which the CI flag --isolate prevents: the lock close (113) and the reset of the synced currency (361). Each statement reads as its comment and error name require. Network features: A1 for 112, 113, 305 and 310; A2 for 360, 361 and 364; A4 and A7 for the Currency and Hooks lines; A8 for 335. None gives an ordinary account a path in the text as written.

leads.question: Answer lead L-117 from the filter contract and its logs on Robinhood Chain: what does an entry identify (a transaction hash, a sender, a contract, any address touched during execution), which account adds entries and by what rule, and can an ordinary account cause an entry or a rule to match transactions that call 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951? Test the levers an ordinary account has: a native take of 1 wei or of zero from the PoolManager to an address that is already listed (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-52), a swap that pays a listed token into the PoolManager, and a pool initialized with a listed contract as hook or currency.
leads.why: F-001 records that the filter also fails forced transactions. If entries follow from what an address touched, any account can make the single PoolManager address touch a listed address at the cost of gas, and every pool on the chain would lose its exit. The lead has been open for four cycles.

attempts.answer: Read from precompile 0x74 and its 6,234 logs. An entry is the hash of one delayed inbox transaction. The single filterer 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7 adds it a median of 10 blocks before the transaction executes as a failure with all gas consumed. 1,389 of 1,491 executed entries name one wallet, 0x42607b2e4fde22e83822d4a86ddac58d847dc289, and none names the PoolManager or its periphery. The filter judges a transaction by the addresses that the transaction itself touches. A native take of zero or 1 wei to a listed address, a payment of a listed token and a pool with a listed hook or currency put the listed address only into transactions that name it, and leave no address in PoolManager storage (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and 117-142). No ordinary account can make another user's transaction on another pool match. The levers could not be run against the sequencer, because the public RPC node does not apply the filter to simulated calls.

leads.question: For the hooks that serve the largest share of pools on each chain (0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 and 0x2c668601193e4a081dd82604785e436aff6a2acc on Robinhood Chain, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium, 0x630e9cac0fff557bd3a01daa111ed253c771bcc0 on X Layer, 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc and 0x580ca49389d83b019d07e17e99454f2f218e2dc0 on Monad, and the two most used hooks on Base, Unichain and Zora): does an initialize call by an ordinary account with its own currencies succeed, do the swap, liquidity and donate callbacks tell that pool from the pools the hook was built for, and does the hook hold ERC-6909 claims or token balances that a callback moves with take, mint, burn or settle? Use the trace method the HyperEVM unit used for its hook census.
leads.why: initialize accepts any PoolKey that names a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), and every later hook call carries caller chosen currencies and hookData (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-335). Users of these pools chose a hook that the attacker did not write, so they are in scope. A hook that keeps state per hook, or that pays from its own claims on a callback from a stranger's pool, lets an ordinary account take funds held at the PoolManager. Lead L-258 was answered for HyperEVM only.

attempts.answer: Answered for Base, Unichain and Zora. The five most frequent hooks in a Base sample and the two most used hooks on Unichain revert when an ordinary account calls initialize with its own currencies. UniMemeHook on Unichain and the only repeated hook on Zora accept any pool, hold no ERC-6909 claims and no ETH, and UniMemeHook pays its fee out inside the same callback in the currency of the calling pool. No hook was found that pays from its own claims on a callback from a stranger's pool. The sources of the Base hooks were not read and a lead asks for them. Robinhood Chain, Elysium, X Layer and Monad are not part of this unit.

leads.question: Build the full currency list of the PoolManager on Base, BNB Smart Chain, X Layer and World Chain from the whole Initialize history (an archive log endpoint or an explorer export), rerun the reconcile script of the balance unit over it, and add one test that does not depend on the window: for every token with a balance, read balanceOf(PoolManager), call each public function without arguments of the token and of the contracts its balanceOf reads (rebase, accrue, poke, harvest, distribute, sync, update), and read the balance again, all in one eth_call.
leads.why: On these four networks only tokens that moved in one day, or an explorer page, were tested. A token whose balance at the PoolManager any account can raise between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289, 349-365) is an in-scope finding when the balance later falls back, and the window method cannot see such a token unless someone used it that day.

attempts.answer: The full Initialize history could not be read on Base or World Chain. The Tenderly gateway for Base caps eth_getLogs at 1,000 blocks, mainnet.base.org refused with a request limit, base.blockscout.com returns HTTP 403, and the World Chain endpoint caps the range at 100 blocks. The second half of the lead was done: the window independent test (balanceOf, 70 public calls, balanceOf again, in one eth_call) ran over 9,108 tokens on Base and 851 on World Chain with no change, and also over the lists of the other five chains of the unit. BNB Smart Chain and X Layer are not part of this unit.

Done for the four networks. The window independent test of the lead is part of assign_sweep.py, which calls every named function without arguments and every function with an address argument for one token per selector family. It found the ibBUSD conversion on BNB Smart Chain. On Base it ran on a set that covers every code family, with the limits stated in the cleared item.

leads.question: Search the logs of each PoolManager for ERC-6909 Transfer events from the zero address whose transaction holds no ERC-20 Transfer of that currency into the PoolManager and no native value sent to it, and for transactions in which the PoolManager pays a token out and receives the same amount back around a call to a third contract. List the tokens, the third contracts called between sync and settle, and whether the PoolManager balance of the token fell again in a later block.
leads.why: This is the trace that the sLGNS takers left on Polygon. It finds use of a public balance trigger without knowing the token, on every network, and it separates a surplus that belonged to nobody from a rise that later falls back and leaves pools short. The balance unit named this search and did not run it.

attempts.answer: (a) Claim mints. I listed every ERC-6909 mint log on 20 networks over the whole history that the endpoints serve and on X Layer over 400,000 blocks: 53.3 million logs in total, of which 29.7 million on Base, 9.9 million on Robinhood Chain and 5.2 million on Unichain. Receipts of sample transactions for each caller and currency pair show unexplained mints on Polygon only, in the three known ids. New facts for F-066: sATH now has 151 mints, all sent by 0x34b6daa3c6b68c1a12b6e6f9e89ca6c0f7861d99 through two contracts, and the third contract called between sync and settle is the staking contract 0x98d21b8e6bf0c1d2dfb0e3fcb82035095dcdd7de with rebase() (trace of 0x5cc3e1803b3990c9a9d93749c855c91117a32c1ae3b26482ab341befa182c2cf); sLGNS stands at 661 mints to six recipients from 636 one use contracts and nine senders, 28 of them in the last seven days. No other network and no other token shows this trace, including sNVB and sSAC on BNB Smart Chain over the whole history and USDI and AMPL on Ethereum. Native claim mints without a pool event are paid by value in every checked case. (b) and (d) Round trips and unexplained outflows. A census of 0.5 to 30 days per network found flash use of take in ordinary tokens only, and no take that is followed by a larger credit. The flagged outflows are protocol fee collection, the Polygon claim mints, Arc's native log mirror, spoof tokens and one real case. (c) Native takes to third parties cannot be listed from logs. The cases seen are takes into the wrapper between sync and settle, which are zero sum, and Arc payouts that are matched by claim burns. What is new and lowers a recorded balance: on Base an ordinary account took the PoolManager's whole DEAD balance through the token's claimIdleTokens (third contract DeadToken 0xf0197f10ea542a67914ecc0ec5304dc9df1faf6f, no sync or settle involved); on Arbitrum One the owner of PUSD burned 41,000 PUSD of the PoolManager's balance; and on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Unichain, Elysium and Arbitrum One token authors burned or moved the PoolManager's balance of about 150 tokens. In the sLGNS, sATH, sKLIMA, USDI and AMPL cases the amount was surplus that belonged to nobody. In the DEAD, PUSD and token author cases the amount was a balance that pools record, and the PoolManager's balance afterwards is lower than what pools record. Ranked by amount within what can be compared. Removed from a recorded balance by an unprivileged account: 14,899.78 DEAD on Base (unpriced). Destroyed by an issuer: 41,000 PUSD on Arbitrum One (41,000 USD if the token held its peg, which I did not check). Removed by token authors: 25,231,970 MAGA, 87,087,301 MEME and 806,756,916 BITCOIN on Ethereum, 601,450,442 CLU on Elysium, and smaller amounts for about 150 more tokens, all unpriced. Booked from unaccounted surplus as claims: 20,418.69 sLGNS (about 3,300 USD at the cycle 4 price), 329.79 sATH and 0.0102 sKLIMA on Polygon. The live PoolManagers are other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so these traces describe tokens and chains and say nothing about a defect in this build.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens count locked, staked, vesting or frozen amounts in balanceOf and let another account assign such an amount to any holder (stakeFor, lockFor, transferWithLock, vest to, deposit for with a hold period)? For each one found, simulate in one unlock: sync, assign a locked amount to the PoolManager, settle, take the same amount, and then check whether a later take of the pooled balance reverts.
leads.why: settle credits any rise of balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364) and take pays with a plain transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). A caller could trade locked units for liquid units at par and leave the PoolManager holding tokens it cannot send, so the last providers cannot withdraw. Transfer logs match in this case, so the reconcile method cannot see it. The verifier checked PYRE only, where stakeFor reverts for an ordinary caller.

attempts.answer: Yes on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Polygon, and no token found on the other eighteen networks. Method: 1,235,609 currencies with a balance on the 21 networks were grouped into 28,560 selector families, and 389,956 read-only trials called every candidate function from an ordinary account with the PoolManager as target while a stub at the PoolManager address measured balances and transfers. Tokens found: old QANX on Ethereum (21,210,277.64 pooled, transferLocked open to any holder, full transfer refused after the call), newer QANX on Ethereum (3,512.31) and BNB Smart Chain (10,297.83), seventeen generator tokens with freezeTo (eleven on Ethereum, one on BNB Smart Chain, five on Polygon, largest priced balance 182 USD), and two tokens with revocable vesting grants on Ethereum (16.5963 old ADX and 310.02 CDT), where the grant can also be revoked after the credit, which turns the freeze into a removal of pooled tokens. In every simulated case the transfer of the liquid amount to the caller succeeds, the reported balance returns to its old value after the assignment, and the full balance can no longer be sent. A later take of the pooled balance therefore reverts for the part that was swapped. PYRE, which the lead names, was not retested.

leads.question: Which addresses appear as operator in OperatorSet logs and as spender in Approval logs of each PoolManager, which of them execute calls that any caller supplies (Multicall3, Across MulticallHandler, aggregator executors, relay forwarders, settlement contracts with user hooks, delegated accounts with public batch functions), and do the owners that approved them hold ERC-6909 claims today?
leads.why: transferFrom and burn accept an operator or an approved spender as msg.sender (src/ERC6909.sol:35-48, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). A claim owner that approved a contract which runs calls for anyone has given every account the right to burn its claims and take the tokens. The verifier of the shared transaction unit found 69 OperatorSet logs on Unichain and classified none.

attempts.answer: Same question as L-302 with delegated accounts added. 56 approved addresses are EIP-7702 delegated accounts on six networks. None exposes a public batch function. One delegate on Ethereum has a handler that makes the account call PoolManager.take to any caller, which alone gives the caller nothing. See the cleared item on delegated accounts and the lead that asks for the rest of that delegate to be read.

leads.question: For the Soneium restriction list, the X Layer TxBlacklist at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 with the rcs-filter of xlayer-reth, and the Arc denylist: are entries added only by hand, or do rules add them from observed behaviour (a count of native transfers per transaction, a counterparty on a list, a volume)? If rules exist, can a caller make the PoolManager meet one with zero amount or dust native takes to chosen addresses, which cost gas only (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297)?
leads.why: Lead L-263 quotes a default limit of 10,000 native transfers per transaction in the X Layer filter. take lets any account make the PoolManager the sender of any number of value calls. On X Layer the deposit blacklist of F-046 also voids forced transactions, so a rule that an ordinary account can trip against the PoolManager address would close every exit.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one fact, as lead L-263 describes: is the risk control filter enabled in the configuration of the X Layer mainnet sequencer? Look for a transaction from an address that the public rule set would deny and that was mined, or for a denied transaction reported by the operator's RPC.
leads.why: F-024 has been plausible for four cycles on this one fact.

leads.question: Settle F-020 with one fact: does HyperCore test an AQAv2 treasury designation against the named address (a signature of that address inside the deployer's action, a refusal of addresses with code), and can the treasury deployer change the address after activation without a new validator vote? Ask the Hyperliquid team or read the testnet behaviour of the designation action.
leads.why: Chain data shows the named address did nothing on chain. If one staked deployer can point the designation at any address, the party that can make the node send transfers in the name of the PoolManager shrinks from the validator set to one account.

leads.question: Settle the open link of F-042: in which order does the MegaETH sequencer take pending transactions, and does a transaction skipped for a block level limit keep its place? Without sending anything, compare for one busy hour the first seen times of pending transactions on a public mempool feed or explorer with their order in mini-blocks, and check whether a deposit that fails for lack of the 60,000 intrinsic gas counts as one new state entry.
leads.why: Under arrival order a queue of state filling transactions delays every exit by its length at about 1.95 ETH per day, which the verifier would rate medium. The deposit route stays below the block budget by 48 entries on the verifier's count.

leads.question: Finish lead L-255 on what the critic did not read: do evm2-jit or evm2-inspectors at revision 66687c18, crates/consensus, crates/zones/node or any macro generated module of tempoxyz/tempo at 697ea97 call State::committed_copy, Evm::call_tx, Evm::transact or the database replacement at crates/evm2/src/evm/mod.rs:701 while a user call is running?
leads.why: A run nested in a user call with an empty transient map and committed writes would let one payment be settled twice (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 322-329, 349-364), and a reset of the map inside an unlock would drop open deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The critic found no such caller outside tests in 241 Tempo files and 137 evm2 files, so the question is down to the parts named here.

leads.question: On Celo the PositionManager 0xf7965f3981e4d5bc383bfbcb61501763e9068ca9 and the first Universal Router hold the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 as their wrapped native address. From their verified source and by simulation: what do the wrap, unwrap, sweep and settle from own balance actions do when the wrapper is the native balance itself, can a later caller in the same transaction spend native value that an earlier caller left in the router through the token face, and which currency id do routes through the 88 pools on the CELO token use when the user sends value?
leads.why: balanceOf(router) on the CELO token equals the router's native balance, so every action that reads a wrapped balance reads the user's msg.value. The stablecoin unit found the matching behaviour on Arc, where the 2.1.2 router pays a debt in 0x3600 out of the value sent with the call. Ordinary users reach the PoolManager through these contracts, and this half of L-218 and L-086 has been skipped for three cycles.

leads.question: On Arc and Celo, with the fee controller of Arc (0x2f2bd3f43880b9644211f16d861b0672aab23782, 3,480 bytes) read from its source or bytecode: who may trigger collectProtocolFees, is the recipient fixed, and can the call run inside another account's unlock? Then walk in the source and by simulation what a collection of address(0) fees does between sync(0x3600) and settle, and what a collection of 0x3600 fees does while a native payment is in flight, for the deployed routers and for a payer in a shared transaction.
leads.why: The guard at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52 skips address(0) with the reason that a native settle uses msg.value. On Arc the token face measures the same balance, protocol fees are set on Arc pools (20, 193 and 1000 pips in the pools the stablecoin unit used), and the lock is never read. A payer whose window contains a collection is credited short by the collected amount (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360) and the difference belongs to nobody.

leads.question: When one currency of a pool rejects transfers from the PoolManager (ViciCoin after its daily allowance is used, G$ on Celo, a paused wrapped stock token, GABAGOOL on Tempo), can a position held through the deployed PositionManager of that network still be closed so that the other currency is paid out? Read the action list of each PositionManager build for a path that mints ERC-6909 claims or clears a delta in place of a take.
leads.why: Core allows the route (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329). The cycle 3 verifier found no call to mint in the Celo PositionManager. If the periphery has no such path, the ViciCoin limit, which any account can exhaust with 6 VCNT of net outflow, blocks the WETH side of those positions as well, and each issuer freeze locks both sides.

leads.question: Is the transfer limit plugin of ViciCoin (TransferLimitHybridPluginV04, or any plugin of the HybridViciERC20 framework) installed on another pooled token on any of the 21 networks, and is the PoolManager of that network on its exemption list? Search by the selectors transferLimitAmountRemaining(address) and getExemptionAtIndex(uint256) over the currency lists in the work directory of the balance unit.
leads.why: The plugin caps the net flow of every address that is not exempt, and the PoolManager is one address for all pools. On Polygon any account can bring the allowance to zero for a day. The token address has no code on the other 20 networks, and other issuers can use the same framework.

leads.question: For each xStocks token and each wrapper of one held by a PoolManager: is a multiplier change pending (newMultiplierActivationTime above the current time), how much of the balance is already above what pools record, and did any pool keep liquidity through the SNDKx activation on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain or Monad? Read the swaps of the first blocks after timestamp 1795167000 in every SNDKx pool.
leads.why: A pool that keeps liquidity through a split quotes the old price for tokens worth a fraction, and the first account to trade takes the other currency from the providers. The activation time is public in advance. The balance unit looked at one pool on X Layer.

leads.question: For the fee and reflection tokens PIT, ASS, CATE and GFH on BNB Smart Chain, and for every token the reconcile marked as fee on transfer, does a transfer of amount a from the PoolManager lower its balance by more than a? Test with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address in one eth_call per token.
leads.why: take debits the caller the requested amount (src/PoolManager.sol:294). A token that charges its fee on top of the amount leaves the PoolManager short on every payout, and a caller can repeat take and settle at no cost to grind the balance down for the other pools and claim holders of that token. RISE on Ethereum shows the safe behaviour and the others were not read.

leads.question: Repeat the special address sweep on Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address for the sixteen shapes that cycle 4 used on Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM, and read core/vm/cas20.go and core/vm/contracts_stateful.go of the Jenner client for what an uncreated address in the CAS20 range, a created token and the precompile 0x70 return to each shape after 2026-12-08. Say whether any CAS20 address reports the native BNB balance.
leads.why: These three chains are the last where lead L-209 is open. The CAS20 range answers every shape today with success and empty data, like an account without code, so a take that names it debits the caller and moves nothing, and that behaviour changes at the fork. A new face of the native balance would need the intra call test recorded in this file's gaps.

attempts.answer: Repeated the sweep with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address on Polygon (55 targets, block 97,807,369), BNB Smart Chain (75 targets, block 135,226,007) and Avalanche (56 targets, block 101,141,646) for the sixteen shapes. No answer differs from the top level call. This closes lead L-209 for the three chains. From cas20.go and contracts_stateful.go and from Chapel: after 2026-12-08 an uncreated address of variant 0 or 1 in the CAS20 range reverts on all sixteen shapes, a created token answers transfer with a 32 byte true and balanceOf with its ledger value and reverts on the rest, addresses with a variant byte of 2 or more stay accounts without code, and 0x70 answers every shape with one timestamp word. No CAS20 address reports the native BNB balance.

leads.question: On the seven OP Stack chains with ETH gas, which addresses from 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff hold code today, and what does each return to the sixteen call shapes when the PoolManager is an inner frame? Name the interop predeploys per chain and say for SuperchainETHBridge and ETHLiquidity whether a value call or a transfer call from the PoolManager changes any balance that balanceOf(PoolManager) reports at another address.
leads.why: The unit for these chains last ran in cycle 2, before the stub method was in use, and the cycle 1 critic already asked for the full range. A predeploy that credits msg.sender in a ledger another address reports is the mirrored ledger shape of cycle 3, and new predeploys arrive with each fork.

attempts.answer: On all seven chains the implementation slot is set at 0x00, 0x02, 0x07, 0x0f, 0x10 to 0x1b, 0x20 and 0x21. 0x2c (ConditionalDeployer) and 0x2d (L2DevFeatureFlags) are set on six chains and empty on Base. 0x30 is set on Base only (BaseTime). WETH at 0x06 and the governance token at 0x42 are plain contracts (0x42 is an empty proxy on Base and has no code on Unichain). No interop predeploy is implemented anywhere: 0x22 CrossL2Inbox, 0x23 L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger, 0x24 SuperchainETHBridge, 0x25 ETHLiquidity, 0x26 and 0x27 the SuperchainERC20 factory and beacon, 0x28 SuperchainTokenBridge and 0x30 UndeliveredMessageExporter are proxies without implementation and revert on every shape, so a value call or a transfer call from the PoolManager to SuperchainETHBridge or ETHLiquidity changes no balance at any address today. The sixteen shapes through a forwarding stub gave the same non reverting targets on every chain: WETH, the four fee vaults and L2ToL1MessagePasser (empty calldata only), L1BlockNumber (every shape, returns the L1 block number) and the governance token. None of them credits msg.sender in a ledger that another address reports, apart from WETH, whose balance is its own ledger. From source, the interop contracts that Lagoon will install on OP Mainnet and Unichain have no receive or fallback and none of the selectors the PoolManager can send. A lead asks for the same sweep on the live contracts after activation.

leads.question: On MegaETH, what does it cost to raise the SALT bucket multiplier for the bucket that holds a given PoolManager storage slot to 2, 10, 100 and 1,000, can entries for a chosen bucket be found without brute force (lead L-174), and which writes of a liquidity removal, a claim mint and a take are zero to nonzero writes that pay the multiplier?
leads.why: The cycle 1 critic kept this open against a clearance: the forced inclusion route buys at most 20,000,000 gas per L1 block, so a multiplier near 1,000 on one new slot would close it. The Tempo unit showed in this cycle how dust positions raise the gas of other users at a storage price of 250,000 per slot. MegaETH lets the attacker raise the price itself.

leads.question: On an endpoint that serves eth_simulateV1 or debug_traceCall for World Chain, replay recent handleOps and PBH bundles with PoolManager.sync(token) placed first, finish the access list sweep over the 820 tokens not covered, and value the balances of Mikami, IDRX, WRC, CAKE and DogeX at the PoolManager together with the second currency of their pools.
leads.why: Three quarters of sampled World Chain swap transactions are bundles and the NodeRouter settles value without sync. A frozen PoolManager address stops every pool of the token, as G$ on Celo shows in F-056, and the World Chain cases were found in passing and not valued.

leads.question: AGL keeps one transient quota per transaction in its hook PoolAGL. When one party of a shared transaction ends its unlock with claims minted and the quota still open, does the AGL payment or take of the next party in that transaction pass against the leftover quota or revert?
leads.why: The quota is added in afterSwap and consumed by token transfers, and nothing resets it between two unlocks of one transaction. The verifier read that a buyer who ends with claims leaves a negative value that makes a later sale fail. The PoolManager holds nearly the whole supply on eight networks, and the liquidity is the issuer's own.

leads.question: Using the endpoint that served the balance unit 286,916 Initialize logs on Arc, list the pools that pair address(0) with 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 or name the USDC implementation 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6, with their liquidity, and obtain the source of the first Universal Router and of the PositionManager on Arc to read every native payment path.
leads.why: The stablecoin unit covered 3 percent of the pools for this question. A pool that pairs the two faces of one balance is a position in one asset against itself, and its price is the only link between the two ids if one face is paused (F-032).

leads.question: For GABAGOOL on Tempo (0x20c000000000000000000000030a4c7f7b8f3586): who holds the admin role, what does the hook 0x55aeb9ebfa15c28ff9d9a675e8574a5bbe186aa8 do on removal, do the two pools hold liquidity from anyone other than the creator, and does the take test over all 73 currencies give the same single failure when repeated?
leads.why: The entry is filed as a live case of the issuer finding F-031 and the verifier reads it as a creator's own token with its own hook. The answer decides the actor value and whether any third party is locked.

leads.question: Does the registrar 0x55f78e37adb9d1f6931c1da7314b374558ae9684 hold the payout group registrar role for USDG on Robinhood Chain, Ink, Ethereum and Arbitrum One, which other addresses were in the batch of 2026-11-19 on X Layer, and can a multiplier record that a live group uses be deleted so that _getMultiplierAtTime reverts on every transfer of a member?
leads.why: The enrolment changed the transfer path of about 390,000 pooled USDG on X Layer without any act of the PoolManager. The PoolManager on Robinhood Chain holds 17 million USDG, and a revert on that path would stop every USDG take and payment.

leads.question: Among the rows the balance unit classed as lending receipt tokens by symbol, and for Aave v2, Radiant, Moola and Neverland deployments in particular, which have a supplier index that a flash loan premium or a public accrual call moves inside one transaction, and what is the PoolManager's share of supply for each? Read balanceOf(PoolManager) before and after each protocol's public accrual call in one eth_call.
leads.why: A token with a stored index that a public call updates belongs with sLGNS and USDI. For a premium the caller pays more than it books unless the PoolManager holds most of the supply, and rzRDNT at 3.8 percent is the largest share found. The class was assigned by pattern and eight tokens were sampled.

leads.question: Does a published revision of hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync replay blocks after 37,597,803, where system transactions carry the AQAv2 treasury address or the CoreDepositWallet as sender, and what bounds the gasLimit field of sendToEvmWithData?
leads.why: If the official client stops at the first AQAv2 block, the only public reproduction of current blocks is the archive client, whose header check leaves out the receipts of system transactions. F-044 rests on a 200,000 gas bound for code that runs ahead of signed transactions, and the documentation states no maximum.

leads.question: For the 20 tokens with the largest value at the Monad PoolManager outside the wrapped stock set, does the transfer path in the verified source or the bytecode hold a per sender volume, count or time rule of any size, and does the wrapped stock implementation at 0x76c6851ea0b2741eedcbbed240715e8817e85583 compile from the Backed source?
leads.why: The census closes L-259 for these tokens on four round trips of the whole balance in one call. A cap in absolute units above four balances, or a rule counted per day, passes that test.

leads.question: Which execution client produces Celo mainnet blocks today, and do op-geth c7ed55b8 and the reth based client give the same result when a listed fee currency leaves a nonzero transient slot at the end of debitGasFees? Read the client name from the extra data or the release notes of the validators, and run the two transaction probe of the cycle 1 critic on an endpoint that names its client.
leads.why: Leads L-238, L-245 and L-256 ask this and no unit took them in cycle 4. Each Celo clearance of cycle 3 holds for one of two clients. A fee currency that calls sync during the debit would leave a synced currency in the user's main call on one client only.

leads.question: Which pools on the Ethereum PoolManager use the V1 EURe address 0x3231Cb76718CDeF2155FC47b5286d82e6eDA273f and which use the V2 address 0x39b8B6385416f4cA36a20319F70D28621895279D, and how much is owed under each id?
leads.why: The Ethereum PoolManager holds 4,188.47 EURe that is readable at both addresses. The issuer hazard found on Polygon applies wherever pools use the V1 id. The other Monerium tokens (GBPe, USDe, ISKe) have the same two address design.

leads.question: How much of the roughly 62,750 EURe in the Polygon PoolManager is owed under the V1 id 0x18ec0A6E18E5bc3784fDd3a3634b31245ab704F6 (pool balances of 21 pools, ERC-6909 claims and 2.27 EURe of fees), and has Monerium published a date for disconnecting V1?
leads.why: The size of the freeze in the EURe finding depends on this split. It needs the liquidity and claim records per pool id, which this cycle did not sum.

leads.question: After 2026-12-08: has GovHub appointed the activation administrator, which features are active, which CAS20 tokens exist on mainnet, which of them have pools, and what do policyId, isPaused and the role holders say for each?
leads.why: Finding F-007 becomes live only when tokens are created and pooled. The Chapel checks of this cycle can be repeated on mainnet in minutes once the registry 0x7020000000000000000000000000000000000001 answers.

leads.question: What is the full list of currencies of pools on the BNB Smart Chain PoolManager? Public endpoints serve its logs for about 250,000 blocks, the Routescan API does not cover the chain, and the Tenderly gateway allows 1,000 blocks per query without an access credential.
leads.why: The shared balance test of this cycle is complete on Polygon and Avalanche and covers only 31 hours of pool creation on BNB Smart Chain. A token with two addresses, as EURe has on Polygon, would be found only with the full list. An indexer export or an archive endpoint is needed.

leads.question: Which contract sends ANTB (0x38dd26788cf2d901e3abf04efe3007d459d0fc53) to the PoolManager when BUTTHOLE (0x020e5f774ca2e84fc80612b2c8503413a549ffff) is transferred from it, how much has accumulated, and can an account book it with sync, a zero amount take and settle?
leads.why: A balance that rises on a third party trigger is the pattern of findings F-060 and F-066. The simulated inflow was 25,751,442,464,642 base units for one transfer, which is small, and other launch platform tokens on the chain may pay larger amounts.

leads.question: After each Bor fork: does the code at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 still return false for transfer without value, and does any new genesis contract or precompile report or move native POL?
leads.why: Uburu replaced the code at 0x1001 at the fork block and reached validators as a private build. A change that let 0x1010 move POL without value would turn the dead credit of finding F-008 into a working second face of the native asset. The existing guard at src/PoolManager.sol:356 would then carry the same weight as on Celo.

leads.question: Do any two pooled currencies share a balance in different units (for example a share token and its underlying read through one ledger), beyond the 170 most pooled tokens per chain?
leads.why: The equal balance grouping finds only faces with a one to one unit. The group test for other ratios was limited to 170 tokens by the 100,000 byte cap on return data. A probe contract that returns one changed flag per token would lift the limit.

leads.question: When the C-Chain rule set for Igloo is published: does it include ACP-209, a new precompile at 0x0200000000000000000000000000000000000006, new opcodes or a change to the storage partition rule of finding F-040?
leads.why: Igloo is the only named upgrade and has no public C-Chain scope. Set code accounts and a precompile that takes value for a named account are the two parts of ACP-209 that meet the PoolManager call shapes.

leads.question: After Lagoon activates on OP Sepolia and Unichain Sepolia (target 10 December 2026), and again on OP Mainnet and Unichain (target 11 January 2027): which implementations sit behind 0x4200..0022 to 0x4200..0028 and 0x4200..0030, and what does each return to the sixteen call shapes with the PoolManager as msg.sender? Confirm from the deployed bytecode that ETHLiquidity, SuperchainETHBridge and SuperchainTokenBridge have no receive or fallback and none of the selectors the PoolManager can send.
leads.why: The clearance of this cycle was read from source on the develop branch and from op-contracts v4.0.0, because the contracts are not deployed. A fallback or a payable receive in the installed version would make one of them a native payout recipient that books value to the PoolManager, the shape of F-048.

leads.question: Build the list of all pool currencies of the Base PoolManager from the full Initialize history with an archive log source that allows wide ranges (an indexer export or a paid endpoint), then rerun the reconcile script and the trigger probe of this cycle over it.
leads.why: Public sources cannot do it: the Tenderly gateway caps eth_getLogs at 1,000 blocks without an access code, mainnet.base.org answered 'request limit reached', and base.blockscout.com answers HTTP 403. Base has about 61 million blocks and the largest pool count of the unit. The tested list holds the 9,108 tokens that moved in one day.

attempts.answer: The Base list is built: 15,540,638 pools, 15,315,529 currencies, no failed window, twelve windows confirmed on a second endpoint. The Tenderly gateway answers 1,000 block windows fast enough to read the whole history in about 15 minutes. The sweeps ran on 59,170 currencies chosen by code hash and code size. A new lead asks for the per token tests of the mass templates.

leads.question: Build the list of all pool currencies of the World Chain PoolManager from the full Initialize history. The public endpoint caps eth_getLogs at 100 blocks.
leads.why: The tested list is the explorer holdings page with 851 tokens. A pooled token that the explorer does not index was never tested.

leads.question: For the Base hooks 0xbdf938149ac6a781f94faa0ed45e6a0e984c6544, 0x0469a4bd3724dc86c9542f4694c976da13c450c0, 0xb429d62f8f3bffb98cdb9569533ea23bf0ba28cc and 0x5e320ea6278107968c119942e57d876c5f922acc: which contract is allowed to initialize pools, can an ordinary account reach that path with a paired currency of its own choice, and what do beforeSwap and afterSwap of 0xb429 and 0x5e32 (both return deltas) do with the hook's ERC-6909 claims?
leads.why: A direct initialize from an ordinary account reverts in all four, which rules out the simplest case only. The sources were not read because the Base explorer API was not reachable. 0xb429 already holds small WETH and USDC claims at the PoolManager.

leads.question: For the pooled tokens whose balanceOf reads a second contract (an exchange, a vault, a rate provider or an oracle): which of those second contracts has a public function that raises the reported balance of every holder? List them by tracing balanceOf(PoolManager) for the tokens with the largest balances on the endpoints that serve debug_traceCall.
leads.why: The trigger probe of this cycle called 70 functions on the token contract itself and found nothing on 19,664 tokens. A rebase that is triggered on another contract, as with USD+ and its exchange, is outside that probe. A public trigger would let a caller run sync, the trigger and settle and take the whole increase (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364).

leads.question: Once interop is live, do any routers, intent settlers or bridges on OP Mainnet or Unichain send tokens or ETH to the PoolManager in one cross-chain message and call settle in a later step or a later message?
leads.why: Relays are permissionless. An account that executes such a relay inside its own unlock, after its own sync, is credited the payment (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). Core is safe, so this concerns periphery that will be written for the fork.

leads.question: When Everest gets an activation time, read the Base Transaction executor again on the release that carries it: does sender and payer authorization still require a secp256k1 signature of that account, and does gas-limit billing change who is debited?
leads.why: The file crates/common/evm/src/eip8130.rs exists at v1.5.6 and returns HTTP 404 on the main branch, so the code has moved or changed since the reading of this cycle. A payer that can be named without its own signature would let the protocol debit an arbitrary account's ETH.

leads.question: Which op-reth commit does the OP Mainnet sequencer run? The official endpoint and publicnode both report op-reth/v0.0.0-dev-unknown.
leads.why: Two released builds that follow the chain have now been read (commit 72fcf947 in cycle 2 and tag op-reth/v2.4.2 in this cycle). The block producer of the chain with the most value in this unit is still unidentified.

leads.question: On every new Base node release and at every fork that adds a B20 logic version or a new stateful precompile: does a DELEGATECALL or CALLCODE to a B20 token, to the B20 factory and to the Policy Registry, made by a contract that the PoolManager has called, still revert, and does the token still take the direct caller as the source of transfer?
leads.why: The PoolManager calls contracts chosen by any account (src/PoolManager.sol:110, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, src/types/Currency.sol:48). In such a frame msg.sender is the PoolManager. At base v1.5.6 one check in the macro base_precompile (input.is_direct_call()) stops that frame from forwarding the PoolManager's identity into the token, and on 23 November 2026 the PoolManager held 5,322,585 OUSD at 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344. A release that drops or bypasses the check would let any account move that balance. The test of this cycle is a single read-only eth_call with two state overrides and can be repeated in seconds.

leads.question: Does revm at the exact version 41.0.0 that op-reth v2.4.2 pins clear transient storage in commit_tx and discard_tx, as the main branch does?
leads.why: The verifier read crates/context/src/journal/inner.rs on the main branch of revm, where both functions call transient_storage.clear(). The file at the pinned version was not read because the matching tag was not identified.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens have a lock, grant or clawback function whose selector the signature database could not name, or whose arguments the fixed patterns did not fit? Take the 52,820 unnamed selectors from the work directory, keep those in tokens with a balance above 1,000 USD, and read the verified sources.
leads.why: The two findings of this unit came from functions with well known names. A token with a private naming scheme and the same balanceOf design would give the same freeze or the same clawback and was not tested.

leads.question: Since which block do yUSD, yETH and xSolvBTC reject the PoolManager, which pools hold them, and does the YieldFi list name the PoolManager address or all contracts?
leads.why: About 976,000 USD at price service figures sits behind these three blocks. The answer shows whether issuers block the singleton on purpose, which would repeat on the new address.

leads.question: Rerun the own transfer test and finish the full balance transfer test on Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arc, and fetch code for every distinct hash on Robinhood Chain in place of the size sample.
leads.why: These three networks hold 1.13 million of the 1.24 million pooled currencies and were covered through families and samples.

leads.question: What is TITHE worth, which pools hold it, and do the three other tokens with its selector set pay rewards to the PoolManager as well?
leads.why: 10,002.56 TITHE can be booked by anyone today. The value decides whether this is a live extraction.

leads.question: Which tokens raise the PoolManager balance only at certain times or after a deposit of a second asset: vault shares with a deposit for function and a holding period for the receiver, reward tokens with nothing due at the time of the test, rebases whose epoch was not due?
leads.why: The trial sweep sees a trigger only when it has an effect in the block of the test and only when the caller needs nothing but the token itself.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens create a lock on the recipient when a distributor, auction, airdrop or vesting contract transfers to an address that an ordinary caller names? Start from FOLD 0xe172e9b6cfbeeb5593bdce3f077356fdb33af904 on Ethereum, where a transfer from CLAIM_SOURCE 0x687cc38d8279df3352b64cf3ec1fe8e033933595 locks the amount at the recipient and the auction pays the bid owner that the bidder chose. List the tokens whose transfer hook treats one sender specially, read that sender, and check whether claim, claimTo, claimFor, release or exit functions on it pay an address chosen by the caller. For FOLD, check the ten bids that are not exited and any later claim source the owner could set.
leads.why: The trial sweep of this cycle called functions of the token only. A lock that arrives through a third contract gives the same exchange of locked for liquid units as the QANX finding and adds a gain for the caller, because the locked amount comes from the caller's own allocation. Tokens sold through the same auction contract with claim locks would be exposed on the new deployment as soon as a pool holds liquid units while claims are open. For FOLD the path is closed today: no bid names the PoolManager and the auction is over.

leads.question: Do holders of locked QANX with allowedHops of at least 1 exist on 0xaaa7a10a8ee237ea61e8ac46c50a8db8bcc1baaa and 0xaaa9214f675316182eaa21c85f0ca99160cc3aaa? Read the LockApplied logs and lockOf for the recipients, and state how much locked QANX could be sent to the PoolManager under transferLocked.
leads.why: Both contracts let a sender pay a locked transfer from its own locked balance. Such a holder can book locked units between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364) and take liquid ones (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), which turns the freeze of the QANX finding into a gain at the expense of the pools.

leads.question: On World Chain the trial sweep recorded that an ordinary account which had just received a third of the PoolManager balance gained 1,874,084 units from withdrawDividend() on 0x5b51b28cb3b7d3dfa2463f3df7ce3929c1464f1b and 2,429.9 units from claimDividend() on 0x98b440dc0491e076ab029bf9fc502a5a721ccce1, with the PoolManager balance unchanged (raw/assign_480.json.gz, class A-gain). Does the payout scale with the balance held at the time of the call, where does it come from, and does it have a price?
leads.why: If a holder of the moment can claim, any account can borrow the whole pooled balance with take, claim the dividend and settle in one unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), which is assumption A5. The payout would come from the token's reward pot and not from pools, so this is a low item. I did not rerun these two trials. The same class in the sweep contains false hits where the test account 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000a11ce already held a balance, for example 29 USDC on Base.

leads.question: Capture the transaction that the hosted Uniswap web application proposes for removing a position in a pool whose token refuses transfers from the PoolManager (G$ on Celo position 178, ViciCoin on Polygon position 60652) and decode its action list. Does it ever use CLEAR_OR_TAKE or MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS, and what does the interface show when the simulation of TAKE_PAIR fails?
leads.why: The published SDK builds removals that end in TAKE_PAIR only. If the application does the same, a block on one token locks the other currency of each position for every user who cannot build a call by hand. The finding rests on the SDK reading for this one link.

leads.question: Decompile the EIP-7702 delegate 0xb0c75276657e80ff04c98a3809dfc39a409a8736 on Ethereum: which handlers run when transient slot 0 is empty, and can any of them make the account call PoolManager.burn with the account 0x82ccba35ad0c7a62230ef8ff337ac67f4cce0ea5 as from?
leads.why: 47 delegated accounts are operators of that account. One handler already makes them call PoolManager.take to any caller. A second handler that burns the owner's claims would let any account pair the two inside its own unlock and take about 740 USD of claims.

leads.question: Read the unlockCallback of the unverified contracts whose public entry reached unlock in the trace and whose burn target was not observed: on Ethereum the routers 0xbc22993a15e16acbf12873f234510d35948f7a59, 0x4531332adecf255c66b5bf6485db73f894ed93d2, 0xad445acd8e2446c652fb47b2d4c5ee9973b150c9 and the implementation 0xa62f9b597225779b430024398b70374e8468ce14 behind proxy 0x37bfb8ac7c960e558657871d41ca70e07e7dbfff, on Robinhood Chain the 47,585 byte hooks with collectPlatform(bytes32[]) and the implementation 0x6b68d5061329f64a087fc894355cb1eacf2a2321. Which account does each burn or transferFrom name, and who chooses it?
leads.why: The reach test used six argument fillings and cannot follow a callback that needs a well formed struct. These contracts hold operator rights from 2 to 7 owners each and are the part of the census that rests on a negative trace alone.

leads.question: Repeat the claim balance step for BNB Smart Chain with an indexed log source, and price the 2,100 unpriced owner and id pairs on Robinhood Chain.
leads.why: The BNB Smart Chain gateway gave differing answers for 1,274 of 17,870 windows, so an id with a balance may be missing. The Robinhood Chain value figure covers 70 of 2,170 pairs.

leads.question: Will the build of this repository be deployed with the existing periphery addresses as its routers, and does any later Universal Router or PositionManager release handle BURN_6909 with a payer that the caller names?
leads.why: The census describes the PoolManagers that run today. A new PoolManager starts with no approvals. The Universal Router already holds an operator right on Robinhood Chain and allowances on Base, and they are harmless only because its code has no call to burn or transferFrom.

leads.question: Which approved operator or spender contracts build the burn or transferFrom selector at run time (signature strings such as burn(address,uint256,uint256) hashed in code, or a selector taken from calldata), and for each of them is the debited account always the caller?
leads.why: The census excluded contracts by searching bytecode for the constants 0xf5298aca and 0xfe99049a. That test missed 0x2834c56d948f063564ff0a3c29483db50c73045a on Robinhood Chain, which holds 120 unlimited allowances and calls burn through a hashed string. My reading clears that contract, and the same test was the stated reason elsewhere. A string search over all approved bytecode and a trace of each hit would close the gap.

leads.question: What calldata does the hosted Uniswap interface or its liquidity API return for a removal when a simulation of TAKE_PAIR fails, and does any widely used front end offer MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS or CLEAR_OR_TAKE?
leads.why: The freeze of the paired currency in this unit's finding is confirmed for calldata built with the published SDK. Whether real users are stuck depends on the interface, which neither the researcher nor I captured.

leads.question: Which transactions left Klik hook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc on Ethereum with 7798353546842757 claims of SPCXon against 79607629840677756 of pending fees, and the Unichain hook 0x9463925bdeee2be5eade2a60857442b4a15ca0cc 10000000000000000 UNI short? Read the ERC-6909 Transfer logs of the PoolManager with the hook as sender and the burn amounts per pool.
leads.why: The difference shows that pending fees of one token were already burned in the currency of other tokens. If one account did it on purpose, the payout step of the finding has been used and the severity should be judged on that.

leads.question: In the Klik factories (0x20839c453a0ed8bcab1095ea068669469098297c on Tempo, 0xb6da931df2ed2c80db47923d4eb46fd913ee01c3 and 0x95e0da371711502eed78bcc3f17856b4415120ca on Ethereum and the factory() of each other hook): may any account call launch, and does collectFees(token) pay creatorFees[token] in pairOf(token) whatever currency the hook credited through creditCreatorFee?
leads.why: If both hold, an ordinary account that launches a token can turn fees credited in a worthless currency into the factory's balance of the real quote currency, which makes the payout step of the finding a direct gain. The Tempo factory holds 2946234 units of pathUSD.

attempts.answer: Yes to both parts. launch has no caller check in the verified KlikLauncher and AnyLauncher sources, and an eth_call from an ordinary account returns a token on the Ethereum and Tempo factories. collectFees(token) pays creatorFees[token] in pairOf[token], and creditCreatorFee records no currency, so fees credited in a worthless currency are paid in the real pair from the factory balance. Collected fees go to creatorOf[token]. Two Ethereum transactions (0xe91af1e1 and 0x341ecc66) took about 0.984 SPCXon and six other pair tokens this way, and the factory now records 0.9887 SPCXon of creator fees against a balance of 0.0043 SPCXon. On Tempo a simulated credit and collect moves the whole 2.946234 pathUSD of the factory.

leads.question: Repeat the debug_traceCall test of the finding on the Klik hooks 0x5b0a864213d49f23ed2a6635cc42b3b4fe7720cc and 0x64746dca345c5652bc251597bd99562216a7a0cc on Base, 0x71b7a448b96a01de73b0caf1267d33558d2620cc on Ink and Arbitrum One and 0xb2c964edbac922f006a09bd293b6c42ee147e0cc on Avalanche once a token has pending fees, with all pools of each hook listed from the Initialize logs.
leads.why: Only the open initialize was confirmed on these four networks. On Base the census kept three sample pools per hook, so tokens with pending fees may exist and were missed.

leads.question: For the launch pad hooks that keep fee ledgers and reject a direct initialize (0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec, 0xe0def4221b9840a610d4e7d55812a79a6431a8ec and 0x3ab88ddc3cf2a012af88b60828edb4553697e5dc on Elysium, CashCatHookV2, PonsV2MemeHook, 0x4eb1976978756bd56802d8162f2271844924e0cc and 0x2c668601193e4a081dd82604785e436aff6a2acc on Robinhood Chain, WonkHook and MinaraFeeHook on Arc, TaxLaunchHook on X Layer, LaunchHook on Ethereum): can an ordinary account launch through the factory with a quote currency of its choice, and is each fee ledger stored per pool id or per token and currency?
leads.why: The Klik finding is a ledger stored per token and paid in the currency of the calling pool. Hooks that hold claims for thousands of pools and let the launcher pick the quote currency can have the same fault behind a factory gate. These hooks hold claims or balances today, for example 178 native units and 20.5 native claims at the first Elysium hook.

leads.question: Complete the hook census where it is partial: Base blocks 37,000,001 to 49,000,000 were sampled one window in four, and X Layer was read only for the most recent 1.4 million blocks because the public endpoints limit eth_getLogs to 100 blocks. Find an indexer or archive endpoint and rerun the count and the probe for the five most used hooks.
leads.why: A widely used hook that created its pools in the unread ranges would be missing from the top five. The X Layer hook named in lead L-258 created no pool in the window that was read.

leads.question: Do routers or interfaces list pools from allPools or getPoolCount of the ERC-4626 wrapper hooks (0xc9987661b047cd73e3b0d66b2b7615a2ca811088 on Polygon, 0x89fcd09773c7c46ea20887c5246033f8a0a1d088 on Arbitrum One, 0x987105e95645d39ad967c8698478e17861271088 on Optimism, 0x8d92ff0a753dbc32e5c9c9f6493a1410d83e1088 on Monad), and what does afterInitialize check about the vault besides asset()?
leads.why: Any account can register a pool for a vault contract it wrote. A swap through such a pool hands the input to that contract. That harms only users who are routed there, so it matters if a router trusts the hook's own list.

leads.question: List every transaction on the nine networks in which a Klik hook burns claims of one currency for an amount it minted in another currency, starting from Ethereum 0xd903d0ada1874646896a5191a2ef25accec3c3db1333914542b6ad9a8c96bfed (sender 0x6356bab9f082de9abf08856ce61b71d294630964, contract 0xbd499416061f78beceb10ac00fdecf0232b38208) and Unichain 0x2b6aab1368b9266b585e655377e5a9431b822e4ff4657fec34166824e372a82e. Did the launcher of 0xfd23280b87514ce09dcb47965f1c5465847422eb collect the 34130246063283906 SPCXon credited by factory call 0xf3937729, and do the deployers 0x690193287a9f3e0095adae116f4260818332ce0a, 0x888ddf6a86fd6e6da39395cd3f333ecba55ff364, 0x02dcd01d534477b5e76628a7284e7fa71c7a7ed7 and 0x3a15cf422307e922645d671cb247e76e8b1ec50d, which created second pools on both Ethereum hooks, belong to the hook author or to third parties?
leads.why: The payout step of the finding has been used on Ethereum and three pools with liquidity are frozen because of it. Whether the creator share was withdrawn decides if this was a test by the author or a theft, and a count over all networks gives the realised loss.

leads.question: Who owns the liquidity positions of the Klik launch pools (for example the three frozen SPCXon pools with liquidity 153845604096252485200300 on Ethereum), can the owner remove them, and how much quote currency do the pools of the nine networks hold in total?
leads.why: An ordinary account can raise pendingClaims of any launched token from a pool without liquidity and stop swaps in that token's real pool. If the positions are locked in the factory, the quote currency paid in by buyers stays in the PoolManager with no swap path, and the severity of the finding should be judged on that amount.

leads.question: Run the census of this unit (Transfer logs that name the PoolManager joined with PoolManager logs per transaction) over the whole history of each network with an indexed log source, and list every transaction where the PoolManager's balance of a token falls without a PoolManager log, whatever the recipient.
leads.why: The full history search of this unit sees only burns. The DEAD case on Base was found because 40 percent of the claim is burned. A token that lets a third party move the PoolManager's balance to an ordinary address is visible only in the windows of 0.5 to 30 days.

attempts.answer: The census covers the whole history on Zora, Celo, Elysium, MegaETH, Tempo and HyperEVM and windows of 3 to 60 days on the other 15 networks. It lists every row where the balance falls without a matching pool amount, whatever the recipient. The busy networks still need an indexed source for the whole history.

leads.question: List pooled tokens that have a public function which moves or burns another holder's balance (idle claims, inactivity decay, reflection sweeps, liquidation of dormant accounts), and test with a read-only call from an unrelated address whether the PoolManager is a valid target today.
leads.why: claimIdleTokens of DeadToken on Base is such a function and an ordinary account used it against the PoolManager. Tokens of the same template may exist on other networks, and the PoolManager is idle for any token whose pools see no payout.

attempts.answer: Three pooled tokens beside the Base DeadToken have a public function that removes the balance of an idle holder with the PoolManager as a valid target: Imperium on Polygon (scanAndClean, valid today, no caller balance needed), the DeadToken copy on Polygon (claimIdleTokens, valid today, 1 base unit pooled) and BankToken on Ethereum (reclaimInactive, valid after the inactivity period in the trial at 91 days, 800 base units pooled). None has a market price. No such function was found among the priced tokens.

leads.question: Finish the burn search for the whole history of Base, Robinhood Chain, World Chain and X Layer, the claim mint list of X Layer, and a dense receipt sample for Base and Robinhood Chain.
leads.why: These searches cover recent windows only, and the two networks with the most claim mints (29.7 million and 9.9 million) were sampled with a lighter rule because of endpoint limits.

leads.question: Part (c) of lead L-318: list native takes whose recipient is not the caller. This needs trace_filter or an explorer export of internal transactions of the PoolManager.
leads.why: Native takes leave no log outside Arc. This unit saw them only through wrapper Deposit logs, through traces of sampled claim mints and through Arc's native logs.

leads.question: Which factory or template produced the tokens that grant the helpers 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 on Ethereum and 0xa25c886dced0e8fc0129082bf597381ea073c925 on BNB Smart Chain an allowance from the PoolManager, and how many pooled tokens of that template still hold a PoolManager balance?
leads.why: The same selector 0x73ed6b13 removed the PoolManager balance of 12 tokens on Ethereum and 18 on BNB Smart Chain. Live tokens of the template can be listed before they are used.

leads.question: Does the deployed PositionManager offer a way to remove liquidity when the PoolManager cannot pay one of the two tokens, for example by taking that side as an ERC-6909 claim or by clearing it?
leads.why: For the pools of MAGA, MEME, BITCOIN, ELX, SNI and DEAD the token side cannot be paid by take. Core allows mint and clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329), and whether ordinary liquidity providers can reach them decides if their other currency is frozen.

leads.question: Record the sSAC payouts on BNB Smart Chain under F-066 and establish how far they go: list every transaction in which the PoolManager pays out sSAC 0x0ae7cd10f94fd16a6f9a29a372708718144c46f8 or sNVB 0x6d6c16a3cbd318f3000e33cfd27662cf00f7e7c1 in a block where the token's rebase log appears, over the whole history, and sum the amounts.
leads.why: The research file cleared this twice and labelled the two rows spoof. Transactions 0xf1c329b6e3e3fa7747c3907e7d449c536977f0e44b79c10db31ff4153b9f098d and 0x27598a81864c463522634ec554d1e69a255353a9d4d6cf7438471a44ebd6ca1e show sync, rebase, settle and take of 2.538 sSAC each by an ordinary account, at epochs 365 and 366. F-066 says the path was unused on BNB Smart Chain. The call enters through lock(bytes) on a second contract, 0x238a358808379702088667322f80ac48bad5e6c4, which calls the taker back and pays it 999,471 base units of sSAC in the same transaction, so a second pool contract with a lock and callback design appears to be used the same way. I did not identify that contract.

attempts.answer: sSAC: 119 payout transactions between blocks 115,986,214 and 135,186,213 among 191 rebase transactions since block 104,200,000, summing to 210.068614 sSAC. The list is in theme-currency-lists.work/raw/ssac_payout_list.json. sNVB was not scanned over the whole history: the endpoint with wide log ranges reached its limit, and the verifier saw no sNVB outflow in the last 1.2 million blocks.

leads.question: Re-read every row the census flagged and the research file explained by a label (393 on BNB Smart Chain, 50 on Polygon, 126 on Arc, 17 on OP Mainnet), with one rule: a row is spoof only when balanceOf(PoolManager) is unchanged by the transfer, and a row is a rebase payout when the amount equals the balance rise since sync. Then run the same census over the whole history for every token whose balance changes without transfers.
leads.why: One of 134 flagged tokens on BNB Smart Chain was a real payout filed as spoof on the strength of the call pattern of the other 132. The census covers 0.5 to 30 days and skips every transaction that holds a pool event, so a capture that sits next to a swap, or that happened before the window, is unseen.

attempts.answer: Every labelled row was re-read. BNB Smart Chain 393: 391 nopool, 2 surplus (nopool means a token that is in no pool and whose balanceOf reverts). Polygon 50: 49 surplus credits and 1 spoof. Arc 126: all balanced by claim burns. OP Mainnet 17 and Arbitrum One 18: fee collection.
