The models never included the fee collection path, which has no lock check and exempts address(0) from the synced check (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52), or two callers that share a transaction. On Polygon and Arc a fee controller exists.

leads.question: Read the code of the seven fee controllers that core-code-loose-guards identified by selector list only (verified source where it exists, bytecode otherwise, and the 3,480 byte adapter on Arc first). Can any account call collect, can the caller choose the recipient, the currency or the amount, and can the call run inside the caller's own unlock? On Polygon and Arc, simulate a collection of address(0) while the native face is synced and state what the next settle of another payer in the same transaction returns.
leads.why: collectProtocolFees checks the caller and the synced token and never the lock (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The clearance that an open adapter moves accrued fees only to a fixed jar rests on the Ethereum source. An adapter that lets the caller name the recipient would hand accrued protocol fees to any account, and an open adapter on a network with a native face is the one input the settlement models never had.

leads.question: Run the sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address (stub_sweep.py under op-stack-custom-gas.work) on Ethereum, Monad and MegaETH against the precompiles, system contracts, predeploys, EntryPoints and wrapped native tokens of each. Add one shape that the sweep lacks: two reads of balanceOf(PoolManager) in one call with a storage clear, a value transfer and a transient write by the stub between them. Does any target answer the two reads with different words, or answer transfer with success while a balance of the stub changes?
leads.why: These three networks are the last ones with the four shape test only. The added shape looks for a ledger that moves inside one transaction without a payment, which is the only way a credit can arise at an address that is no token. Tempo has one such address (StorageCredits), found by reading and not by the sweep. MegaETH has an oracle and a timestamp service and Monad a staking precompile that were swept with single reads.

leads.question: For Dinari USD+ on Arbitrum One: decompile the implementation 0xff5bff8081eaee966bd74e9c0c059949df2345e1 and the public contract 0xb7541f225385104347539397a4e01abc1d4ea8bd. Which account signs the storage writes, does the signed message bind the chain id, the token address and a nonce, and which slots may a write name? Then find by code hash every other network of the 21 where the PoolManager holds a token that accepts selector 0x8078438b from the same kind of contract, and test whether a write signed for one network is accepted on another.
leads.why: The verifier found that the index of a token of which the PoolManager holds 1.07 million units moves through a signed write that any sender can submit, and that used writes revert on replay on Arbitrum One. A write that is valid on a second network, or one that an ordinary account can see before it lands, can be placed between that account's own sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-364). A write that may name any slot is an issuer power over balances that the finding does not yet describe. The behaviour was found on Arbitrum One, and no unit checked whether the PoolManagers of the other networks hold tokens that take writes the same way.

leads.question: Do the Robinhood stock tokens and USDG on Robinhood Chain have any path on which transfer returns true while the amount is credited to an account other than the named recipient, or held by a second contract, as TIP-20 does on Tempo for a recipient whose receive policy rejects the sender? Read the token implementation behind the proxies and send transfer(recipient, 1) from a stub at the PoolManager address to a restricted recipient, a paused share class and an unregistered recipient, reading both balances before and after.
leads.why: Lead L-214 asked this for three networks and was closed on the BNB Smart Chain part alone. A take that reports success and delivers nothing costs the withdrawing user the amount (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is finding F-033 on Tempo. Robinhood Chain has transfer rules enforced by the issuer and by the sequencer filter, and nobody ran the test there.

leads.question: Read WETH9() of the PositionManager and the wrapped native parameter of each Universal Router on these seven networks, as op-stack-custom-gas did for Celo. Which deployments name the native face itself, a contract that always reverts, or a token with other decimals than the native asset? For each, send the WRAP and UNWRAP actions and a native settle through the Quoter or by eth_call and state whether the call reverts, succeeds one to one, or succeeds with a different amount.
leads.why: On Celo the PositionManager and the first router name the CELO token, which is the native balance, as wrapped native, and on Arc they name a contract that reverts, as cycle 4 recorded. The other networks with a native asset other than ETH, or without one, were not read. Tempo has no native asset, HyperEVM and Elysium run a shorter PositionManager build of 19,965 bytes, and a wrapper with six decimals beside a native unit of eighteen would misprice every wrap. Most liquidity of ordinary users sits behind these contracts.

leads.question: For the 20 hooks per network that theme-hook-ledgers ranked by holdings: does the hook have any function that an ordinary account can call and that makes the hook call swap, modifyLiquidity or donate on the PoolManager with a PoolKey, amounts or hookData that the caller chooses? Read the source or the selector list and test by eth_call inside an unlock. Where the answer is yes, state what the skipped callbacks would have enforced and whose positions the hook address owns.
leads.why: The PoolManager skips every callback when msg.sender is the hook itself (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217, 253 and 293), and a position belongs to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161). A hook that forwards caller chosen calls therefore lets an ordinary account swap in its pools without the fee or the access rule that its callbacks apply, and act on liquidity that the hook owns for its users. No unit tried this lever. The probes of cycles 5 and 6 tested who may initialize a pool on a hook and which ledger the callbacks use.

leads.question: Read the four audit reports that arbitrum-family listed and did not open (Sequencer Feed Ticketing and Upgrade Action Contract, Yield Bearing Bridge, Tip Collection Toggler, OSP Soundness Guard) and the Stylus Permissioned Deployer report. Does the yield bearing bridge change the native balance or a bridged token balance of an account on the child chain without a transfer, is it deployed for Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain or Elysium, and does the tip toggler or the permissioned deployer change who may send a transaction or deploy code?
leads.why: The known weakness angle of the unit stopped at one of six reports. A bridge that pays yield by changing balances would touch assumption A2 for the native asset and for bridged tokens on a chain that adopts it, and Elysium already bridges its native asset from another chain.

leads.question: Elysium reports the client nitro/vlocal+unknown-unknown. Run the opcode and call pattern probes that the critic of cycle 1 used (TSTORE rollback in a reverted frame and in a reverted outer frame, TSTORE under STATICCALL, CALL with value to an account without code, return data of a failed call, the delegation probe of this cycle) in one eth_call each on Elysium and on Arbitrum One at the same ArbOS version, and compare the words. Does the Elysium team publish the commit it builds from?
leads.why: Every Elysium clearance assumes stock Nitro at v3.12.4. The network has 131,786 pools and 9,964 native units in the PoolManager, its node is a local build, and an upgrade that adds a predeploy and a precompile is announced. A difference in one probe word would show that the assumption fails before the upgrade arrives.

leads.question: On the first day after T14 activates on Tempo (2026-12-08): repeat the sixteen shape sweep and the inherited caller test, and answer one new question from the source at the activated commit. Can any party register or change a configuration of the ConfigurableAccount precompile for an address it does not control, and can a registered rule make a call reach the PoolManager with msg.sender equal to an account that holds ERC-6909 claims or positions without a signature of that account's root credential?
leads.why: The cycle 4 item read T14 from source before activation and covered the call shapes P1, P2, P3 and P5. Claims and positions are booked to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161, 301, 326 and 334, src/ERC6909.sol:25-48), so a new way to act as an account is a way to move its claims. F-051 already shows that a delegated credential with a token spending limit moves claims without limit.

leads.question: Which results of cycles 5 and 6 on BNB Smart Chain rest on eth_getLogs through bsc.api.pocket.network for blocks older than a few days? List them, repeat each through a second source, and add a count that does not depend on logs where one exists. On Base, confirm the Initialize census of 15,540,638 pools against the pool count of a second source for ten random windows.
leads.why: The verifier showed that the endpoint returned 191 of 323 logs without an error. A census that silently loses four logs in ten cannot support a statement that no row shows funds leaving without a debit.

leads.question: Repeat the Celo sweep of this cycle through a second endpoint and record web3_clientVersion beside every batch. Do the answers of the 319 addresses to the sixteen shapes differ between the reth build and the op-geth build that forno still serves, in particular for 0xfd, the CELO token and the four fee currency adapters?
leads.why: forno answered one of three version calls from a client that Celo no longer supports. The clearances for the native face on Celo cite probes through that endpoint, and the transfer precompile is implemented separately in each client.

leads.question: Does Nitro v3.12.4 contain the ArbOS 61 rules that Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain run under the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9, and has the source of that build or its consensus release been published since 2026-11-23? If it has, repeat the reading of parse_l2.go, tx_processor.go and the resolveCode change at that tag.
leads.why: All source readings of this cycle for the two chains were made at a release older than the one the nodes report. The transaction type walk and the filter analysis are only as good as the match between the two.

leads.question: Settle F-020 with one fact. Has any token other than USDC been activated for AQAv2 on HyperCore, and was its treasury address a contract or an address that had sent no transaction before? Read the spot deploy state from the info API and the first system transactions from each treasury address. If the HyperCore documentation or a validator release note states a check on the designated address, quote it.
leads.why: F-020 has been plausible since cycle 1 and leads L-065 and L-116 name this fact. If a designation needs proof of control, the PoolManager can never be named and the finding drops to info. If a contract address was accepted once, the operator hazard is confirmed.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one fact: a statement by OKX, in documentation, release notes, a governance post or an answer to a direct question from the owner, on whether the mainnet sequencer of X Layer starts xlayer-reth with the risk control filter enabled. Chain data cannot show it, as this cycle established.
leads.why: F-024 has been plausible since cycle 1. The filter is in the mandatory release and switched off by default, and the only rule independent trace would need a transaction of about 69,000,000 gas that this review does not send.

leads.question: Settle F-062 with one fact: read the payload builder of the MegaETH sequencer in the public repositories of megaeth-labs for the order in which it takes candidates from the pool and for what it does with a candidate that the block limiter skipped. Does a skipped transaction keep its place ahead of newer arrivals in the next block?
leads.why: F-062 is plausible on an inference from block contents, and lead L-170 has one inconclusive attempt. Arrival order across blocks would make the delay a standing one for every user at a known price per day, and fee order would bound it at one block.

leads.question: In crates/evm and crates/precompiles of arc-node at the commit that mainnet runs: can native value reach an account without a call to it, through SELFDESTRUCT, a block reward, a fee refund, a system transfer or the Native Coin Authority, in an amount that is not a multiple of 10^12 wei? State the rule for each of the five.
leads.why: Three models agree that the only gain on Arc needs such an inflow while 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 is synced and that it stays below 10^12 wei per settle. This one fact closes the open point of two cycle 2 items and of the verifier lead of this cycle.

leads.question: Robinhood Chain answers eth_call and eth_estimateGas without applying its transaction filter. Is the same true on Soneium for the restricted list of F-030 and on X Layer for the builder filter of F-024: does a simulated call that touches a listed contract succeed on the public endpoint while the sequencer would leave the transaction out?
leads.why: Wallets and routers simulate before they send. Where simulation and inclusion disagree, a user of a pool that touches a listed address learns of the block only when the transaction fails or never lands. The behaviour was shown on Robinhood Chain in this cycle and was not tested on the two other networks with an operator list.

leads.question: X Layer gives zero priced transactions to listed target and selector pairs. List the pairs of the whitelist at 0x19787404b0c70021b4752028f7e3a92313885B27 from its storage or logs, and check for Tempo sponsored transactions and for Arc whether any public sponsor or paymaster pays for calls that reach the PoolManager through a router or an account abstraction entry point.
leads.why: Filling a boundary tick to the liquidity cap (F-038) and other griefing cost gas today. A free path into the PoolManager would remove that cost inside the budget of the sponsor. The X Layer whitelist has more than two hundred storage branches and only six targets were tried.

gaps.note: MegaETH. The high-throughput unit cleared assumption A1 with the statement that the KeylessDeploy sandbox has its own journal and cannot see the parent's transient storage. That property alone is the dangerous shape named in the settlement unit's high lead: a nested run with an empty transient map whose storage and balance changes are merged back would let a caller sync a token outside, pay, settle and mint a claim inside, and settle again outside for the same tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364, 322-329). Critic check on 2026-11-22, read only: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/system/intercept.rs returns no interception when ctx.is_inside_sandbox() is true or depth is nonzero (lines 298 to 303), and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/sandbox/mod.rs states that a call from a contract reaches the Solidity fallback and reverts with NotIntercepted. A sandbox therefore starts only as the first frame of a transaction, when the PoolManager has no transient state yet. The clearance stands for that reason and the recorded reason should be replaced. Still open: which mega-evm release and spec the mainnet sequencer runs, since both files were read on the main branch.

The special address sweeps on these chains are recorded as eth_call with the from field set to the PoolManager, or record no forwarding stub. In such a call tx.origin equals msg.sender and the caller looks like an account that sends a transaction. In a real take, sync or hook call the PoolManager is an inner frame and the origin is another account. The Ethereum, OP Stack, Monad and MegaETH units used a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override, and the MegaETH unit saw L2StandardBridge accept the top-level call and reject the inner one. A target that requires its caller to be a contract, or that reads tx.origin for credit or refunds, would answer the two shapes differently. The eleven sweeps should be repeated with the stub for every target that did not revert and for every target that reverted with an origin or account type message.

Monad, Tempo and BNB Smart Chain. The opcode probes of both cycles ran as freshly created init code through eth_call. The Monad client runs bytecode in an interpreter first and switches to compiled native code once enough gas has been spent on that code (critic read of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/vm.cpp, lines 130 to 170), Tempo pins the evm2 JIT crate with unknown activation, and the BNB Smart Chain changelog records an opcode fusion interpreter with two consensus fixes whose location in the current client was not found. A probe made of new init code does not show how the deployed PoolManager bytecode runs under those paths. The liquidity unit reproduced modifyLiquidity amounts through the deployed PositionManager on 20 networks. No unit reproduced swap results through a deployed contract on any network, and Tempo was probed with one zero payment position only.

Tempo. The L3 profile lists balance writes and issuer roles and says nothing about gas, so assumption A9 is untested there. Critic reads on 2026-11-22: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tempoxyz/tempo/main/tips/tip-1000.md prices a write to an empty storage slot at 250,000 gas in place of 20,000 and sets the gas cap per transaction to 30,000,000. Block 50,314,865 on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz reports gasLimit 500,000,000 and mainBlockGeneralGasLimit 30,000,000. eth_feeHistory over the last 1,024 blocks returned a base fee of 600,000,000 in every block, and two block timestamps 3,745 blocks apart give 0.54 seconds per block. I did not establish whether PoolManager transactions count against the general limit, whether the base fee can move, or how a proposer orders transactions inside that limit.

HyperEVM. The A1 clearance and the system transaction rules rest on the archive client. The validator node is closed source. The unit could not confirm how HyperCore orders several system transactions in one block or how early an action must be sent to land ahead of signed transactions, and finding 1 of the unit has evidence marked inferred. The treasury designation rule behind F-020 and the new AQAv2 finding is still unread.

Elysium. Blocks are produced by a Conduit sequencer on a separate stack and only the RPC node, a locally built Nitro binary of unknown commit, was tested. The announced ArbOS upgrade with a HyperCore read precompile and an ElysiumCoreWriter predeploy is unscheduled on chain and lead L-001 is still open. More than 10,000 pools exist and their currencies and hooks were not enumerated.

Arc. Every source claim of both cycles was read on the arc-node main branch while the endpoint reports arc/v1. Whether Zero8 is active, and whether mainnet contains the ruint correction of v0.8.0 that concerns shift and overflow handling, is unknown. The pool math depends on those operations.

OP Mainnet. The endpoint reports op-reth/v0.0.0-dev-unknown. The source reading for this chain was taken from the commit that Unichain, Ink and Soneium report. The largest OP Stack deployment by value therefore has no client reading of its own.

Zora, Ink, Soneium and World Chain. The four L3 profiles repeat one sentence about the WETH predeploy, and the World Chain L3 profile cites no source at all. No unit listed the tokens these four PoolManagers hold or classified them for rebasing balances, second entry points or issuer controls. The cycle 1 critic raised the same point for three of them.

World Chain. The unit states that the parallel validation path for flashblocks with block access lists was not read to the end. That path decides whether each transaction runs on its own journal with a clean transient map.
Polygon. The unit states that the merge step of the BlockSTM executor was not read line by line. The clearance of A1 for parallel execution rests on the serial message path.

Unichain. The predeploy of 24,050 bytes is still assumed to behave like src/. The owner has ruled out a comparison of code copies. A behaviour test through eth_call with a caller contract placed by state override compares no code and was not tried: the outcomes of sync, settle with and without value after a token sync, settleFor, take, clear, mint and burn can be checked against src/PoolManager.sol line by line.

BNB Smart Chain and Tempo. Jenner and T14 both activate on 2026-12-08. Today the CAS20 address range, 0x70 and the ConfigurableAccount address 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 answer every call shape with success and empty data, as accounts without code do, so a take that names them debits the caller and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). The sweeps on both chains describe the state before the forks and expire on that date.

Seven units wrote the same open lead: list the currencies of all initialized pools from an indexer and classify them. The public endpoints limit eth_getLogs, so every unit sampled a token list. The samples found tokens whose balance changes without a transfer on five chains (AMPL and stETH on Ethereum, aTokens on Arbitrum One and MegaETH, USD+ on Base, stHYPE on HyperEVM). The full lists are missing on every chain.

titles: A native payout sent to L2ToL1MessagePasser, an ERC-4337 EntryPoint or the L1BlockNumber predeploy is booked to the PoolManager's own address and is lost to the caller
A native payout sent to a withdrawal predeploy, a fee vault, an EntryPoint or a Celo core contract is lost to the caller on Celo and X Layer
A payout sent to an EntryPoint, a precompile address or a protocol custody address is lost to the caller on Arc and Tempo
Three more recipients on HyperEVM accept a PoolManager payout and strand it: the L1 block number precompile, the ERC-4337 EntryPoints and a system address reached through the stHYPE contract
A payout sent to a HyperCore bridge address is credited to the PoolManager's HyperCore account and cannot be recovered
duplicates.note: One hazard on twelve chains. The caller who names the recipient is the only party that loses, as each verifier wrote. The four new entries carry actor unprivileged with effect freeze or degrade, which reads as an in-scope item. Merge them into F-021 as one low finding about recipient choice, and record for Ethereum, Monad, MegaETH, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche and the Arbitrum family, where the same behaviour was filed under cleared, that it is the same item.

titles: Issuer block lists on USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC cover the single PoolManager address on Arbitrum One
Role holders on GHO, syrupUSDC, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD can pause, burn, move or replace balances that the Monad PoolManager holds
A pause of the USDC token on Arc stops the ERC-20 face and leaves native transfers open over the same PoolManager balance
Elysium USDC is a bridge representation whose backing on HyperEVM sits at one address that the issuer can block
One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
duplicates.note: Same issuer control hazard as F-011, F-015, F-019, F-028 and F-032, now reported for Arbitrum One, Monad, Arc and Elysium. Keep one finding with a per chain token table. The Arc pause variant and the Elysium backing variant add a second step and should stay as named variants.

titles: The USDC implementation address on Arc mirrors the PoolManager's USDC balance, so a third currency id can be credited and never paid out
Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
Cleared: Faces, tokens with more than one entry point: SNX on OP Mainnet is reachable at the proxy and at its target
Cleared: Faces on Celo: the CELO token proxy, its implementation address, the four fee currency adapters
Cleared: Faces, native asset with the read only LegacyERC20ETH view
duplicates.note: Contradiction in filing. An address that answers balanceOf with a balance the PoolManager holds under another id and rejects transfer is a low finding on Arc and Polygon and a cleared item on OP Mainnet, Zora and Celo. The behaviour and the consequence are the same on all five: a credit under the mirror id needs a real payment and can never be taken out. Record it once, with one rule for the status.

titles: Aave aTokens held by the Arbitrum One PoolManager grow outside pool accounting and the growth cannot be claimed
Rebasing stETH held by the PoolManager gains and loses balance outside pool accounting
Any account can book a balance increase it triggers at the PoolManager as its own payment, and EIP-7702 removes the origin check that guards Ampleforth's public rebase
stHYPE and wstHYPE are two currency ids over one share balance, so a loss in the rebasing face is paid from the shares of pools in the other face
Cleared: Aave aTokens and other yield tokens at the MegaETH PoolManager
duplicates.note: One class: balanceOf(PoolManager) moves without a transfer. The general statement is the Ethereum finding. The Arbitrum One and MegaETH entries are the passive case and the HyperEVM entry adds two ids over one balance. The units also disagree on a fact that decides the active case for aTokens: the Arbitrum One unit says the whole flash loan premium goes to the protocol, while the Ethereum unit says premiums raise the supplier index inside the transaction. Both can be true per deployment and each chain should state which holds.

titles: Any account can fill a boundary tick to the per tick liquidity cap for a dust payment, which blocks later deposits that use that tick
Cleared (cycle 1): tick spacing bounds, bitmap arithmetic, the liquidity cap per tick and overflow of in range liquidity
duplicates.note: The cycle 1 critic asked for one rule. Cycle 2 filed the item as a low finding with effect degrade. The cycle 1 cleared entry should be withdrawn so the state holds it once.

titles: X Layer voids blacklisted L1 deposits at the execution layer, so forced inclusion is no guaranteed exit from the PoolManager
X Layer block builder can exclude PoolManager transactions through a rule driven risk control filter, which leaves L1 deposits as the exit
Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
duplicates.note: The new X Layer finding removes the mitigation that F-024 names, so F-024 should be updated in place and its severity aligned with F-001, which describes the same end state on Robinhood Chain.

titles: The swap loop pays for every bitmap word and every initialized tick on its way, and a HyperEVM small block holds 3,000,000 gas
The MRB hard fork raised the price of seven precompiles by 5 to 40 times, which can push a hook past the 3,000,000 gas fast block
duplicates.note: Both rest on the 3,000,000 gas block of HyperEVM and assumption A9. The first has evidence marked inferred from repository snapshots. One measured gas figure for an empty bitmap word and for a tick crossing on the deployed contract settles the first and bounds the second.

titles: A HyperCore transfer makes the node call a linked contract with 200,000 gas ahead of every signed transaction in the block
HyperCore sends unsigned system transactions from addresses outside the system range, which moves ERC-20 balances without any call by the holder
duplicates.note: The two entries give different answers to who can cause a system transaction. The new one says an ordinary account that links a spot token can make the node call its contract at the top of a block. F-020 carries actor operator. They describe two sender classes and the state should say which system transactions an ordinary HyperCore account can cause and which need a validator vote.

titles: Cleared: A1 from the node source: does transient storage end with the transaction, and does the KeylessDeploy sandbox share it
Lead (settlement unit, high): does any execution feature run code inside a call in a context whose transient storage is separate from the caller's
duplicates.note: Contradiction between units, resolved by the critic check recorded under gaps for chain 4326. The sandbox is safe because it starts only at depth zero, and the cleared entry should say so.

titles: Lead: do the deployed routers and position managers call sync(address(0)) before a native settle (settlement verifier, all chains)
Lead: do the Universal Router and PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle
Lead: which tokens raise a holder's balance through a call that any account can make (Ethereum, OP Stack, established L1, HyperEVM, Monad, Arbitrum and X Layer units)
Lead: enumerate currency0 and currency1 from the Initialize events (HyperEVM, Monad, Elysium, Arbitrum One, Ethereum units)
duplicates.note: Three questions were each written by several units for their own chains. Each needs one method applied to all 21 chains: one read of the router source, one indexer query for pool currencies, and one classification pass over the result.

gaps.note: All 21 networks. The mirrored ledgers unit took its token lists from explorer pages (Blockscout, Routescan), from a pool listing site (GeckoTerminal) and from a hand list on HyperEVM, 9 to 16 tokens per chain and 248 in total. No unit has listed the currencies of initialized pools on any chain in three cycles. The tokens with special behaviour that the review knows (AMPL, stETH, aTokens, USD+, stHYPE, G$, ELO, v4CRCL, qiAVAX, sAVAX) were each found by an odd probe result on a sample. One method would list all of them without knowing the token: compare the change of balanceOf(PoolManager) between two blocks with the Transfer logs that name the PoolManager in between. It has not been run on any chain.

World Chain, Celo, X Layer, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Arc and HyperEVM. These endpoints refuse eth_simulateV1 and debug_traceCall, so the statement that a zero amount transfer from the PoolManager touches no second token rests on the gas of the inner call and on the balance of the token itself. The verifier of the mirrored ledgers unit did not test the wrapped native token on Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Monad and Arc, did not repeat the sweep of the 248 tokens, and its EntryPoint v0.8 probe on Monad was cut off by a rate limit.

Tempo, Arc, HyperEVM, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche. The cycle 2 critic asked for the special address sweeps to be repeated with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, so that the PoolManager is an inner frame with another transaction origin. Cycle 3 did this in full for the Arbitrum family only (ten call shapes on 64 to 70 targets). The mirrored ledgers unit used a stub on all chains for four shapes (value with empty calldata, zero value, transfer of 0 and of 1). The hook selectors, unlockCallback and balanceOf under STATICCALL were not sent through a stub on these six chains, and lead L-209 stays open for them.

Base. The B20 token precompile is the one enshrined token whose node source has not been read for balance writes that an account without a role can cause. Cycle 2 did that reading for TIP-20 on Tempo (every balance write listed) and for the USDC implementation on Arc. Lead L-119 has asked for it since cycle 1 and lead L-214 since cycle 2, and the unit that holds Base did not run in cycle 3. The PoolManager on Base held about 5.34 million OUSD in a B20 token when cycle 1 looked.

BNB Smart Chain and Tempo. Jenner and T14 activate on 2026-12-08, fifteen days after this cycle, and neither chain had a unit in cycle 3. The leads L-029, L-124 and L-105 are worded as questions for after activation. The Jenner source is public today: the callvalue unit read core/vm/cas20.go and core/vm/contracts_stateful.go on the master branch of bnb-chain/bsc. The CAS20 questions can be answered from source before the fork, and the current sweeps of the CAS20 range, of 0x70 and of 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 expire on that date.

Celo. The public endpoint answered web3_clientVersion with reth/v2.2.0-74cc8bb eight times and with Geth/v0.1.0-untagged-c7ed55b8 four times in the verifier's runs. The nested transient unit read only the op-geth fork and the custom gas unit read only celo-kona, and the two texts differ on whether transient storage written by debitGasFees survives into the main call. Three verifier leads of this cycle ask which client produces blocks. Until that is known, each Celo clearance of cycle 3 holds for one of two clients, and the revision 74cc8bb did not resolve in the celo-kona repository.

Robinhood Chain and Elysium. The Arbitrum unit closed the question of the unpublished node build (v3.13.0-rc.9 on two chains, a local build on Elysium) with the argument that the rollup contract pins the consensus-v61 replay binary. That binds the sequencer only if a validator challenges a wrong state. validatorWhitelistDisabled() is false on the Robinhood Chain rollup, and validation on Elysium is limited to listed validators, so the argument rests on parties the review files as operators. The unit was assigned lenses L1 to L4 only, so L5 and L6 had no pass, and lead L-117 about the Robinhood filter list is still open.

MegaETH. The clearance of the KeylessDeploy sandbox rests on two things that were not confirmed: which mega-evm revision mega-reth v2.2.3 pins (the files were read on the main branch), and that every accepted transaction type has exactly one frame at depth zero. The unit saw types 0x7e, 0x0 and 0x2 in one block and states that it did not enumerate the types the node accepts.

Tempo. The verifier found that evm2 at the pinned revision 66687c18 ships committed_copy, a facility for a transaction nested in the running one with committed writes and an empty transient map, and could not search the whole tree for a caller. The JIT path for TSTORE is unread, and the Tempo unit did not run in cycle 3. Two critic reads on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz (client tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97). First, a creation payload sent with eth_call near block 50,356,289 returned 0 for BALANCE(PoolManager) and for SELFBALANCE while eth_getBalance returns a placeholder, which supports the statement that the native branch is inert. Second, the StorageCredits precompile at 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 answered balanceOf(PoolManager) with 13 at block 50,356,964 and rejected transfer(address,uint256) with UnknownFunctionSelector. https://tips.sh/1060 says this counter rises by one for the account whose storage slot goes from nonzero to zero, inside the transaction, and that creations by any sender consume it at the end of the transaction. The mirrored ledgers unit did not list it, because its probes raised ledgers by value calls and zero amount transfers only. A liquidity removal between sync and settle would give a credit under that address as currency id (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), which can only become a claim because the precompile has no transfer.

Monad. The self-destruct probe of the callvalue unit left a balance of 0 for a contract that names itself as beneficiary, where 19 endpoints kept the 9 wei and Arc reverted. The unit could not say whether this is a burn rule or an effect of the state override. It is the one opcode result of three cycles that differs without an explanation. The compiled execution path of the Monad client is still unread for TSTORE, and the swap results of the deployed contract on Monad were reproduced for six mined swaps or fewer.

HyperEVM. No unit ran for this chain in cycle 3. The validator binary is closed, so each theme answer for it rests on documentation, on the two public replay clients and on probes of the RPC node. F-020 stays plausible, and the fact that would settle it (lead L-215: must the address named as AQAv2 treasury sign or send anything) was not looked up.

Unichain. The behaviour test that the cycle 2 critic described (lead L-217: a caller contract placed by state override that walks sync, settle with and without value, settleFor, take, clear, mint and burn on the predeploy) was not run. Every Unichain clearance of cycle 3 still assumes that the 24,050 byte predeploy behaves like src/.

All 21 networks. Part of the evidence in the cleared list describes the PoolManagers that are deployed today: sync accepted while locked, ManagerLocked on settle, the mined swaps and Quoter quotes that the libraries verifier reproduced. Those contracts are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. Such results show how each chain executes the deployed contract and say nothing about the custody code of this build. The two tests replay units showed that the source satisfies every test and comment of the repository. Nobody asked the converse: which guards and accounting statements in src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 279-378, src/types/Currency.sol:40-96 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 are exercised by no test. The repository's tests run on a plain EVM with ordinary tokens and one model of a native face (src/test/NativeERC20.sol), so behaviour that only matters on another network is the part they are least likely to pin.

Critic check of assumption A1 on 2026-11-23, read only. The probes of cycles 1 to 3 wrote and read transient slots inside one contract and its delegate, with slot numbers 1 and 2. None checked that transient storage is scoped by address, or that slot indexes with an odd first byte are kept apart (Avalanche rewrites the first byte of persistent slot indexes, F-040). I sent one 529 byte creation payload with eth_call and no to address to the 21 endpoints of state/networks.json. It writes 0xaa to the three slot constants of src/libraries/Lock.sol:8, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-10 and src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:13, lets a second contract read the same slots, and reads each slot again with the lowest bit of its first byte flipped. All 21 endpoints returned the same nine words: the second contract read zero (it returns the value plus one, and returned 1), the flipped index read zero, and the writer read 0xaa. I also recomputed the four slot constants from the strings in their comments with a local Keccak, and they match. The result describes the RPC node of each network.

Seven open leads need a compiler: L-016, L-024, L-028, L-151, L-152 and the two build leads written by the tests replay units in cycle 3, one of them marked high (does a build reproduce the creation code hash and the 24,009 byte size recorded in snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json). forge and solc are not installed and the rules forbid installing them, and L-151 came back inconclusive for that reason. These leads cannot be answered by any unit in this environment. They should be parked or handed to the owner, so that the planner stops spending slots on them.

Celo, Arc, Polygon, OP Mainnet and Zora, the chains where an ERC-20 address reports the native balance of the PoolManager. Cycle 3 walked the core paths across the two ids again and found no gain. The leads about the deployed periphery are unanswered after two cycles: L-019 (is sync called before every payment), L-086 (the Celo PositionManager returns the CELO token from WETH9()), L-104, L-199 and L-218. Ordinary users reach the PoolManager through those contracts, and a router that treats the native face as a wrapped token, or settles native value without sync(address(0)), meets the revert at src/PoolManager.sol:356 or the stale sync of F-014.

Robinhood Chain, Elysium and X Layer. The samples of this cycle show that one hook serves a third of recent pools on Robinhood Chain (0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544), four fifths on Elysium (0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec), and that seven hooks serve the 110 listed pools on X Layer. The units asked who owns these hooks. No unit asked what an ordinary account can make the PoolManager say to them: initialize accepts any PoolKey that names the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), and every later hook call carries caller-chosen currencies and hookData (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-335). The hook is not an indexed field of Initialize, so the pools of one hook cannot be listed with a topic filter, and the counts are samples.

gaps.note: All 21 networks. Cycle 4 ran three themes in place of the source readings, so no unit read src/ this cycle and leads L-260 and L-204 were not taken up. Every replay of this cycle ran against the PoolManagers deployed today, which are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. The stablecoin unit, the HyperEVM unit and the verifier of the shared transaction unit state this limit in their own files. The places where the source is looser than the repository's own text are recorded in F-006, F-054 and F-055 and were each judged under Ethereum rules only: src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says fee collection reverts when the contract is unlocked, while src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 never reads the lock and exempts address(0) from the synced check; src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 says only initialize and updateDynamicLPFee run without an unlock, while sync has no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279); src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts when the amount is not available, while a currency without code makes the transfer succeed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74); src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:58, 151, 156, 163, 176 and 181 put noDelegateCall on unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn, while src/PoolManager.sol has it on initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate only (lines 117, 148, 190, 259). No unit has asked, for each of these four, on which of the 21 networks the missing guard meets a chain feature. The fee controller holds code on eight networks (4,544 bytes on chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 42161, 4663, 137 and 56, and 3,480 bytes on Arc), and Arc is also a network where an ERC-20 address measures the native balance that the exemption for address(0) leaves open.

Tempo. Critic check of lead L-255 on 2026-11-23, read only. I fetched 241 source files of tempoxyz/tempo at commit 697ea97 by following the mod declarations from the lib.rs of crates/evm, crates/precompiles, crates/payload/builder, crates/primitives, crates/node, crates/transaction-pool, crates/contracts, crates/zones/evm and crates/zones/precompiles, and 137 files of the evm2 crate at revision 66687c18b34d3bdbb899f5eb7605070615c03475, which Cargo.toml line 322 pins. State::committed_copy is defined at crates/evm2/src/evm/state/mod.rs:135 and its only caller is the unit test at lines 1036 to 1056 of that file. Evm::call_tx is defined at crates/evm2/src/evm/mod.rs:1316, and every call to it in the 378 files sits inside a test module, including crates/zones/evm/src/executor.rs:1173. In evm2, clear_transaction_state is called outside tests where a transaction, a system call or a validation ends or fails (evm/mod.rs:990, 1306 and 1333, system.rs:135, tx.rs:226 to 244), when the base database is replaced (state/mod.rs:271, called from evm/mod.rs:701) and when an inspector scope is dropped unfinished (evm/mod.rs:1211). In the Tempo crates the calls outside tests are in genesis setup (crates/evm/src/genesis.rs:76), and the one partial removal of transient storage takes the slots of the StorageCredits address only (crates/evm/src/handler/config.rs:452-454). I found no path that empties or replaces the transient map while a user call is running. I did not read the evm2-jit and evm2-inspectors crates, crates/consensus, crates/zones/node, files that a macro or a path attribute pulls in, or who calls the function at evm2 evm/mod.rs:701. The cycle 4 unit for Tempo did not answer L-255. The lead can be narrowed to those points.

Arc, Celo, Polygon and OP Mainnet, the networks where an ERC-20 address reports the native balance. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only. The clearance of assumption A3 needs that address to follow the native balance inside one call frame, and earlier cycles compared the two at block boundaries. I sent one eth_call with a probe contract placed by state override and a value of 5,000,000,000,007 wei to the four endpoints of state/networks.json. The probe reads balanceOf(self) at the face and SELFBALANCE on entry, after sending 3,000,000,000,000 wei to a second address by CALL, and after calling transfer(second address, 2) on the face. On Celo (0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438) the two numbers were equal at all three points and the transfer moved 2 wei. On Arc (0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000) the face read 5, 2 and 0 against native balances of 5000000000007, 2000000000007 and 7, so it is the native balance divided by 10^12 and rounded down at every point, and the transfer of 2 units moved 2 * 10^12 wei. On Polygon (0x1010) the readings were equal and transfer returned false without value. On OP Mainnet (LegacyERC20ETH) the readings were equal and transfer reverted. No face lags behind the native balance inside a call. The result describes the RPC node of each network. On Arc the seven wei that the face cannot see stay in the account, so a credit taken through the face can differ from the native amount by less than 10^12 wei per account.

OP Stack chains with ETH gas. The unit that holds these seven chains last ran in cycle 2, and Base and OP Mainnet carry the largest value after Ethereum. The sweep of 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff with the sixteen call shapes through a forwarding stub, which cycle 4 ran on Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM, has not been run here. No unit has listed which interop predeploys (CrossL2Inbox, L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger, SuperchainETHBridge, ETHLiquidity, SuperchainTokenBridge) hold code on each of the seven chains today. Lead L-213 about deposit filters on these clients is open.

Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche. The established L1 unit last ran in cycle 2. The cycle 3 critic asked for the hook selectors, unlockCallback and balanceOf under STATICCALL to be sent through a stub on these three chains, and cycle 4 did that for Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM only, so lead L-209 stays open here. Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain on 2026-12-08, fifteen days after this cycle. The cycle 3 critic noted that core/vm/cas20.go is public on the master branch, and no unit has read it for the call shapes P1 to P5. Leads L-029, L-124 and L-158 are still worded for after activation.

Base, BNB Smart Chain, X Layer and World Chain. The files currencies_8453, currencies_56, currencies_196 and currencies_480 in the work directory of the balance unit hold no Initialize log (nInit is 0). On Base, BNB Smart Chain and X Layer the list is the tokens that moved in a one day window, and on World Chain it is the explorer holdings page. A pooled token that sat still for a day was never tested on the two chains with the highest swap counts. The same limit applies to the take and repay census of the quota unit on these chains (253 tokens on Base, 39 on BNB Smart Chain).

All 21 networks, method of the balance unit. The comparison of a one day balance change with Transfer logs finds a token only when its balance moved in that day. The HyperEVM unit compared the whole history and found one token that emits no logs (SMK4), while the balance unit reports no mismatch on HyperEVM for the same list. A token whose balance any account can raise for the length of one transaction leaves no trace unless someone did it in the window. The 177 lending receipt rows were classed by a symbol pattern, and the verifier sampled eight of them. One of the 661 sLGNS transactions was traced. The search for claim mints on BNB Smart Chain covered 1,344,000 blocks, and a payout by take leaves no claim log.

Celo. The Celo half of leads L-218 and L-086 is unanswered for the third cycle: the PositionManager and the first Universal Router return the CELO token, which is the native balance itself, as their wrapped native address. Both units that touched L-218 in cycle 4 left that half out. The currency list of the balance unit shows 88 pools on the CELO token address and 18 on address(0), so most native liquidity on Celo sits under the face that the periphery treats as a wrapper. Leads L-238, L-245 and L-256 about which client produces Celo blocks are also still open.

Arc. The stablecoin unit read two million blocks of Initialize logs and reports 7,481 pools. The balance unit read the whole history through another endpoint and holds 286,916 Initialize logs, with 229,191 pools on 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 and 53,208 on address(0). The question whether any pool pairs the two faces was therefore answered for 3 percent of the pools. The file of the balance unit stores counts per currency and no pairs. The first Universal Router and the PositionManager on Arc have no verified source, and only their SETTLE action was simulated.

HyperEVM. The validator node is closed. The verifier found that the official replay client derives the sender of a system transaction from its target and has no case for the AQAv2 treasury address or the CoreDepositWallet (hyper-evm-sync src/run.rs lines 223 to 227), so for blocks after 37,597,803 the clearance of assumption A1 rests on the third party archive client, whose header check leaves out the receipts of system transactions. F-020 stays plausible on one unread rule.

MegaETH. F-042 was re-reported with a queue mechanism that rests on arrival order in the sequencer's pool, and the verdict is plausible. Leads L-170, L-176 and L-177 came back inconclusive. The payload builder is closed source, the dependency line of mega-reth v2.2.3 is unread, and the margin by which deposits stay below the block budget for new state is 48 entries by the verifier's count, with one case (a deposit that fails for lack of intrinsic gas) not confirmed.

Monad. 2,774 hook addresses appear in Initialize logs, 4,726 pools use 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc and 900 use 0x580ca49389d83b019d07e17e99454f2f218e2dc0, and neither was read. The unit filed this as a low lead. The transfer census moved the whole balance four times in one call, so it detects a quota below four balances and a cooldown inside one block, and the verifier notes that a caller can repeat take and settle hundreds of times per transaction. The wrapped stock token source was matched by 46 selectors and not by bytecode.

World Chain. The access list sweep of the verifier covered 30 of 851 tokens. The public endpoint refuses eth_simulateV1, so no bundle was replayed on the network where three quarters of sampled swap transactions are bundles. Mikami answers Sender is frozen for the PoolManager, which holds 15,912 tokens, and IDRX, WRC, CAKE and DogeX are paused or locked. None of these balances was valued. The token list comes from an explorer page.

All 21 networks. The cells for lenses L5 and L6 are at depth 2 or lower on every network in state/ledger.json, because revisits were assigned lenses L1 to L4 in cycles 3 and 4. Lead L-117 about the transaction filter of Robinhood Chain has been open since cycle 1. The rules by which an address or a transaction enters the filter of Robinhood Chain, the restriction list of Soneium, the TxBlacklist and risk control filter of X Layer and the denylist of Arc were not read by any unit. F-001 and F-046 record that two of these filters also apply to forced transactions.

Tempo. Three statements about GABAGOOL in this cycle do not agree. The stablecoin unit says the token carries policy 0, which rejects every sender and recipient, and files it under the issuer finding F-031. The quota unit says the token refuses the test recipient because of its TIP-403 list. The verifier says the token was created through a factory without a role check, both of its pools use the hook 0x55aeb9ebfa15c28ff9d9a675e8574a5bbe186aa8, and the class is pool-creator. The statement that 72 of 73 currencies pass a full take rests on one run that the verifier did not repeat.

Zora, World Chain, Soneium, Celo and Arc. No public endpoint served debug_traceCall, so the quota unit has no state diff for the pooled tokens of these five networks. Its test rules out a cap below 25 balances. The verifier's access list method shows which contracts a transfer touches and cannot tell a read from a write. Seven Celo tokens read two slots of 0x796dff6d74f3e27060b71255fe517bfb23c93eed on every transfer, and that contract is not identified.

Elysium. The PoolManager has 131,786 pools over 129,516 currencies. The hook 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec serves four fifths of sampled pools and lead L-258 about it was not assigned in cycle 4. The bridge gateway that holds the escrowed tokens was not read (the HyperEVM unit takes its behaviour from the standard design). The announced ArbOS upgrade is still unscheduled and leads L-001 and L-134 stay open.

X Layer. F-024 has been plausible for four cycles on one fact, whether the builder filter is switched on for the mainnet sequencer, and lead L-263 names a way to settle it that no unit took. The registrar of USDG enrolled the PoolManager address in payout group 2 on 2026-11-19, four days before this cycle, so an issuer side role is acting on the PoolManager account now. No Initialize history was read on this chain.

Unichain. The behaviour test of lead L-217 was not run for the third cycle. Every Unichain result of cycle 4 (5,149 tokens reconciled, 34 tokens traced, router code matched) describes the predeploy of 24,050 bytes.

gaps.note: All 21 networks. No unit has read the custody path of src/ against network features since cycle 3. Cycle 5 again ran four themes in the code slots, and the high leads L-313, L-314 and L-260 and the leads L-204, L-232 and L-016 were assigned to nobody for the second cycle in a row. The one source reading of this cycle is the claim transfer and burn checks (src/ERC6909.sol:35-48, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) by theme-claim-operators. Its verifier repeated the reading and added that no selector the PoolManager sends to a caller chosen address equals a claim selector. Every other test of cycles 4 and 5 ran against the PoolManagers that are deployed today, while the review is about a build of this checkout, which no unit could compile. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only: I placed a stub at the fee controller address by state override on Ethereum, Polygon and Arc (eth_call on the endpoints of state/networks.json). The stub calls unlock and, inside unlockCallback, calls collectProtocolFees(stub, 0x00000000000000000000000000000000deadbeef, 0). The call returned success with 32 bytes of return data on all three, and the same call sent directly from the controller address while the manager is locked also returned zero without reverting. The deployed PoolManagers therefore collect fees inside an unlock, as src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 reads. The cycle 1 cleared items for chain ids 1, 137, 56 and 5042 already walked that case for a gain and found none, so the first of the four places that L-313 lists is answered. The other three (sync without a lock, take on an address without code, and unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn without noDelegateCall) were not walked against network features by any unit, and I did not test them.

Monad, World Chain, Celo and Avalanche. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only: one eth_simulateV1 request with two calls in one simulated block to a contract placed by state override. The first call runs TSTORE(0, 1) and the second returns TLOAD(0). The second call returned zero on 17 networks: on the endpoints of state/networks.json for chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 130, 7777777, 57073, 1868, 42161, 4663, 99901, 137, 56 and 4217, on arc.drpc.org for Arc, on rpc.purroofgroup.com and hyperliquid.drpc.org for HyperEVM, on xlayer.drpc.org for X Layer and on megaeth.drpc.org for MegaETH. The endpoints I tried for Monad (rpc.monad.xyz, rpc2.monad.xyz, monad.drpc.org), World Chain, Celo (forno.celo.org, celo.drpc.org) and Avalanche refused the method or failed. For these four networks assumption A1 rests on source readings alone. The test exercises the simulation path of an RPC node. It says nothing about block production on HyperEVM and MegaETH, where the producing node or the payload builder is closed, and the HyperEVM endpoints run third party clients. Cycle 5 added two source readings for this lens. For World Chain the unit read the flashblock validation path at tag v2.8.2: every transaction runs in its own EVM instance over its own State object. For OP Mainnet the unit and its verifier read op-reth v2.4.2, where the transaction handler calls commit_tx and discard_tx, and they read the journal of revm on the main branch because the tag that matches the pinned version 41.0.0 was not found. Both are readings of released builds. The build of the OP Mainnet sequencer is still unknown.

Base, BNB Smart Chain, World Chain and X Layer. Two units of this cycle say that the Initialize history of these PoolManagers cannot be read from public endpoints (established-l1 for BNB Smart Chain, op-stack-eth for Base and World Chain), while theme-shared-hooks read it in the same cycle: 341,033 Initialize logs on BNB Smart Chain from block 45,970,610 through a NodeReal endpoint, 15,572,154 pools on Base through base.gateway.tenderly.co (one window in four between blocks 37,000,001 and 49,000,000), 4,758 pools on World Chain through a QuickNode endpoint and 2,833 pools on X Layer for the last 1.4 million blocks. The token tests of this cycle ran on much smaller lists: theme-assigned-balance tested 9,108 currencies on Base, 3,369 on BNB Smart Chain, 851 on World Chain and 96 on X Layer, the trigger probe of op-stack-eth used the same Base list (tokens that moved in one day), and the shared balance test of established-l1 covered 1,364 currencies from 31 hours of pool creation on BNB Smart Chain. A pooled token on these four networks that did not move in the sampled day has never been tested for a lock, a clawback, an idle sweep or a second address. Leads L-317 and L-291 came back inconclusive for this reason. The claim census of theme-claim-operators met the same limit on BNB Smart Chain: the gateway it used gave differing answers for 1,274 of 17,870 log windows.

Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arc hold 1.13 million of the 1.24 million pooled currencies. theme-assigned-balance covered them through families and samples: on Robinhood Chain one token per code hash for hashes shared by more than three tokens and three tokens per code size for the rest, and the unit's own lead says the full balance transfer test did not finish on the three networks. The test for a balance that rises on a transfer was not run on them. Function names came from a signature database that knew 85,092 of 137,912 selectors, so 52,820 selectors were never tried. Tokens that run as precompiles (TIP-20, B20) were covered by one transfer test and by documentation. The cleared item that lists tokens refusing a full transfer from the PoolManager records counts per network (Optimism 110, Arbitrum One 178, Polygon 104, Monad 62, World Chain 43, Ink 39, Unichain 37, Base 27, BNB Smart Chain 21, Avalanche 20, Robinhood Chain 2,439, Arc 115). The verifier confirmed the cause for the five Ethereum tokens priced above 100,000 USD and nobody valued or classed the others, so that item is a list of open cases and should not be filed as cleared.

Ethereum, Arbitrum One and Base, tokens above 10,000 USD. theme-assigned-balance cleared the pooled tokens whose function list has lock, freeze, vest, cooldown or escrow words (FOLD, WLFI, sUSDe, sENA, apyUSD, aptUSD, syrupUSDC, syrupUSDT, yUSD, ondo, skl, DPR, AST, RNDR and TITANX on Ethereum, SPA on Arbitrum One, launch pad tokens on Base) by calling their functions from an ordinary account, without reading a source. The verifier read two of them. WLFI keeps vesting in a separate contract and is safe. FOLD counts locked units in balanceOf, and a lock is created by any transfer from its claim source, an auction that pays the bid owner whom the bidder names. The trials could not see that path because it runs through a second contract. It is closed today only because the auction ended at block 25,502,753 and no bid names the PoolManager, which holds about 23.8 million FOLD. The other tokens of the list rest on trials alone. The same limit applies to the 389,956 trials on all 21 networks: they see a lock, a grant or a clawback only when the token contract itself offers the function.

Hook census. theme-shared-hooks ranked hooks by pools per address and probed 111 hooks on 21 networks. On Arc 206,554 pools name a hook and 194,252 distinct hook addresses appear, and the most used address serves 2,003 pools, so more than nine tenths of the hooked pools on Arc sit behind addresses that were not read and that probably share a few code templates. The census did not group by code hash on any network. It did not rank hooks by what they hold, and the one finding (Klik) came from a hook family with small claim balances. On Base one window in four was read for 12 million blocks and three sample pools per hook were kept. On X Layer 1.4 million blocks were read. The probes called callbacks outside an unlock, so every path ends at ManagerLocked on the first take, mint or burn and later steps were not observed. Several top hooks have no verified source (for example 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec with 104,615 pools on Elysium and 0xf0e1b03731fa1c94b30e90a9a61368e2f5968088 on Optimism) and were judged from revert selectors. The unit names further parts that it did not read: pools that an ordinary account creates through the Doppler Airlock with a quote currency of its choice, the engine, oracle manager, fee manager and limit order manager that AegisHook on Ink calls with a foreign PoolKey, the account behind the OnlyStrategy check of Arc hook 0x4ab0bf61327761fffc5910052d9e0b9a94f960cc (35.4 units of native claims), and the older Clanker hook versions. The verifier confirmed the Klik finding and three cleared hooks (FeeHookV3, the Clanker V2 hook, the Doppler initializer) from verified source.

Ethereum, Celo, X Layer, Monad and MegaETH. The sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address (empty calldata with and without value, transfer with 0 and 1, balanceOf, the ten hook selectors, unlockCallback) has now run on Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM (cycle 4), on Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche and the seven OP Stack chains with ETH gas (cycle 5), and in an earlier form on the three Nitro chains (cycle 3). These five networks have only the four shape test of lead L-166. Lead L-209 stays open for them.

OP Mainnet and Unichain. The Lagoon clearances rest on source from the develop branch and from op-contracts v4.0.0. Slots 0x22 to 0x28 and 0x30 hold no implementation on any chain today, the activation timestamps are not set, and the notice gives 10 December 2026 for the two Sepolia chains and 11 January 2027 for mainnet pending a vote. The OP Mainnet sequencer still reports a build without a version, so the client reading for that chain is of two releases that follow it. The unit states that after Lagoon any account can make 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000023 the msg.sender of a call to the PoolManager. No unit asked which ERC-6909 balances, operator rights or positions exist under addresses that execute calls for any caller, on any network. The verifier repeated the predeploy sweep with its own stub on all seven chains and agrees with the present state.

Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche. Three statements of established-l1 leave the upgrade lens thin. Polygon distributed Uburu, the security release v2.11.1 and Purley as private builds and published the source at or after activation, and Uburu replaced the code at 0x1001, so the next change to 0x1010 cannot be read in advance and the probe of F-008 must be repeated after every Bor release. On BNB Smart Chain Jenner activates on 2026-12-08: the CAS20 behaviour was observed on the Chapel testnet (12 tokens by the unit, 18 by the verifier), mainnet token creation stays closed until an administrator appointed through GovHub acts, and the v1.7 source with the fused opcodes was not read. The verifier read core/paymentlanemeta, which the unit had left out, and found one STATICCALL from the zero address to 0x2007 on a snapshot that is reverted afterwards. On Avalanche the Igloo rule set for the C-Chain is unpublished. Cells for lenses L5 and L6 are still at depth 2 from cycle 1 on all 21 networks.

Eleven networks in six families. The two angles of this cycle (upcoming forks, and one balance under two currency ids) ran for established-l1 and op-stack-eth only. Ethereum was last visited in cycle 2 although six findings of this cycle name chain id 1, and no unit has asked which Ethereum fork is scheduled. The equal balance grouping that found the two EURe addresses is complete on Polygon and Avalanche, partial on BNB Smart Chain, and was not run on the other networks. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only: ArbOwnerPublic.getScheduledUpgrade() (selector 0x81ef944c at 0x6b) returns two zero words on Elysium, Robinhood Chain and Arbitrum One, and ArbSys.arbOSVersion() returns 0x74 on all three. No ArbOS upgrade is scheduled on Elysium today, so leads L-001 and L-134 still cannot be answered.

theme-unbacked-claims, reach of the search. The verifier disagreed with two cleared items. The research file states twice that no row shows a rebase surplus paid out by take on BNB Smart Chain. Two of the 393 flagged rows there, filed as spoof logs on the strength of the call pattern of the other tokens, are payouts of 2.538 sSAC each (transactions 0xf1c329b6e3e3fa7747c3907e7d449c536977f0e44b79c10db31ff4153b9f098d and 0x27598a81864c463522634ec554d1e69a255353a9d4d6cf7438471a44ebd6ca1e, epochs 365 and 366): sync, rebase, settle and take by an ordinary account. The rows explained by a label were not re-read one by one (393 on BNB Smart Chain, 50 on Polygon, 126 on Arc, 17 on OP Mainnet). Most claim mint rows were counted as explained because the transaction holds a Swap, ModifyLiquidity or Donate log (45,277 of 48,939 sampled rows on Ethereum, 10,401 of 10,782 on Unichain, all 440 on HyperEVM), and of 17 such rows the verifier tested on Unichain 4 cannot be confirmed from logs. The search for balance falls sees transfers to burn addresses only. A token that lets a third party move the PoolManager balance to an ordinary address is visible only in census windows of 0.5 days on Base, 2 days on World Chain, 3 days on Ethereum and up to 30 days elsewhere. The burn search covers recent windows on Base, World Chain and Robinhood Chain and 400,000 blocks on X Layer. Base and Robinhood Chain hold 39.6 of the 53.3 million claim mints and were sampled with a lighter rule. Part (c) of lead L-318, native takes to a recipient other than the caller, was not done. The eleven empty placeholders in the second finding are filled by the verdict: Ethereum 54,048 rows over 1,277 tokens, 78 flagged, 53 with a balance fall and 25 spoof, and BNB Smart Chain 29,326 rows over 1,801 tokens, 97 flagged, 91 with a balance fall.

Tempo and Elysium. protocolFeeController is the zero address on both (state/networks.json). The question whether any transaction type, system call or precompile can call a contract with msg.sender equal to address(0) has a cleared item for Avalanche, Celo, X Layer, the five OP Stack chains without a controller, Monad, MegaETH and HyperEVM. I found no such item for Tempo or Elysium in state/cleared.json. The checks at src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48 compare msg.sender with that stored value and nothing else.

Carried over without work. The Celo half of lead L-218 (the PositionManager and the first Universal Router return the CELO token, which is the native balance, as their wrapped native address) is unanswered for the fifth cycle. F-024 on X Layer stays plausible on one fact and lead L-263, which names the observation that would settle it, was not taken. The behaviour test of the Unichain predeploy (lead L-217) was not run. Lead L-315 about the rule by which the Robinhood Chain filter gains entries has been open at high priority since cycle 4 and its parent L-117 since cycle 1, and no unit has read the filter contract or its logs.

Tempo. No cleared item recorded whether a contract that the PoolManager calls (an unlock callback, a hook, a recipient of a native payout) can reach a TIP-20 token by DELEGATECALL with the PoolManager as the inherited caller. That test exists for B20 on Base (cycle 2, revert 0x0d89438e), for the Celo transfer precompile and for the Native Coin Authority on Arc, and for CAS20 from source only. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only, on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz (client tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97, block 50,425,160). A 45 byte stub placed by state override forwards its calldata to the token, and the eth_call is sent with from set to the PoolManager, so the stub frame has the PoolManager as caller. Through DELEGATECALL, balanceOf(PoolManager) and transfer(address,uint256) with amount 1 revert with 0x0d89438e on pathUSD 0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000000 and on OUSD 0x20c0000000000000000000006a37da5c996874be. Through CALL the same stub returns the PoolManager balance (18,595,278,947 and 409,943,492,388 base units) and the transfer fails with InsufficientBalance for the stub address, which shows that the stub works. This can be recorded as cleared for the two tokens. I did not test CALLCODE, the other Tempo precompiles that keep ledgers (StablecoinDEX, FeeManager, TIP20ChannelReserve) or any address on Arc, and the test must be repeated when a release adds a precompile with a ledger.

HyperEVM, Elysium and Arc, periphery. A position made through the PositionManager belongs to that one contract inside the PoolManager (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so its caller checks decide who can remove most of the liquidity that users hold. No unit was assigned the periphery in five cycles. The PositionManager has 19,965 bytes on HyperEVM and Elysium against 23,877 bytes on the other 19 networks (raw/posm_actions.json of theme-claim-operators), nobody established what the shorter build leaves out, and the cycle 4 critic recorded that the PositionManager on Arc has no verified source. Critic check on 2026-11-23, read only: modifyLiquidities with DECREASE_LIQUIDITY for the full liquidity followed by TAKE_PAIR, sent once from the token owner and once from an unrelated address, and the ERC-721 transferFrom sent from the unrelated address. I used HyperEVM token 123 at block 52,030,929, Elysium token 150073 at block 9,898,289, Arc token 334139 at block 32,730,757 and, as a control, Ethereum token 528992 at block 26,477,682. On all four the owner call returns, the unrelated call reverts with 0x0ca968d8 followed by the caller, which is the selector of NotApproved(address), and transferFrom reverts with NOT_AUTHORIZED. BURN_POSITION from the unrelated address reverts the same way on HyperEVM, Arc and Ethereum. Not tested on any network: modifyLiquiditiesWithoutUnlock from an account that holds the PoolManager lock itself, the signature paths (permit, permitForAll, Permit2), the subscriber callbacks, and the Universal Routers.

theme-claim-operators, what its clearance rests on. The unit cleared 765 approved operator and spender addresses. The verifier found that 0x2834c56d948f063564ff0a3c29483db50c73045a on Robinhood Chain, which holds 120 unlimited allowances, does call burn: it hashes the signature string at run time, so the search for the constants 0xf5298aca and 0xfe99049a missed it. The verifier read the code and clears the contract, because every request is bound to its caller. The same constant search was the stated reason for other exclusions. Not read: the unverified routers 0xbc22993a15e16acbf12873f234510d35948f7a59, 0x4531332adecf255c66b5bf6485db73f894ed93d2 and 0xad445acd8e2446c652fb47b2d4c5ee9973b150c9 and the implementation 0xa62f9b597225779b430024398b70374e8468ce14 on Ethereum, the 47,585 byte hooks with collectPlatform(bytes32[]) and the implementation 0x6b68d5061329f64a087fc894355cb1eacf2a2321 on Robinhood Chain, the 677 byte proxies on Base and Robinhood Chain, and most of the 24,384 byte delegate 0xb0c75276657e80ff04c98a3809dfc39a409a8736 behind 47 delegated operators of one Ethereum account. The reach test used six argument fillings, so a function that needs a well formed struct or a signature shows up as not reaching, and 33 traces failed. On Robinhood Chain 2,100 of 2,170 owner and id pairs have no price. The priced exposure on all networks is about 44,000 USD.

Zora, Ink and Soneium. The profiles of op-stack-eth for lenses L1 and L2 say that nothing is new, and the lens L3 and L4 profiles repeat the predeploy sweep and the trigger probe over 41, 3,438 and 70 tokens.
